title: Bullying Victimization and Youth Psychotic-Like Experiences: Evidence From a Longitudinal Discordant Twin and Sibling Design
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Childhood bullying victimization is a common and potentially modifiable stressor associated with psychotic-like experiences (PLEs), which confers risk for later psychiatric disorders. The present work examines reciprocal associations between bullying victimization and PLEs in youth, testing whether bullying victimization contributes to distressing PLEs independent of shared familial liability using longitudinal and genetically informed within-family analyses.

METHOD: Participants were 11,868 youth (baseline age 9-10 years) from 6 waves of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study across 21 U.S. sites. Any bullying victimization was assessed using both caregiver- and youth-report across multiple waves. Significantly distressing PLEs were defined as endorsement of ≥1 psychotic-like experience with high associated distress on the Prodromal Questionnaire-Brief Child Version. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models tested bidirectional longitudinal associations. Genetically-informed analyses compared bullying-discordant twin and sibling pairs to distinguish individual-specific environmental effects from shared familial influences.

RESULTS: Bullying victimization was associated with increased odds of distressing PLEs (OR=3.62, 95% CI=3.31-3.96). Longitudinal models demonstrated reciprocal associations, with bullying victimization predicting subsequent PLEs and PLEs predicting later bullying victimization exposure. Critically, within-family analyses indicated evidence for both shared genetic (OR=6.87, 95% CI=5.37,8.78) and individual-specific contributions (OR=2.55, 95% CI=1.99,3.28) to the association between bullying victimization and significantly distressing PLEs.

CONCLUSION: Bullying victimization is associated with elevated risk for distressing psychotic-like experiences through both individual-specific environmental processes and shared familial liability. These findings provide evidence highlighting bullying prevention and early identification of affected youth as potential targets for reducing risk for later psychiatric disorders.

title: Not all food avoidance is the same: a latent profile analysis informed by the Appetite Self-Regulation model
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Food avoidance is a common problem for some children and negatively affects their dietary quality. The Appetite Self-Regulation (ASR) model proposes that food avoidance phenotypes arise in children due to interactions between bottom-up and top-down processes. However, it is unknown how these factors combine within children to produce distinct food avoidant profiles. This study aimed to better understand different types of food avoidance by identifying food avoidant profiles in middle childhood and examining their neurodevelopmental correlates.

METHODS: Participants were 517 parents of children aged 5-12 years. Latent profile analysis was conducted using multiple ASR domains, including appetitive traits (satiety responsiveness, slowness in eating, food responsiveness, enjoyment of food and food fussiness), temperament traits (fear, shyness, inhibitory control, impulsivity), food avoidance behaviours (food avoidance, texture sensitivity and cognitive rigidity) and liking of low- and high-energy-density foods (vegetable and snack liking). Multinomial logistic regression examined associations between profile membership and neurodevelopmental disorders.

RESULTS: Five profiles were identified, including two food avoidant profiles. Multi-Domain Food Avoidant profile (n = 114, 22%) was characterised by a multi-domain form of avoidance, particularly showing higher levels of fear and shyness, suggesting greater bottom-up emotional reactivity to foods. The Rigid Texture-Sensitive Avoidant profile (n = 66, 13%) showed the highest texture sensitivity and cognitive rigidity, indicating a sensory-driven pathway to food avoidance. The Rigid Texture-Sensitive Avoidant profile was also characterised by the lowest inhibitory control, reflecting reduced top-down regulatory capacity. Children with neurodevelopmental disorders were disproportionately represented in the food avoidant profiles.

CONCLUSIONS: Food avoidance in middle childhood reflects heterogeneous behavioural patterns shaped by different combinations of bottom-up avoidance processes and top-down regulatory control. Identifying distinct avoidant profiles may improve understanding of the processes underlying children's food avoidance and inform more targeted approaches to supporting children with persistent avoidant eating behaviours.

title: Child chaos: parent-reported sibling differences in chaos at home in association with externalising and internalising behaviours
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Household chaos has long been associated with children's adjustment, relating to both externalising and-though somewhat less so-internalising behaviours. Original conceptualisations view chaos as an aspect of the home environment that may be shared by family members and/or differentially influence or be influenced by them. There is increasing recognition that home experiences can differ for siblings in ways important for their outcomes. To capture this for chaos, examining differential sibling perspectives has gained attention, but the extent to which parents perceive sibling differences in chaos and their relation to adjustment remains unstudied. In a preliminary study, for the first time, we distinguished family-wide and child-specific parent-reported chaos in association with sibling externalising and internalising behaviours.

METHODS: In a UK sample of 261 families with young sibling pairs (3-11 years; 522 children), we adapted the response format of the widely used measure, CHAOS, to assess parent reports of child chaos, that is, chaos 'for and around' each child in the home. Multilevel modelling examined family-wide (family average) and child-specific (child differentiation from the family average) chaos reported by mothers in the prediction of between- and within-family variances in externalising and internalising behaviours.

RESULTS: As hypothesised, accounting for key demographic and parenting confounders, family-wide chaos was associated with both externalising and internalising behaviours, whereas child-specific chaos was associated only with externalising behaviours.

CONCLUSIONS: Exploring parent perceptions of child chaos may offer key insights into associations between household chaos and young children's adjustment.

title: Maternal thyroid function in the first half of pregnancy and child internalising and externalising problems over time
abstract: Adequate gestational thyroid function is important for offspring neurodevelopment, yet behavioural implications of variation within the normal range are unclear. We examined associations with externalising and internalising problems across repeated assessments in childhood and adolescence. 2,606 mother-child dyads from the Amsterdam Born Children and their Development (ABCD) cohort with maternal free thyroxine (FT4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) measurements in the first half of pregnancy and at least one child SDQ assessment. Primary analysis excluded women with overt thyroid disease or thyroid medication use and children born < 32 weeks or < 1500 g. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) scores at 5-6, 11-12 and 15-16 years, via mother-, teacher-, and self-report. Secondary analyses included logistic regression for borderline SDQ cut-offs, sex interactions, and effect modification by TSH. FT4 showed a U-shaped association with teacher-reported externalising problems (quadratic β = 9.49, FDR-adjusted p = 0.03), with higher scores at both low and high FT4. Higher FT4 was associated with lower child-reported internalising problems (β = -0.17, FDR-adjusted p = 0.04). For both primary associations, there was no evidence of FT4-by-age interaction, suggesting differences in problem levels rather than thyroid-related differences in symptom change over time. At age 5-6, FT4 showed a non-linear association with teacher-reported hyperactivity/inattention above the threshold, with a negative linear term (OR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.72 to 0.97) and a positive quadratic term (OR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.02 to 1.20). At age 11-12, higher FT4 was associated with fewer self-reported peer problems (OR = 0.84, 95% CI:0.71-0.99). In exploratory analyses, curvature of the FT4-externalising association varied by maternal TSH; no sex modification was detected. Within a cohort free of overt thyroid disease, maternal thyroid function in the first half of pregnancy was associated with domain- and rater-specific differences in child internalising and externalising problems. We found no evidence that these associations changed across the available repeated assessments, suggesting differences in average problem scores rather than differences in how symptoms changed with age.

title: Pornography use in adolescence: a gender perspective on co-occurring behavioural, psychosocial, and health outcomes
abstract: This study examined associations between pornography use and gender identity, sexual attraction, sexual behaviours, substance use, adverse social experiences, and health and wellbeing among secondary school students from a gender perspective. This cross-sectional study used data from the 2025 FRESC Health Survey on Adolescence in Barcelona, Spain (3,690 students aged 13-19 years). Occasional or regular pornography use was contrasted with no use or one-time use. Sex-stratified survey-weighted complex-samples logistic regression models accounted for sampling strata and classroom clustering and were adjusted for age, family socioeconomic status, and family structure. Pornography use was more frequent among boys than girls (55.6% vs. 13.8%). Associations with ever having had sexual intercourse, daily smoking, recent drunkenness, lifetime cannabis use, peer aggression, and hyperactivity/inattention were observed in both sexes. Among girls, associations were additionally observed with transgender/nonbinary gender identity, non-exclusively heterosexual attraction, poor family relationships, peer victimization, sexual harassment, poor self-reported health, and life dissatisfaction; body dissatisfaction was significant only before correction for multiple testing. Among boys, conduct problems were also associated with pornography use. Following Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 21 outcomes per sex, seven of eight initially significant associations in boys and 13 of 14 in girls remained significant. Overall, these findings suggest that pornography use should not be understood as an isolated behaviour but rather in relation to a broader range of behavioural, psychosocial, and health characteristics during adolescence, although the cross-sectional design does not permit causal or temporal conclusions.

title: Prenatal alcohol exposure and adolescent sleep in clinical pathways: a commentary on Devine et al
abstract: Devine et al. provide timely evidence that parent-reported adolescent sleep disturbances are associated with prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development cohort, even when most exposure was low to moderate. This commentary argues that the central contribution of the study is not only the replication of a sleep signal after PAE, but the identification of a clinically recognisable phenotype: sleep-wake transition problems, excessive somnolence, and possible sleep breathing symptoms. We highlight three implications: sleep should be treated as a developmental mediator and modifiable target, future studies should triangulate retrospective PAE and parent-reported sleep with objective measures, and prevention messages about alcohol in pregnancy should be paired with non-stigmatising family support. Building clinical pathways from screening to intervention may transform small epidemiologic effects into meaningful benefits for affected adolescents.

title: Childhood competence, adverse childhood experiences, and sociocultural context: Understanding resilience processes from childhood to young adulthood
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Childhood competencies in mental health, social, and academic domains could support (or promote) low levels of stress later in life. These competencies could also protect those highly exposed to ACEs from experiencing elevated perceived stress (PS).

METHODS: Participants (N = 2,004, ages 5-17 at Waves 1-3; ages 15-29 at Wave 4) were from the Boricua Youth Study, a sample of Puerto Rican children recruited from the South Bronx, New York, and the metropolitan area in San Juan and Caguas, Puerto Rico. The current study examined longitudinal patterns of childhood competence (stable, unstable, not reaching) across three domains (mental health, social adjustment, and academic achievement) in relation to PS in young adulthood. We also investigated the role of childhood competencies as a protective factor, buffering the association between ACEs and PS. We explored whether associations varied across two sociocultural contexts with varying levels of ACEs (South Bronx vs. Puerto Rico).

RESULTS: Childhood mental health competence, in relation to never reaching competence, was the only type of competence that promoted (b = -1.72, p < .001) lower PS in young adulthood. Childhood mental health competence also modified the association between ACEs and PS among those recruited in the South Bronx (F (2, 776) = 4.45, p = .01), such that among those with stable childhood mental health competence, higher ACEs were associated with more PS (b = 0.56, SE = 0.22, p = .01) while the same was not observed in the other two trajectories (Unstable: b = 0.44, SE = 0.23, p = .053; Not reaching competence: b = -0.59, SE = 0.33, p = .08).

CONCLUSIONS: Experiencing competence in mental health during childhood may alleviate PS in young adulthood. For those growing up in a sociocultural context where adversities are frequent experiences and who have stable levels of mental health competence, ACEs were related to high PS in young adulthood.

title: Treatment patterns among US children and adolescents with recorded depressive disorders
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To characterize depression-linked treatment, annual trends, and factors associated with receipt of both psychotherapy and antidepressants among youths in the United States.

METHODS: This repeated cross-sectional study used 2016-2023 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey data. The population included children and adolescents aged 6-17 years with depressive disorders. We linked condition records to psychotherapy visits and antidepressant fills, estimated survey-weighted treatment percentages, and used survey-weighted logistic regression to examine factors associated with receipt of both treatments during the same survey year.

RESULTS: The analysis included 865 person-year observations, with adolescents comprising 90.3% of the weighted sample. Any treatment was recorded for 82.7% (95% confidence interval [CI], 79.6-85.7%), psychotherapy for 62.7%, and antidepressant treatment for 50.1%. Psychotherapy alone accounted for 32.5%, both treatments for 30.2%, and antidepressants alone for 20.0%. Neither treatment was recorded for 17.3%. The percentage receiving any treatment increased from 58.9% in 2016 to 89.8% in 2023 (P for trend < 0.001). Compared with non-Hispanic White youths, Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black youths had lower adjusted odds of receiving both modalities (0.44 [95% CI, 0.26-0.76] and 0.35 [95% CI, 0.13-0.89], respectively). Comorbid anxiety disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder were associated with higher adjusted odds (1.54 [95% CI, 1.04-2.29] and 1.60 [95% CI, 1.07-2.41], respectively).

CONCLUSIONS: More than one in six participants had neither depression-linked treatment recorded, and receipt of both treatments differed by race and ethnicity. Small subgroup sizes limited precision, particularly for younger children. The linked records measured treatment receipt without establishing clinical indication or adequacy.

title: Neurocognitive profiles structure heterogeneous treatment response to bumetanide in neurodevelopmental disorders: secondary analysis of a multiple baseline single-case experimental design
abstract: We performed a secondary analysis of the Bumetanide for Developmental Disorders (BUDDI;EUDRA-CT-2020-002196-35) trial to examine whether baseline neurocognitive profiles are associated with differential behavioral and cognitive treatment response. Participants (7-19 years) with atypical sensory reactivity and ASD, ADHD, epilepsy, or TSC diagnoses received 6-months of bumetanide treatment (max 3.0 mg/day) within a multiple-baseline SCED. Neurocognitive functioning was assessed across multiple domains and used to derive subgroups via cluster analysis. Behavioral outcomes were captured using a parent-reported PROMset and standardized questionnaires. Linear mixed models and subgroup comparisons were used to evaluate change over time. Of 119 participants enrolled, 105 completed baseline and 85 follow-up assessments At the group level, memory improved after six months (B = 0.65, 95%CI = 0.45to0.85, pFDR < .001, d = 1.07), while processing speed decreased (B = - 0.25, 95%CI = - 0.42to - 0.07, pFDR < .001, d = - 0.49). Cluster analysis identified four neurocognitive subgroups with distinct baseline profiles and differential treatment responses: individuals with weaker functioning showed the largest memory improvements, whereas those with preserved functioning showed greater behavioral improvement alongside declines in processing speed and visuomotor integration. Across subgroups, neurocognitive and behavioral changes did not align, and correlations were small (r < 0.30). In this study, neurocognitive profiling based on a standardized test battery was associated with distinct patterns of change during treatment. The dissociation between neurocognitive and behavioral outcomes indicated domain-specific and non-linear treatment effects. These findings provide a basis for linking variability in real-world change to individual neurocognitive characteristics within a defined clinical context.Trial registration: EudraCT (2020-002196-35) registration date 24-04-2020. Protocol: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-022-04033-8.

title: Analysis of the placebo response model and its influencing factors in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a model-based meta-analysis
abstract:
PURPOSE: A robust placebo response continuously challenges the evaluation of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) therapies. This study utilized model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) to quantify the longitudinal trajectory of the placebo response, identify trial- and patient- level predictors, and compare response magnitudes between pediatric and adult populations to optimize future trial designs.

METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science identified placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs) for ADHD. Longitudinal changes in placebo groups were mathematically modeled based on the ADHD Rating Scale (ADHD-RS) and Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S). Covariate modeling and subgroup analyses were applied to evaluate the impact of demographic and trial design factors.

RESULTS: Data from 79 RCTs were analyzed. Placebo responses exhibited non-linear dynamics, plateauing at approximately 6 weeks for the ADHD-RS and 10 weeks for the CGI-S. Larger trial sample sizes significantly predicted increased ADHD-RS placebo scores. Placebo magnitudes were also more pronounced in recent, multicenter, three more trial arms, industry-sponsored trials, trials using a stimulant as the active comparator, as well as in cohorts with fewer male or White participants and more severe baseline disease. Crucially, The time-course trajectories and amplitudes of the placebo response were similar in pediatric and adult populations.

CONCLUSION: This study provides a quantitative description of the placebo response trajectory in ADHD trials, together with the trial-level factors that modify it. The concordance between pediatric and adult placebo trajectories is supportive. These findings offer parameters for baseline-adjusted sample size estimation and endpoint selection in future trials. PROSPERO registration CRD420251171116.

title: Changing characteristics, treatment patterns, and risk among children and young people with a first recorded common mental disorder symptom or diagnosis in primary care in England (2001-23): a retrospective, population-based cohort study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Presentations to primary care by children and young people (CYP) for common mental disorders (anxiety and depression) have risen steeply in the past two decades. In this study, we aimed to describe changes in the case mix of CYP with an incident record of a common mental disorder, treatment patterns after the incident record, and whether these trends were accompanied by secular changes in the demographics of those presenting, their treatment patterns, and whether the clinical risk profile of those presenting changed between 2001 and 2023 in England.

METHODS: In this retrospective, population-based cohort study, we used anonymised primary care health records data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum (2001-23). We identified children and adolescents (aged 10-18 years) registered with English general practices with linked hospital admission and mortality records. We estimated trends in incidence of common mental disorders (using both symptom and diagnosis codes) in primary care and, among CYP with an incident record of a common mental disorder, changes in demographic and comorbidity profiles, referrals to Child And Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS), and antidepressant prescribing. We compared CYP with incident common mental disorders to matched controls on hospital admission for self-harm, alcohol misuse, and drug misuse, and tested for change in these associations using common mental disorder-by-calendar-year interactions. People with lived experience were not involved in the design or conduct of this study.

FINDINGS: Between Jan 1, 2001, and Dec 31, 2023, 6 220 923 CYP were registered with CPRD-Aurum practices. 379 802 CYP had a first recorded common mental disorder symptom or diagnosis. 250 315 (65·9%) of 379 802 CYP were girls and 129 353 (34·1%) were boys, with a mean age of 15·2 years (range 10-18; SD 2·1), 304 544 (80·2%) were White, and 35 082 (19·2%) were from minoritised ethnic groups. From 2001, the incidence of common mental disorders increased by four times from 57 per 10 000 person-years to 240 in 2019, followed by a decrease to 163 in 2023. The age of CYP with an incident record of a common mental disorder became younger (mean age 15·5 years [SD 2·1] to 15·0 [SD 2·1]), the proportion of White CYP became increasingly overrepresented relative to the general population, and the prevalence of psychiatric or neurodevelopmental comorbidities almost tripled (5·1% in 2001, 13·8% in 2023). After an incident common mental disorder, CAMHS referrals increased from 6·8 to 17·8 per 100 person-years (rate ratio [RR] 2·64 [95% CI 2·48 to 2·79]); antidepressant prescribing halved (38·8 to 17·9 per 100 person-years; RR 0·46 [0·45-0·48]), while prescriptions per treated CYP increased from 4·1 to 6·2 (RR 1·50, 1·48- 1·52). Between 2001 and 2019, the association between common mental disorders and adverse outcomes in the 2 years after the index date remained broadly stable over time (ratio of hazard ratios [HRs] per calendar year 1·01 [95% CI 1·00-1·02] for hospital admission for self-harm; 1·00 [0·99-1·01] for alcohol misuse; 1·01 [0·99-1·02] for drug misuse).

INTERPRETATION: The increase in recorded common mental disorders among CYP was not accompanied by declining clinical risk as would be expected if young people were increasingly being recorded at lower levels of severity, whether through readier presentation to primary care, greater clinical recognition, or more liberal recording. These findings highlight the need for greater consistency, better recording of psychometric measures, and transparency in care pathways.

FUNDING: NIHR, Wellcome Trust, Place2Be.

title: Cannabidiol for Severe Behavioral Problems in Youths With Intellectual Disability: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: There is a high level of interest in cannabidiol (CBD) as treatment for severe behavioral problems in children with intellectual disabilities. Given the lack of evidence, clinical trials are needed to inform practice.

OBJECTIVE: To investigate the efficacy of CBD to reduce severe behavioral problems in children and adolescents with intellectual disability.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This parallel design, double-blind placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial was conducted between May 11, 2021, and May 8, 2025. Participants were children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 years with an intellectual disability and severe behavioral problems from 3 children's hospitals in Australia: The Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Monash Children's Hospital in Melbourne, and The Children's Hospital Westmead in Sydney.

INTERVENTION: Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive CBD isolate in oil (10 mg/kg/d) or placebo orally for 8 weeks, with a 4-week follow-up period.

MAIN OUTCOME AND MEASURE: The primary outcome was parent-reported score on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist, Irritability (ABC-I) subscale assessed at the end of the 8-week maintenance phase.

RESULTS: Of 131 participants randomized after exclusion of 1 participant randomized in error, 65 were in the CBD group and 66 were in the placebo group. Overall, mean (SD) age was 11.2 (3.1) years, and 98 participants (74.8%) were male. A total of 110 participants (84.0%) had comorbid autism. Primary outcome data were available for 61 participants in the CBD group and 63 in the placebo group. Mean (SD) ABC-I subscale scores at baseline were 32.2 (7.3) and 30.0 (6.3) in the CBD and placebo groups, respectively. Intention-to-treat analysis showed similar mean (SD) ABC-I subscale scores at the end of treatment: 21.7 (11.0) in the CBD group and 19.2 (10.7) in the placebo group (mean difference, 2.4; 95% CI, -1.5 to 6.3). A similar proportion of participants experienced at least 1 adverse event in the CBD group (41 [63.1%]) and the placebo group (40 [60.6%]).

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial, CBD was not effective in treating severe behavioral problems in youths with intellectual disability. The results suggest that CBD should not be used to treat severe behavioral problems in this population.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04821856.

title: School-Based Health Centers and Student Health Care Use, Need, and Health Outcomes
abstract:
This cross-sectional study evaluates 10 years of survey data to determine the association of access to school-based health centers with health, unmet health care need, and health care receipt for high school students in Oregon.

Key Points Question Does having access to a school-based health center (SBHC) improve the physical and mental health outcomes of high school students? Findings This cross-sectional study using Oregon data found that SBHC access reduced suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts, and unmet emotional health care need among students in grade 11. No changes in physical health or unmet physical health care need were observed. Meaning SBHCs may help improve the mental health of high school students.

Importance School-based health centers (SBHCs) are health clinics located in schools that provide comprehensive primary medical care at low or no cost to students. SBHCs are well positioned to improve health outcomes and health care use by eliminating transportation and cost barriers and to reduce disparities by primarily serving communities with low household incomes and high health care needs. Objective To determine the association of SBHC access with health, unmet health care need, and health care receipt for high school students in Oregon. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used 10 years of student survey data during 2006 to 2023 linked to information on SBHC access in high schools in Oregon. Participants were students in 11th grade statewide who took the health survey. Using entropy-balanced staggered difference-in-differences regressions, we estimated the association of having an SBHC at a student’s school with their outcomes. Data analysis was performed from July to September 2026. Exposure School-level measure of whether an SBHC was present in a high school in Oregon. Main Outcomes and Measures Three measures of mental health and suicidality, 2 measures of physical health, 2 measures of unmet health care need, and 1 measure of medical care received. Results Among 87 871 students at 180 schools, 43 397 (49.7%) were female, 42 824 (49.0%) were male, and 1157 (1.3%) were another gender. A total of 14 933 students attended a school with an SBHC during the study period. SBHC access was associated with statistically significant improvements in student mental health, with decreases in suicidal thoughts (−2.7 percentage points [pp]; 95% CI, −4.5 to −0.7 pp) and suicide attempts (−1.4 pp; 95% CI, −2.3 to −0.5 pp) and decreases in reports of unmet emotional health care needs (−2.1 pp; 95% CI, −3.8 to −0.6 pp). No other statistically significant associations with SBHC access were observed. Heterogeneous treatment effects by gender, sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, and rurality were observed. Conclusions and Relevance This study found that SBHC access was associated with improved mental health among high school students. There are nearly 4000 SBHCs in the United States, and they are primarily in schools with a high share of students from low-income families. Expanding access to SBHCs may help reduce mental health disparities.

Introduction School-based health centers (SBHCs) are health centers located in schools that offer a range of physical, behavioral, and preventive health services at low or no cost. There are nearly 4000 SBHCs nationwide. SBHCs offer an opportunity to reduce disparities in health outcomes and access to care, as schools with SBHCs have a higher share of students from low-income households and Black and Hispanic students compared with schools without SBHCs. Much of the evidence about the impacts of SBHCs on health care use and health outcomes is based on studies examining correlations. Among more rigorous evaluations of SBHCs, there are mixed findings on the associations of receipt of health care and health outcomes, likely due to the variety of contexts and outcomes examined. Nationwide research suggests that SBHC openings reduce teen birth rates, but may not change high school dropout rates, and that the opening of an SBHC in a county increases the likelihood of an adolescent having a usual source of care, but does not change receipt of a mental health visit or improve overall health. Positive changes on students’ mental health following SBHC openings were observed in Tennessee and Oregon, with reductions in emergency department (ED) visits for mental health concerns and increased outpatient mental health visits among youth insured by Medicaid after the opening of an SBHC in a district in Tennessee and reductions in student-reported depression, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts among high school students after the expansion of mental health services in existing SBHCs in Oregon. However, a study of SBHCs offering mental health care in California found no changes in student-reported depression and suicidality. Nearly all of these studies looked at SBHC access at the school district or county level, which may understate the benefits that students attending schools with an on-site SBHC experience. The 2 studies that examined access to on-site SBHCs may have limited generalizability because one examined the expansion of services at existing SBHCs and the other examined a subtype of SBHCs that offer mental health care with or without primary care services. Our study extends previous work by examining SBHC access among students attending these schools and by examining a broad array of measures of physical and mental health. The objective of this study was to determine the changes in physical and mental health outcomes, unmet health care need, and receipt of care for high school students in Oregon after an SBHC opens. We used 10 years of survey data and a difference-in-differences study design to compare outcomes for students in grade 11 in schools with an SBHC to schools that did not have an SBHC during the study period. Methods This cross-sectional study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guidelines for cross-sectional studies and was determined exempt by RAND’s human participants protections committee with a waiver of informed consent. Data and Setting We use 10 years of survey data from the Oregon Healthy Teens survey (fielded annually from 2006-2009, biennially from 2011 to 2019) and the Student Health Survey (2023). Both are statewide surveys that provide information about the health and health behaviors of students in grade 11. These data were obtained from the Oregon Health Authority with school identifiers, allowing us to link on information about SBHCs. Information on Oregon’s SBHCs, including school location and open (and close) date, was obtained from the Oregon Health Authority SBHC program. Data analysis was performed from July to September 2026. Exposure Oregon certifies SBHCs and requires that they are open at least 3 days per week and at least 15 hours per week during the school year. SBHCs are required to have a primary care clinician, such as a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant, working on-site at least 10 hours per week and at least 2 days per week. They are also required to have a qualified mental health professional, with at least a master’s degree in a mental health field, available on-site or through referral who can provide mental health care, substance use treatment, and other services supporting student emotional well-being. A student was considered exposed if they attended a school with a certified SBHC. Outcomes We examine 8 outcome questions that were asked in all survey waves. This includes 3 outcomes related to mental health and suicidality. Students were asked if during the past year they ever (1) felt so sad or hopeless almost every day for 2 weeks or more in a row that they stopped doing some usual activities and (2) seriously considered attempting suicide. We constructed 2 dichotomous variables to compare responses of yes with no. Students were also asked how many times they attempted suicide during the past year (3). We constructed a dichotomous variable to compare 1 or more times with 0 times. We examine 2 health outcomes. Students responded to 2 questions asking them to rate their (4) emotional and mental health and (5) physical health. We constructed 2 dichotomous variables to compare responses of excellent and very good with good, fair, and poor. We examine 2 measures of unmet health care needs. Students responded to 2 questions asking them if, during the past year, they had any (6) physical health care needs or (7) emotional or mental health care needs that were not met. We constructed 2 dichotomous variables to compare responses of yes with no. For all aforementioned outcomes, responses of not sure, don’t know, and prefer not to answer were coded as missing and excluded from analysis. We examine 1 outcome related to receipt of health care. Students were asked (8) when they last went to a doctor or nurse practitioner for a checkup when they were not sick or injured. We constructed a dichotomous variable to compare responses of during the past year with between 1 and 2 years ago, more than 2 years ago, never, and not sure. Statistical Analysis We used a difference-in-differences (DiD) regression approach, fit via ordinary least squares, to estimate the association of SBHC access with student outcomes. Our analytic approach leveraged a natural experiment in which we compared the mean outcome in 37 schools that opened SBHCs to the mean outcome in schools that never opened an SBHC, both before and after the SBHC opened. All DiD regressions used entropy balancing weights to make students at schools without SBHCs more similar to students at schools with SBHCs with respect to student gender, race and ethnicity, sexual orientation, language spoken at home, and presence of an asthma diagnosis. More details on these variables are provided in eMethods 1 in Supplement 1 . We included school and year fixed effects in the DiD regressions; the school-level fixed effects adjusted for observed and unobserved school characteristics that were consistent over the study period, while the year fixed effects controlled for statewide changes in student outcomes over time. To adjust for the staggered opening of SBHCs throughout the study period, DiD regressions were fit separately in each SBHC opening cohort, relative to not-yet-treated controls, and then aggregated across cohorts by weighting cohorts proportional to the number of treated students in that cohort. We hypothesized that treatment effects could vary by rural location and by self-reported student gender, race and ethnicity, and sexual minority status. To test whether associations differed for these subgroups, we fit DiD regressions in which we interacted the treatment status with subgroup indicators and estimated separate effects in each group. We used multiple imputation via chained equations to address small quantities of missing data on some covariates. More information on missing data and multiple imputation are given in eMethods 1 in Supplement 1 , while additional details on model specification, fitting, and inference are provided in eMethods 2 in the Supplement 1 . We conducted sensitivity analyses in which we adjusted for additional covariates, did not use entropy balancing, removed survey data from after the COVID-19 pandemic (ie, 2023 data), conducted a complete case analysis, and analyzed self-reported emotional and physical health ratings using the full range of student responses. More details on these analyses are given in eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 . All analyses were conducted in R version 4.5.0 (R Foundation). A P value less than .05 was considered significant. Results Across the 10 survey waves, there were 107 781 grade 11 student respondents at 254 schools. After applying exclusion criteria, 87 871 students at 180 schools were included in the main analysis (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 ), reflecting an annual average of 20% of high schools and 21% of grade 11 students in Oregon. Missing data were generally less than 5% for key variables (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 ). During the study period, 37 schools opened an SBHC, and 14 933 student respondents attended a school with an SBHC (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 ). Table 1 presents demographic characteristics of students in the sample, while Table 2 provides outcome prevalences. eFigures 1 through 8 in Supplement 1 provide information on how outcome prevalences changed over time. Among 87 871 students at 180 schools, 43 397 (49.7%) were female, 42 824 (49.0%) were male, and 1157 (1.3%) were another gender. The sample was representative with respect to gender, and the composition of student race and ethnicity largely reflected Oregon demographics. Most students were heterosexual (n = 74 069; 87.8%) and spoke English at home (n = 57 723; 84.0%). Around 10% of the sample (n = 9070) had asthma at the time of survey, and 15 298 students (17.4%) attended schools in rural areas. Negative mental health outcomes were common in the sample, with around a quarter of students reporting depression (n = 22 360; 27.0%), 12 360 reporting suicidal thoughts (15.0%), and reporting a suicide attempt in the last year (n = 4698; 5.7%). Around half reported having very good or excellent physical health (n = 43 205; 49.6%); 39 010 students (45.0%) reported having very good or excellent emotional health. A total of 51 299 students (60.1%) had seen a doctor for routine care (ie, not for acute illness or injury) in the last year. The estimated association of SBHC access with each outcome is given in Table 3 , along with unadjusted differences in the prevalence of the outcome before and after SBHC opening for comparison. Event study results are given in eFigure 9 in Supplement 1 . When not adjusting for other confounders, SBHC access appears associated with almost uniformly worse health outcomes. However, after adjusting for confounders, we found that SBHC access was associated with significant improvements in student mental health. Students at schools with an SBHC were 2.7 percentage points (pp) (95% CI, −4.5 to −0.7 pp) less likely to consider suicide and 1.4 pp less likely to attempt suicide (95% CI, −2.3 to −0.5 pp) in the past year. SBHC access was also associated with a 2.1–percentage point statistically significant decrease in the likelihood of reporting an unmet mental health care need (95% CI, −3.8 to −0.6 pp). In addition, there was a 2.2–percentage point increase in reporting very good or excellent emotional health among students at schools with an SBHC (95% CI, −0.01 to 4.5 pp). We did not find statistically significant associations with physical health outcomes or receipt of medical care. Sensitivity analyses found that these results were mostly robust to a range of model specifications and exclusion criteria (eFigure 10 and eTable 4 in Supplement 1 ). We also considered how the association of SBHC access with each outcome varied across key subgroups.

title: Reduced Social Media Use and Change in Internalizing Symptoms Among High-Risk Young Adults
abstract:
Key Points Question Among young adults with elevated internalizing problems and frequent social media use, is reduced social media use associated with subsequent improvement in internalizing symptoms? Findings In this cohort study of a nationally representative sample of 2358 US young adults (3788 observations) with elevated internalizing symptoms and frequent social media use at baseline, reductions in social media use frequency were associated with subsequent improvement in internalizing symptoms. Meaning The findings suggest that reducing social media use may represent a modifiable target for prevention and early intervention in young adults with elevated symptoms and frequent use.

This cohort study evaluates associations between reduced social media use and changes in internalizing problems among young adults in the US.

Importance National cohort analyses of the association between reduced social media use and subsequent improvement in internalizing problems among high-risk young adults—ie, those most likely to benefit from intervention—remain limited. Objective To assess whether reduced social media use is associated with improvements in internalizing problems among US young adults with frequent social media use and elevated internalizing problems. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used data from the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study (2013-2021). Repeated observations were organized into 4 consecutive, overlapping 3-wave intervals, each comprising 3 sequential survey waves ( t , t + 1, and t + 2); for example, interval 1 included waves 1-3, and interval 4 included waves 4-6. Young adults aged 18 to 24 years with elevated internalizing problems (all 4 symptoms) and frequent social media use (several times a day) at wave t were included. Data were analyzed from February to August 2026. Exposures Self-reported social media use frequency at wave t + 1 (nonfrequent [≤once daily] vs frequent [several times daily]). Main Outcomes and Measures Past-year internalizing problems (nonelevated [≤3 symptoms] vs elevated [4 symptoms]) at wave t + 2 via the Global Appraisal of Individual Needs–Short Screener (depression, anxiety, psychological distress, sleep difficulties). Results A total of 3788 person-interval observations (2561 [64.7%] female; aged 18-24 years at baseline) were included. Approximately 14% (n = 540) transitioned to nonfrequent use at t + 1. Reduced use was associated with greater likelihood of nonelevated internalizing symptoms at t + 2 (0.57 vs 0.49; prevalence difference, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.02-0.13; prevalence ratio, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.04-1.27). Findings were generally consistent across sensitivity analyses, including alternative exposure definitions (weekly or less vs several times daily social media use: prevalence ratio, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.04-1.33), alternative missing-data handling approaches (prevalence ratio, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.04-1.25), design-based analyses (prevalence ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.28), concurrent models (prevalence ratio, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.01-1.26), and alternative outcome definitions using internalizing symptom counts, with non-frequent use associated with fewer symptoms (adjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.85-0.96). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, reduced social media use was associated with subsequent improvement in internalizing symptoms among US young adults with elevated symptoms and frequent use. These findings identify reduced social media use as a potentially modifiable target for prevention and early intervention in this high-risk population.

title: Lithium for Suicide Prevention: Umbrella Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Lithium has anchored suicide-prevention guidelines for five decades, yet quantitative syntheses of the randomized evidence have produced divergent estimates. The authors evaluated the contemporary randomized evidence on lithium for suicide-related outcomes in patients with psychiatric disorders.

METHODS: Five databases were searched from inception to April 6, 2026, for systematic reviews with meta-analyses of randomized trials comparing lithium with placebo, treatment as usual, or active comparators; all eligible trials were re-extracted, with an updated six-source primary-trial search from January 2024. Prespecified outcomes were completed suicide, suicide attempt, deliberate self-harm, all-cause mortality, composite suicide-related events, and treatment discontinuation. The primary estimator was the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio without continuity correction, and certainty of evidence was rated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.

RESULTS: Ten systematic reviews, one reanalysis, and 20 trial publications (22 strata; 3,675 participants) were included. For completed suicide (11 informative comparisons, 2,292 participants; six events with lithium vs. 16 with comparators), the pooled estimate favored lithium but included the null (odds ratio [OR]=0.39, 95% CI=0.15, 1.00; I²=0%). A Peto sensitivity estimate reached statistical significance (OR=0.42, 95% CI=0.18, 0.98), whereas excluding the most influential comparison attenuated the estimate (OR=0.43, 95% CI=0.13, 1.40). In exploratory subgroup analysis, the signal concentrated in trials enrolling mixed mood-disorder populations (four trials; OR=0.25, 95% CI=0.07, 0.90). Treatment discontinuation favored lithium over placebo but active comparators over lithium. No significant effects emerged for suicide attempt, deliberate self-harm, all-cause mortality, or composite suicide-related events. GRADE certainty was low to very low.

CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence indicates greater uncertainty than suggested by earlier syntheses, with a sparse completed-suicide signal that was estimator-sensitive and with no consistent evidence across related outcomes. Lithium remains a treatment option when clinically indicated, but adequately powered pragmatic trials that prespecify suicidal behavior and balance clinical contact between arms are needed.

title: Growth Differentiation Factor 15 as a Body-Brain Stress Signal in Major Depression and Insulin Resistance
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is linked to insulin resistance, which is associated with increased risk, chronicity, and poor treatment response in depression. Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a stress-induced cytokine linking peripheral to central energy metabolism, may mediate this link, but its role in MDD is unclear. The authors assessed associations of MDD and insulin resistance with GDF15; links between GDF15, symptoms, and stress; and whether baseline GDF15 levels predict symptom persistence.

METHODS: In this preregistered secondary analysis, 190 participants with MDD and 183 control participants provided blood, underwent interviews, and completed questionnaires. GDF15 values were log-transformed and analyzed with linear models. The association between GDF15 and depression severity was validated in an independent cohort of medication-free MDD patients (N=168).

RESULTS: Both MDD diagnosis and insulin resistance were significantly associated with elevated GDF15 (adjusted for age and sex). Across all participants, elevated GDF15 was significantly associated with greater depressive severity, childhood trauma, and perceived stress. In stratified analyses, the association with depression severity and perceived stress was significant only in healthy control subjects. In MDD patients, baseline GDF15 was associated with persistence of symptoms across time. In the second independent sample of medication-free MDD patients, depression severity was significantly associated with GDF15.

CONCLUSIONS: GDF15 is elevated in MDD and insulin resistance, indicating convergent stress-energy pathway activation, and in MDD higher GDF15 predicted symptom persistence. These findings position GDF15 as a mechanistic biomarker at the interface of psychiatric and metabolic health and reinforce the need for integrated care of metabolic and mental health.

title: Implication of the ADCY1 Gene in Lithium Response in Bipolar Disorder by Genome-Wide Association Meta-Analysis
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Efforts to examine the influence of genetics in the efficacy of lithium using genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several loci. Here, we report new cases and meta-analyses to combine previous efforts.

METHODS: We report data from 1259 participants with bipolar disorder (BD) recruited at University College London who had been treated with lithium. The data come from three waves of genotyping on different arrays. The GWAS data from each array was analysed separately and then meta-analysed with two published lithium response GWAS datasets. Post-GWAS analyses were conducted to examine lithium response heritability and its genetic correlations with other traits. We also attempted to replicate past polygenic risk scores (PRS) results.

RESULTS: SNP rs116927879 (A/G) was associated with lithium response at a genome-wide significance level (p = 4.509 × 10 -08 ) with a consistent effect across all cohorts. rs116927879 is located on chromosome 7 and maps to the protein-coding gene ADCY1 and two pseudo-genes, GTF2IP13 and SEPT7P2. The sQTL results suggested that rs116927879 genotypes may influence the splicing of ADCY1 across different brain regions. We estimated the SNP heritability (h 2 ) for good lithium response as 20.3% and 15.6% for subjective/objective response definitions, respectively. We did not observe any genetic correlation or PRS association between the lithium response and schizophrenia or major depression disorder. However, we found weak evidence to suggest that males are more likely to be good responders.

CONCLUSIONS: Our GWAS identifies a genome-wide significant finding and provides updated heritability estimates for lithium efficacy.

title: The efficacy of ketogenic interventions on neuropsychological & metabolic outcomes in serious mental illness & neurocognitive disorders: a systematic review & meta-analysis
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Ketogenic interventions have garnered attention for their potential benefits in individuals with psychiatric and neurocognitive disorders. This review analyzed findings from studies investigating the impact of ketogenic interventions on clinical outcomes in individuals with serious mental illness (SMI) and neurocognitive disorders.

METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted to identify studies reporting on psychopathology or cognitive performance in individuals with schizophrenia spectrum, major mood, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or major neurocognitive disorders/dementia treated with a ketogenic intervention. Changes in body composition, metabolic parameters, adherence, and safety were also assessed. Evidence was organized by population and outcome of interest, and supplemented by a quantitative meta-analysis.

RESULTS: Seventy-three studies (SMI k = 31; neurocognitive disorders k = 42) were included, with treatment durations ranging from single-dose interventions up to 12 years. Evidence in SMI was largely limited to case reports and single-arm trials reporting symptom remission, reductions in positive and negative symptoms, and mood improvements. Controlled trials in neurocognitive disorders provided more substantiated evidence amenable to meta-analysis. Ketogenic interventions improved cognitive performance (SMD 0.24, 95% CI [0.06, 0.43], p = 0.01, n = 587, k = 14, I² = 61%) and reduced body weight (MD - 3.13 kg, 95% CI [-5.91, -0.35], p = 0.03, n = 80, k = 3, I² = 6%) in this population. Gastrointestinal symptoms were the most frequently reported adverse event.

CONCLUSION: While the evidence for ketogenic interventions differs by population, promising findings emerge. In neurocognitive disorders, controlled trial data support modest cognitive and metabolic benefits. In SMI, preliminary evidence highlights the evolving nature of this field and the need for more rigorous investigation, including RCTs, to establish clinical safety and efficacy.

title: Unreliability of Biomarker Research in Psychiatry
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Biomarker discovery is a key research area in psychiatry, with the goals of identifying susceptibility to conditions, improving diagnostic accuracy, and predicting treatment response. Most biomarkers in psychiatry fail to be externally validated.

OBJECTIVE: To discuss 5 key principles used in unreliable biomarker discovery and provide alternative strategies for rigorous internal validation of biomarkers that can improve rigor and replicability.

EVIDENCE REVIEW: Six articles were reviewed for biomarker discovery in major depressive disorder and their use of the 5 principles.

FINDINGS: Well-documented unreliable practices have contributed to failed biomarker research. Modern methods are subject to the same unreliable principles.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Rigorous biomarker discovery is rare and remains a challenge with complex data augmentation, synthetic data, and cross-validation strategies.

title: Effects of specialised and centralised versus generalised and decentralised outpatient treatment for progressed bipolar disorder: Results from the CAG Bipolar randomised controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical Academic Group (CAG) is a new organization of treatment bringing together clinical services, research, education, and training to provide evidence-based care. We aimed, for the first time, to investigate whether specialized and centralized outpatient treatment (CAG Bipolar) versus decentralized community-based treatment improves patient outcomes and satisfaction with care in patients with progressed bipolar disorder.

METHODS: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial was undertaken with individual randomization to 1) specialized and centralized outpatient treatment in CAG Bipolar or 2) generalized and decentralized community-based outpatient treatment. The 12-month outcomes were 1) cumulated number and duration of psychiatric hospitalizations, and 2) psychotropic medication, coercion, self-rated depressive and manic symptoms, quality of life, perceived stress, and satisfaction with care.

RESULTS: There was no difference among 1,134 included patients in cumulated number (RR: 0.94 (95% CI: 0.74-1.14),  p  = 0.6) or duration (0.16 days, (95% CI: -4.10-4.42;  p  = 0.9) of psychiatric hospitalizations. Lithium (RR: 1.19 (95% CI: 1.05-1.33) and antipsychotics (RR: 1.09 (95% CI: 1.01-1.17), specifically quetiapine (RR: 1.17 (95% CI: 1.03-1.30), were prescribed more in the CAG Bipolar group, and CAG Bipolar patients were overall more satisfied with care including the skills of the professionals, information and the efficacy of the service. There was no difference in coercion, self-rated depressive or manic symptoms, quality of life or perceived stress.

CONCLUSIONS: Specialized and centralized outpatient treatment for progressed bipolar disorder does not result in improvement in robust outcome measures such as hospitalization and coercion, but in the use of psychotropic medication concordant with international guidelines, and increased satisfaction with care.

title: ALE meta-analysis of cognitive control, motivation, and effort in schizophrenia and mood disorders: implications for multidimensional apathy
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Apathy is present in about 50% of patients suffering from schizophrenia (SZ) and mood disorders (MD). Even though these two disorders are different, in psychiatry, apathy refers typically to the same unidimensional clinical entity, sharing the same pathophysiological processes and symptoms regardless of the underlying diagnosis. Neurology proposes another perspective: three forms of apathy-emotional, executive, and initiative-are related to a disturbance in motivation, cognitive control, and effort-based decision-making, respectively. We explored whether this latter model can be applied in psychiatry by identifying differences between SZ and MD through a PRISMA meta-analysis of imaging studies on reward processing, cognitive control, and effort-based decision-making networks.

METHODS: We searched the Sleuth BrainMap and PubMed databases for studies on SZ, MD, and/or healthy controls using tasks probing reward processing, cognitive control, and effort-based decision-making. Twenty-three functional MRI studies were identified and included for a coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation analysis.

RESULTS: In SZ, hypoactivity in reward-processing structures, a specific hyperactivity in the right cerebellar vermis that has previously been linked to emotional blunting and apathy, and a lack of activation during effort-based decision-making that could imply an impaired reward processing, suggest a dominant form of emotional apathy. In MD, hypoactivity in both cognitive control and reward-processing structures, which has previously been linked to the co-occurrence of executive difficulty and amotivation, suggests a mixed emotional/executive apathy profile.

LIMITATIONS: The main limitations include the use of two databases, a small number of existing studies, a lack of control over treatment, age, and disorder severity, as well as the inherent heterogeneity of each diagnosis.

CONCLUSION: By highlighting different dominant forms of apathy in SZ and MD, these results could help target new individualized treatment strategies in precision psychiatry based on a multidimensional conceptualization of apathy.

REGISTRATION: This review was not prospectively registered.

title: [Child suicide: a developmental perspective]
abstract: Suicide before puberty is rare but can affect children as young as 6. Suicidal behaviour should be viewed from a developmental perspective, at the intersection of individual vulnerabilities and family, school and social factors. Abuse, trauma, family conflicts, mental health problems, bullying, rejection and isolation increase the risk. Conversely, parental support, a sense of belonging at school and the presence of reassuring adults act as protective factors. Any expression of suicidal thoughts must be taken seriously and form the subject of a comprehensive assessment. Prevention involves a combination of child and adolescent psychiatry, family support, cooperation with schools and public policy.

title: Intolerance of Uncertainty Among US and Canadian Young Adults Attending College 1992-2023: A Meta-Analysis
abstract:
This meta-analysis investigates the evolution of intolerance of uncertainty (IU), a transdiagnostic risk factor for anxiety, in US and Canadian young adults attending college between 1992 and 2023.

Key Points Question How did intolerance of uncertainty, a transdiagnostic risk factor for anxiety, evolve in US and Canadian young adults attending college between 1992 and 2023? Findings In this meta-analysis including 137 studies and 37 298 participants, average intolerance of uncertainty grew between 1992 and 2023. The annual rate of change was 3-fold higher between 2012 and 2023 than between 1992 and 2011. Meaning Study results suggest that intervening on intolerance of uncertainty may curb the growth of anxiety prevalence in young adults.

Importance Rising anxiety prevalence among young adults may relate to intolerance of uncertainty (IU), difficulty enduring the perceived absence of important information. A prior meta-analysis found increasing long-form Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS) scores among US and Canadian undergraduates from 1992 to 2014, but recent evidence is lacking. Objective To estimate IU trends among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023 by extending the prior meta-analysis and including the short-form IUS. Data Sources Web of Science was used to track English-language articles from Canada or the US citing the source articles for the long-form or short-form IUS across 13 databases. Study Selection Eligible studies were peer-reviewed empirical articles with nonclinical undergraduate samples from the US or Canada that reported sample size and mean long-form or short-form IUS. Data Extraction and Synthesis Following MOOSE guidelines, 2 investigators extracted study characteristics and mean IU, resolving discrepancies jointly. Studies were merged with the prior meta-analysis and analyzed using fixed-effect meta-regression. To assess IU across scale forms, mean IU was converted into SD units and regressed onto data collection year, weighted by sample size, and adjusted for mean age and sex or gender distribution. Study data were analyzed from September 2025 to July 2026. Main Outcome and Measure Mean IU. The hypothesis was preregistered before data collection. Results Of 799 abstracts screened and 294 full texts reviewed independently by 2 investigators, 92 articles (11%) met selection criteria. After merger with prior meta-analysis and removal of duplicates, this meta-analysis included 137 studies (62 long-form IUS and 75 short-form IUS) comprising 37 298 participants (unweighted median [IQR] of sample mean age, 20.1 [19.4-21.3] years; 69.5% female [unweighted mean of sample sex/gender distribution]). Mean long-form IU increased from 1992 to 2023 by 0.66 points annually (95% CI, 0.47-0.84 points) on a scale from 27 to 135. Mean short-form IU increased from 2005 (first sample) to 2023 by 0.60 points annually (95% CI, 0.43-0.76 points) on a scale from 12 to 60. In the combined sample, mean IU grew by 0.04 SD per year from 1992 to 2023 (95% CI, 0.03-0.05 SD per year), with 3-fold faster growth during 2012-2023 (0.06 SD per year; 95% CI, 0.04-0.08 SD per year) than during 1992-2011 (0.02 SD per year; 95% CI, 0-0.04 SD per year). Conclusions and Relevance Results of this meta-analysis suggest that IU increased among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023, with a steeper increase after 2012. This supports further investigating the role of uncertainty in the epidemiology of anxiety.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Psychotic Disorders: Mechanistic Convergence and Therapeutic Implications for Brain and Metabolic Health
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to review and synthesize the mechanistic rationale and emerging clinical evidence for the use of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) in psychotic disorders.

METHODS: The authors conducted a systematic review of the clinical literature relevant to GLP-1RA use in people with psychotic disorders. Searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycInfo, and Cochrane CENTRAL were conducted from database inception through March 7, 2026, and were supplemented by searches of ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and reference-list screening. The findings were integrated into a narrative synthesis of preclinical and translational evidence relevant to novel metabolic mechanisms in the pathophysiology of psychotic disorders.

RESULTS: Preclinical and early human mechanistic studies suggest that GLP-1RAs may influence several pathways relevant to psychotic disorders, including systemic and central glucose homeostasis, gut-brain signaling, inflammatory processes, redox alterations, mitochondrial function, and reward-related signaling. Clinically, the clearest evidence of benefit is for antipsychotic-associated weight gain and cardiometabolic risk, with most randomized clinical trials reporting meaningful improvements in body weight and metabolic outcomes. Relevant to comorbidities in psychotic disorders, the evidence for GLP-1RA effects on alcohol and nicotine use is suggestive but inconclusive. Available studies have not yet demonstrated consistent improvements in psychotic symptoms, cognition, or functioning. Limitations to the clinical evidence include small samples; short follow-up; heterogeneity in agents, dosing, and endpoints; and minimal incorporation of mechanistic endpoints.

CONCLUSIONS: GLP-1RAs represent a clinically and mechanistically grounded strategy to address the substantial cardiometabolic burden in psychotic disorders, with the potential for reduced substance use and other neuropsychiatric benefits.

title: Eight-Week Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled 2-Site Trial Assessing the Efficacy and Safety of Mixed Amphetamine Salt as an Adjunctive Therapy for Bipolar Depression
abstract: Objective:  This study examined the efficacy and safety of adjunctive mixed  d -amphetamine/ l -amphetamine salt (MAS; Mydayis) in adults with  DSM-IV-TR -confirmed bipolar I or II depression.  Methods:  In this 8-week, randomized, placebo-controlled 2-site study of adjunctive MAS, the primary outcome was baseline-to-end point change in the Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Secondary outcomes included, in part, treatment response and remission (≥50% MADRS reduction, MADRS <10) and illness improvement as measured by the Clinical Global Impression for Bipolar Disorder (CGI-BP). The primary safety assessment was the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS). The 8-week controlled trial was followed by an 8-week open-label extension.  Results:  Thirty-two (14 with bipolar I disorder, 18 with bipolar II disorder; 10 male, 22 female; mean age=38.2 y) patients enrolled in the study. Baseline symptoms (MADRS = 27.0±6.3, Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Clinician-Rated = 15.3±3.2, Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Self-Report = 14.8±4.7, and YMRS = 4.0) were consistent with moderate depression and absence of hypomania. Baseline demographics showed no significant group differences. In age-adjusted analyses, participants receiving adjunctive MAS (n = 15) showed significantly greater improvement on MADRS compared to placebo (n = 17, mean percent reduction: 62.3% vs 15.4%;  P = .002), with higher rates of remission (63.3% vs 8.5%;  P = .002) and response (79.5% vs 7.3%;  P <. 001). CGI-BP ratings of "much improved" or "very much improved" were higher with MAS (67.0% vs 10.2%;  P = .001). No significant differences were observed in YMRS (last observation 2.9 vs 3.3;  P = .72). The open-label extension (n = 24) showed maintenance of response, with 1 participant experiencing a switch to mania and 2 participants with drug misuse.  Conclusions:  Adjunctive MAS was associated with effective reduction in depression symptoms with broad safety profile for most participants. Secondary analyses are encouraged to examine differential response rates by mood stabilizer and item analyses of attention and eating behavior.  Trial Registration:  ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04235686.

title: Mitochondrial Bioenergetics in Schizophrenia: a Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and GRADE-Based Certainty Assessment
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been linked to schizophrenia, but findings remain inconsistent. No previous systematic review has quantitatively synthesized mitochondrial function and biomarker outcomes while also evaluating risk of bias and certainty of the evidence in schizophrenia.

STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of functional outcomes and mitochondrial biomarkers in schizophrenia, including human studies and animal models published through December 2025. Meta-analyses were performed separately by experimental system. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-E/ROBINS-I and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE.

STUDY RESULTS: Forty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria. Human studies showed reduced ATP-related respiratory capacity. Mitochondrial Complex activity was reduced in schizophrenia for Complexes III and IV, but not for Complex II, which lacks mitochondrial DNA-encoded subunits. Human meta-analyses showed high heterogeneity (I2 > 90%), effect estimates varied with study quality, and pooled estimates were unstable. Animal studies showed similar trends but were imprecise. Overall, the certainty of the evidence was very low due to the risks of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness.

CONCLUSIONS: The available evidence supports altered mitochondrial function in schizophrenia, particularly impaired respiratory capacity. However, substantial methodological heterogeneity, risk of bias, and indirectness limit confidence in the magnitude and biomarker specificity of these findings, highlighting the need for larger, standardized, and independently replicated studies.

title: A state-dependent glymphatic dimension in major depressive disorder: implications for treatment resistance
abstract: The glymphatic system refers to cerebrospinal fluid-interstitial fluid exchange and proposed drainage pathways shaped by sleep, arousal, vascular dynamics, and astrocytic organization. This physiology offers a way to connect disturbances that often coexist in major depressive disorder (MDD): disrupted sleep, fatigue, cognitive slowing, and stress-related abnormalities. We propose that difficulty establishing or maintaining a coordinated sleep-astrocyte-vascular state may contribute to illness persistence in some patients. Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) provides a setting in which this possibility can be examined across the course of treatment. Preclinical studies link stress and depressive-like behavior to astrocytic injury, aquaporin-4 dysregulation, and altered fluid transport. Human imaging findings vary across depressive phenotypes. In a dedicated TRD study, a higher diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) ratio was partly driven by reduced denominator diffusivity, illustrating the importance of interpreting this indirect index at component level. Whole-brain spatiotemporal models provide a complementary account of the neural activity accompanying these physiological states. Ketamine/esketamine, transcranial magnetic stimulation, and chronobiological interventions offer different ways to investigate treatment-related change; serotonergic psychedelics provide an exploratory extension. Longitudinal studies can establish how changes in sleep, fluid-sensitive imaging, and neural dynamics relate temporally to clinical recovery. This Perspective therefore develops a potentially modifiable physiological dimension of persistent depressive illness and defines how it can be tested.

title: Assortative mating can mask non-additive genetic contributions to individual differences
abstract: Assortative mating impacts trait variation and covariation among individuals within populations. Here, we examine how direct and indirect assortative mating influence additive and non-additive genetic contributions to individual differences. In an extended twin design, we show by simulations that correlations between mating partners can mask non-additive genetic influences. Accounting for assortative mating can unmask non-additive genetic contributions, revealing upward biases in additive genetic estimates. We applied our approach to anthropometric (height), personality (openness to experience), and psychiatric (borderline personality disorder features) traits in a large dataset of 9000 Dutch families of twins, siblings, and spouses of twins. Our results demonstrate that accounting for partner correlations (r = 0.21-0.29) unmasks non-additive genetic influences (13-19% of trait variation), leading to additive genetic estimates that are 14-39% smaller than those obtained from models ignoring assortment. Our findings clarify the impacts of assortative mating on both additive and non-additive genetic variance components, contributing to a better understanding of the heritability gap between twin and molecular-based studies, and highlight a refined framework for modelling the genetic transmission of behavioural and psychiatric traits.

title: Remodeling stress-responsive networks following early life adversity: Insights from preclinical models
abstract: Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup. Preclinical models using primates and rodents have allowed for fine control over these variables, providing substantial evidence of pathways and related biomarkers impacted by ELA. The present review aims to bridge findings from human clinical data with preclinical research, highlighting well-supported ELA-induced changes in the functional connectivity of stress-sensitive pathways, as well as alterations in additional cortical and subcortical pathways which are susceptible to disturbances during development. We also present key neuromodulatory mechanisms contributing to connectivity changes observed in preclinical models, and sex-specific nuances. Addressing these critical gaps could enhance the potential of connectivity-based therapeutic approaches. Lastly, we consider the translatability of functional connectivity analyses using various preclinical techniques for studying the influence of ELA on the developing brain.

title: Working memory capacity moderates stress-related drinking in alcohol use disorder: An intensive one-year ecological assessment study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stress is a trigger for alcohol consumption, with working memory capacity (WMC) proposed as a protective factor. While several laboratory-based and cross-sectional studies point toward an interaction between WMC, stress, and alcohol consumption, ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) are needed to establish this relationship in real-life contexts, where alcohol consumption and stress experiences actually take place.

METHODS: In this one-year longitudinal EMA study, we collected data from a gamified, smartphone-based WMC task (every 4 weeks) and EMAs of stress and alcohol consumption (every two days) from n=603 participants diagnosed with alcohol use disorder (AUD). We then integrated this data with structural brain imaging data to explore the neural correlates of the hypothesized moderating effect of WMC.

RESULTS: As preregistered, we found that WMC moderated the within-subject association between stress and alcohol consumption. Participants with low WMC, but not participants with high WMC, consumed more alcohol in more stressful compared to less stressful months. In further analysis, within-subject fluctuations in WMC also moderated the within-subject association between stress and drinking. Although effects were in the expected direction, the moderating effect of WMC was not mediated by neural correlates of interest (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and insula).

CONCLUSIONS: We provide first real-life evidence that greater WMC might increase resilience to stress-related drinking in individuals with AUD. This advances our neurocognitive understanding of individual susceptibility to stress-related drinking, which could inform the development of future, personalized interventions.

title: Mapping the shared genetic architecture between anorexia nervosa and metabolomic biomarkers
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anorexia Nervosa (AN) has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder yet lacks effective treatments. While recent genomic efforts have reframed AN as a metabo-psychiatric condition that overlaps with cardiometabolic traits, AN's relationship to circulating metabolomic markers remains unknown.

METHODS: We examined shared genetic architecture between AN and 249 metabolomic biomarkers, and compared profiles with related mental health, anthropometric and cardiometabolic traits. Genetic and biological overlap was assessed with global genetic correlations, conjunctional false discovery rate, bivariate Gaussian mixture modeling, and gene set enrichment analysis across body tissues. We also explored putative causal relationships between AN, body mass index (BMI), and metabolomic biomarkers.

RESULTS: Significant genetic correlations emerged between AN and 142 metabolomic biomarkers, which were opposite in direction to cardiometabolic traits such as BMI and type 2 diabetes (r s <-0.94), and stronger than correlations with anxiety. Shared variants between AN and metabolomic biomarkers, particularly lipid-based metabolites, exhibited a mixture of positive and negative effects. These were mapped to genes involved in lipid-related cell signals, developmental growth, and inflammation, and were widely expressed in the brain, most internal organs and female reproductive organs. Bidirectional associations between AN and metabolomic biomarkers were found to act through their respective influence on BMI.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings reveal a complex, bidirectional mixture of positive and negative genetic relationships between AN and systemic metabolism, which would be obscured by examination of broader cardiometabolic traits. Uncovering specific shared lipid and developmental pathways provides a genetically-anchored mechanistic understanding of the illness, while highlighting promising metabolomic targets for weight restoration approaches.

title: When resilience breaks down: Erosion of the protective role of intelligence in PTSD under extreme combat stress
abstract: Resilience factors play an important role in shaping posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) trajectories, yet their protective effects may depend on the severity of trauma exposure.
