Prior research has linked higher premorbid IQ to lower PTSD risk, with longitudinal evidence from deploying soldiers showing more favorable symptom trajectories among those with higher IQ during routine combat deployment. The present study examined whether this protective effect persisted under conditions of extreme and protracted combat exposure during the Israel-Hamas war. Male Israel Defense Force infantry reservists ( N  = 192; Mean age at enrollment = 19.60 years, SD = 0.78; range = 19-23) were assessed for IQ at age 17 and followed across four time points: three during mandatory service with routine deployments and one during active reserve duty in the war. Ethnicity data were not collected. A mixed-design ANCOVA revealed an interaction ( η 2 p  = 0.017) indicating that higher IQ was associated with greater resilience under routine combat deployment conditions. However, this advantage disappeared under the extreme and protracted combat conditions of the war. Findings highlight that the protective role of cognitive ability is context-dependent, supporting diathesis-stress and threshold models of PTSD risk and resilience. Developmental implications associated with war-related trauma exposure during the critical period of emerging adulthood are discussed.

title: Hands-on or screen-on? The role of training approach in spatial skill development and transfer to mathematics
abstract:
Growing evidence suggests that spatial skills are crucial for learning and everyday functioning and can be improved through training. However, which approaches are most effective remains unclear. The present study compared improvement in children's spatial skills and math performance across four carefully matched spatial training approaches and examined whether individual differences in working memory, spatial anxiety, and gender moderated these changes. Fifth- and sixth-graders from Dutch schools (N = 349; Mage = 11.5 years; 57% girls) were randomly assigned to four training approaches: (1) physical manipulatives (hands-on), (2) virtual manipulatives (hands-on), (3) video demonstration (hands-off), or (4) practice without materials (baseline). Children completed a pretest 1-2 weeks before training, an immediate posttest, and a follow-up assessment 1-2 weeks later (data collected January-March 2024). Results indicated that the two hands-on conditions and the practice-without-materials condition produced comparable gains across all spatial and math outcomes, whereas the video demonstration condition generally showed smaller gains. Additionally, children higher in working memory improved more, regardless of training approach. Interestingly, while girls and children with higher spatial anxiety performed lower overall, they improved to a similar extent as boys and low-anxiety children. Finally, we found that gains were sustained at follow-up, indicating durability.

Spatial skills are fundamental for academic achievement and everyday life, and research shows they can be improved with training. This study compared children's improvements in spatial and math outcomes following one of four spatial training approaches: physical manipulatives, digital manipulatives, video demonstrations, or practice without materials. In total, 349 fifth- and sixth-graders completed tasks 1–2 weeks before training, immediately after training, and 1–2 weeks later. Children using physical and digital manipulatives and those practicing without materials showed similar improvements, whereas those watching video demonstrations showed smaller improvement. Gains were maintained at follow-up, suggesting durability. Overall, these findings suggest that hands-on materials are not always necessary for spatial training, and simpler approaches may be sufficient when hands-on methods are not feasible.

title: Adverse childhood experiences and later overweight and obesity: Findings from an 11-year longitudinal follow-up study-The HUNT Study
abstract: Aims:  Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with unfavorable health consequences. This study aimed to examine the longitudinal associations between ACEs and overweight/obesity in young adulthood.  Methods:  Up to 1942 participants aged 13-19 years in Young-HUNT3 (2006-08) were followed into adulthood 11 years later in HUNT4 (2017-2019). Associations between ACEs (violence/threats, sexual abuse, death/serious illness of someone close, and disaster/serious accidents) reported in adolescence as either a total sum score or sub-scores and adult body mass index (BMI) or waist circumference were estimated by linear regression, stratified by sex and adjusted for age and socioeconomic position.  Results:  Among the participants, 80% (82.6% females and 76.7% males) reported at least one ACE. However, the highest cumulative ACE burden (7-10 ACEs) was slightly more common among males (2.3%) than females (1.7%). Among females, but not males, a positive association was found between the total ACE score and BMI and waist circumference.  Conclusions:  Female adolescents reporting ACEs are at risk of increased overweight and obesity in adulthood. This finding underscores the importance of early interventions targeting ACEs in obesity prevention strategies.

title: Associations between adverse childhood experiences and later-life multiple functional limitation in older adults across four cohorts
abstract:
Background The aim of this study is to evaluate the association between Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and multiple functional limitation in older adults across various international settings. Methods We used longitudinal data from 78,417 adults aged 50 years or older in four ageing cohorts: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), and the Health and Retirement Study (HRS). Six ACE indicators were assessed retrospectively (physical abuse, emotional neglect, parental death, foster care placement, financial hardship, and parental unemployment) and analyzed in two ways: as the cumulative number of ACEs (categorized as 0, 1, 2, or ≥ 3), and as four ACE types (physical abuse, emotional neglect, adverse family environment, and economic adversity). At each survey wave, multiple functional limitation was measured as the number of impairments across six domains (hearing, vision, physical functioning, mobility, mental health, and cognition), giving a score from 0 to 6. Within each cohort, we used survey-weighted generalized estimating equations with a Poisson distribution to estimate associations with functional limitation, adjusting for age, sex, and survey wave. Cohort-specific risk ratios (RRs) were then combined using random-effects meta-analysis. Results Across all cohorts, the proportion reporting at least one ACE ranged from 32.6% in ELSA to 66.9% in CHARLS. Compared with those reporting no ACE, the RRs (95% CI) for functional limitations were 1.17 (1.09–1.26) for one ACE, 1.29 (1.17–1.43) for two ACEs, and 1.39 (1.20–1.61) for three or more ACEs. Among the four ACE types, physical abuse (RR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.08–1.29), economic adversity (RR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.10–1.23), and emotional neglect (RR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.02–1.20) were each associated with higher functional limitation. Increased risks were observed across all six domains, with the strongest associations for mental disorders among individuals with three or more ACEs (RR, 1.82). The findings were consistent across cohorts and robust in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions ACEs were consistently associated with a greater risk of experiencing multiple functional limitations in later life, emphasizing the importance of mitigating childhood adversity to promote healthier ageing.

Background The global population is aging at an unprecedented rate, presenting significant challenges to public health systems worldwide [ 1 ]. Healthy aging prioritizes maintaining functional independence and quality of life, rather than merely extending lifespan. Multiple functional limitation, characterized by a decline in sensory, physical, cognitive, and psychological function, poses a major obstacle to this goal and places a significant burden on individuals, families, and society [ 2 ]. The life-course perspective suggests that health trajectories in adulthood and later life are influenced by experiences in early life. One such critical early-life factor is Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs). ACEs encompass potentially traumatic events that occur before the age of 18, such as physical abuse, emotional neglect, and household dysfunction [ 3 ]. These experiences are recognized as key stressors associated with long-term health outcomes. Previous studies have consistently demonstrated an association between ACEs and a range of adverse health outcomes in adulthood and later life. Individuals who have experienced multiple ACEs are at a significantly higher risk of developing depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders, as well as cardiovascular disease, dementia, and multiple chronic conditions [ 4 – 8 ]. Beyond these clinical conditions, ACEs have also been linked to impairments in specific functional domains, including poorer cognitive function, greater difficulty with activities of daily living and mobility, and accelerated decline in hearing, vision, and dual sensory function [ 9 – 12 ]. These associations may arise through neuroendocrine and inflammatory dysregulation, accelerated biological ageing, and adverse socioeconomic pathways that contribute to decline across multiple domains jointly. Despite the growing body of evidence on ACEs and specific health issues, there are still several research gaps. First, most studies have examined the association between ACEs and individual diseases or health dimensions, but the comprehensive impact of ACEs on overall functional status, particularly multiple functional limitation that better reflects general health, remains poorly understood [ 9 , 13 , 14 ]. Second, existing evidence predominantly derives from single-country or culturally specific contexts [ 10 , 15 ]. Large-scale, cross-national comparative evidence is lacking to determine whether findings can be generalized across populations with diverse socioeconomic backgrounds. Third, while some research has explored the effects of cumulative ACEs effects, the relative and independent contributions of different types of adversity to later-life functional limitation requires further examination [ 16 , 17 ]. To address these limitations, we investigated the prospective association between ACEs (both cumulative number and specific types) and multiple functional limitation (including hearing, vision, physical activity, mobility, mental health, and cognition) in a comprehensive study using data from 78,417 adults aged 50 years and older in the United States, England, Europe, and China. We hypothesize that there is a dose-response association between the cumulative number of ACEs and functional limitation in later life. Furthermore, we hypothesize that each sub-type of ACE (physical abuse, emotional neglect, adverse family environment, and economic adversity) is also associated with an increased risk of functional limitation in each domain. Methods Study design and participants In this cross-national cohort study, we used longitudinal data from four ageing cohorts from the program on Global Ageing, Health and Policy: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE, covering 28 European countries and Israel), and Health and Retirement Study (HRS) in the United States [ 18 – 25 ]. These studies recruited nationally representative samples of middle-aged and older adults using stratified multistage probability sampling and conducted follow-up surveys every two or three years according to comparable study protocols (Additional file: Additional Methods ). Participants were followed longitudinally across survey waves, and refreshment samples of adults were periodically introduced to compensate for attrition due to mortality and loss to follow-up. Individuals were excluded if they (1) had no information on ACEs; (2) were aged below 50 years across all waves; (3) had more than 20% missing values across all covariates and outcomes in each wave, as imputation may be less reliable when a large proportion of information required for modeling is missing; [ 26 ] (4) without sample weights information. As no participants from the Netherlands or Ireland remained after applying these criteria, both countries were excluded from the SHARE analytic sample. Furthermore, survey waves were excluded if any outcome variable was missing for > 50% of participants, as extensive imputation of outcome variables in waves with limited observed information may reduce the reliability of the estimates. This led to the exclusion of SHARE wave 3, which lacked all outcome data, and HRS wave 1, which lacked the required cognitive outcome data. The final analytical sample comprised data from CHARLS (waves 1–4, 2011–2018), ELSA (waves 1–10, 2002–2020), SHARE (waves 1–2, 2004–2006/2007; waves 4–9, 2011–2021/2022), and HRS (waves 2–15, 1993–2020). The baseline was defined as the first wave in which a participant was aged 50 years or older. In total, 78,417 individuals were included in the analysis (Fig. 1 ). We adhered to STROBE guidelines for reporting observational studies (Additional file: Table S1 ). Assessment of ACE ACEs were defined as potentially traumatic events occurring during childhood that are beyond a child’s control, encompassing various forms of abuse, neglect, and household adversity [ 3 ]. Guided by this definition and previous studies, we compiled 21 candidate indicators and assessed the availability and cross-cohort comparability of each in CHARLS, ELSA, SHARE, and HRS (Additional file: Additional Methods ) [ 27 – 30 ]. Six indicators were retained because a comparable measure was available in all four cohorts: physical abuse, emotional neglect, parental death, placement in a foster family or foster home, financial hardship, and parental unemployment. Detailed reasons for not including the remaining indicators, including sexual abuse, are provided in the Additional Methods in Additional file. With the exception of parental death, all ACE indicators were obtained from the dedicated life history surveys conducted in each cohort, which were designed to collect retrospective information on childhood: the 2014 Life History Survey in CHARLS, the 2006 Life History Interview in ELSA, the 2017 SHARELIFE survey in SHARE, and the Childhood Family and Health Study (1992–2016) together with the Life History Mail Survey (2015–2019) in HRS. Parental death was ascertained from a different source. In CHARLS, HRS, and SHARE, the core questionnaire administered at every wave asked whether each biological parent was alive and, if not, the year of death; this was combined with the participant’s year of birth to determine whether either parent had died before the participant reached age 16, drawing on all available waves to maximize completeness. In ELSA, parental death before age 16 was obtained from the 2006 Life History Interview. Specifically, physical abuse was assessed using cohort-specific questions on parental physical abuse during childhood. CHARLS and SHARE used frequency-based questions to assess the physical abusive behaviors by guardians or parents. Responses of “sometimes” or “often” were classified as physical abuse. HRS and ELSA used direct questions assessing whether participants had experienced physical abuse by their parents [ 30 , 31 ]. Emotional neglect was assessed with questions on the emotional support participants received from their parents in CHARLS, HRS, and SHARE, and with a question on whether a parent had been emotionally cold towards the participant in ELSA [ 29 , 31 ]. Parental death was defined as the death of one or both parents before the participant reached age 16. In CHARLS and SHARE, it was derived from the participant’s year of birth and the reported year of parental death; [ 27 , 32 ] in ELSA, it was based on participant reports of parental death before age 16 [ 33 ], and in HRS, parental death was determined using both sources. Placement in a foster family or foster home was assessed with cohort-specific measures. Participants were classified as exposed if they reported having lived with a foster family or in a foster home before age 16 in HRS, having been fostered by another family during childhood in ELSA and SHARE, or having been raised mainly by an adoptive parent in CHARLS [ 27 , 32 ]. Financial hardship was assessed using indicators of poor childhood socioeconomic status, which differed across cohorts: relative financial disadvantage compared with the average family in the same community or village in CHARLS, financial difficulties requiring help from relatives in HRS, severe financial hardship in ELSA, and family poverty before age 16 in SHARE [ 27 , 28 , 31 ]. Parental unemployment was assessed using available measures of parental or guardian joblessness during childhood. Participants were classified as exposed if their father had been unemployed for several months or longer before age 16 in HRS and SHARE, if one or both parents had been unemployed for more than six months before age 16 in ELSA, or if a male or female guardian had ever been unemployed while actively seeking work during their childhood in CHARLS [ 27 , 30 ]. Detailed descriptions of the assessed ACEs across cohorts were provided in Table S2 in Additional file. ACE exposure was operationalized in two ways. The first was cumulative ACE exposure: each of the six indicators was coded as a binary variable (yes or no) and summed into a total ACE score (range 0–6). This score was used in two forms, as a four-category variable (0, 1, 2, and 3 or more ACEs) for the main analysis and as a continuous variable (0–6) for testing the dose-response relationship. The second was specific ACE types: the six indicators were grouped into four types according to their nature. Physical abuse and emotional neglect each comprised a single indicator and were retained as separate types. The remaining four indicators were combined into two composite types: adverse family environment, defined as exposure to parental death or placement in a foster family or foster home, reflecting disruption of the family structure; and economic adversity, defined as exposure to financial hardship or parental unemployment, reflecting childhood socioeconomic deprivation. For the broader definitions of two ACE types used in the sensitivity analysis (see statistical analysis), three additional childhood indicators were assessed in CHARLS, HRS, and ELSA: parental substance abuse, parental separation or divorce, and father’s occupation. These indicators were unavailable in SHARE: parental substance abuse and father’s occupation were collected only in the Wave 3 SHARELIFE survey, which had been excluded, and parental separation or divorce was not assessed. Parental substance abuse was defined as a parent having experienced problematic alcohol or drug use during the participant’s childhood. This was based on reports of parental alcoholism or drug use in CHARLS, parental drinking or drug use causing family problems before the age of 18 in HRS, and parental drinking, drug use, or mental health problems before the age of 16 in ELSA. Parental separation or divorce was defined as the biological or adoptive parents having separated or divorced before the participant turned 16. A father’s occupation was categorized based on his or the male guardian’s usual occupation during the participant’s childhood. Non-white-collar occupations (e.g. manual, agricultural, or service work) were classified as exposed, reflecting a lower childhood socioeconomic position. Detailed question wording for each cohort is provided in Table S2 in Additional file. These additional indicators were incorporated into two types. title: Adverse childhood experiences, social isolation and loneliness across adulthood: A nationwide cross-sectional study of Chinese adults
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Loneliness and social isolation are distinct risk factors for depression and other affective disorders but are often conflated. Whether adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) relate differently to the two, and whether this varies across adulthood, is unclear.

METHODS: We analysed 24,219 adults from the nationwide 2024 Psychology and Behaviour Investigation of Chinese Residents. Seven ACE domains were assessed with items adapted from the WHO ACE-IQ. Social isolation (three-item structural index, score ≥ 2) and loneliness (two-item functional index, score 2) were defined using indices adapted from the UK Biobank. Adjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) were estimated by modified Poisson regression with city-clustered standard errors; a stacked model compared the two outcomes.

RESULTS: Social isolation (30.0%) and loneliness (11.0%) overlapped weakly (kappa 0.17). Each additional ACE was associated with higher prevalence of loneliness (PR 1.24, 95% CI 1.20-1.28) and, more weakly, isolation (PR 1.04, 1.01-1.08; ratio of PRs 1.19, 1.17-1.22). All seven domains were associated with loneliness; only emotional abuse, witnessed violence and, marginally, physical abuse were associated with isolation; sexual abuse, household substance use, household mental illness and parental incarceration were not. The association of ≥4 ACEs with loneliness strengthened with age (P for interaction <0.001; PR 2.71, 1.98-3.72, at ≥60 years).

LIMITATIONS: The cross-sectional design and retrospectively self-reported ACEs preclude causal inference.

CONCLUSIONS: ACEs were more strongly associated with loneliness than with social isolation, particularly in later life. Among adults with ACE histories, asking about loneliness may capture disconnection that structural indicators such as living arrangements or contact frequency miss.

title: Adverse childhood experiences and oral health outcomes among adults in the United States: 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) can have lasting effects on oral health. The authors examined the relationships between ACEs and dental outcomes among adults in the United States.

METHODS: The authors used the 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data (with an overall response rate of 45.0%). The study included 73,537 adults from 12 states. The authors used SAS Release 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc) to conduct multiple logistic regression analyses to assess the association of ACEs with tooth loss and past-year dental visits, and they examined the interactions between ACEs and covariates (age, sex, race, education, income, cigarette smoking status, general health, diabetes, health insurance).

RESULTS: Less than one-half (48.5%) of the study population was male; 62.5% were White, 38.0% had no college education, and 51.5% reported at least 1 ACE. Those with ACEs had higher odds of missing 6 or more teeth than those without ACEs after adjusting for covariates. The adjusted odds ratios of participants with 1, 2 through 3, and 4 or more ACEs were 1.22 (95% CI, 1.06 to 1.40), 1.20 (95% CI, 1.04 to 1.38), and 1.45 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.68), respectively, compared with those without ACEs. Adults with 4 or more ACEs were less likely to have had a past-year dental visit than those without ACEs (adjusted odds ratio, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.67 to 0.82]).

CONCLUSIONS: Having 1 or more ACEs was significantly associated with a higher risk of tooth loss, and having 4 or more ACEs was significantly associated with a lower likelihood of a past-year dental visit among adults in the United States.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: Dental care providers should be encouraged to incorporate trauma-informed care into their practice through patient-centered communication, shared decision making, and strategies that promote safety and trust for patients with ACEs.

title: Adverse and Positive Childhood Experiences among US Bereaved Youth (2022-2024)
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To describe associations of adverse and positive childhood experiences (ACEs and PCEs) and social demographic characteristics with exposure to parent or guardian death among a nationally representative sample of US youth (6-17 years).

METHODS: We pooled cross-sectional data from the 2022-2024 National Survey of Children's Health (N=101,617). We estimated stepwise Poisson and Negative Binomial regression models testing the association of parent or guardian death with ACEs and PCEs accumulation in both the full sample and racial and ethnic stratified subsamples.

RESULTS: Approximately 4% of youth experienced parent or guardian death and were disproportionately non-Hispanic Black, Native American/Other Race, or from low-income households. Bereaved youth were more likely to be exposed to all ACEs and less likely to be exposed to the majority of PCEs relative to their non-bereaved counterparts. Youth exposed to parent or guardian death exhibited significantly more ACEs (β = 0.40, IRR = 1.49, SE = 0.03), yet a similar number of PCEs (β = -0.02, IRR = 0.98, SE = 0.01), relative to their non-bereaved peers. The association between parent and guardian death and ACEs was no longer significant among non-Hispanic Black (β = 0.15, IRR = 1.16, SE = 0.08) and Native American/Other Race (β = 0.12, IRR = 1.12, SE = 0.11) youth relative to other racial and ethnic groups.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings underscore the elevated and unequal exposure of adversity among youth exposed to parent and guardian death. Implications for targeted pediatric supports that address heightened adversities and inequities within this population are discussed.

title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths
abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

title: Noncoding functions of FMR1 transcript in riboregulation of human neurodevelopment
abstract:
SUMMARY The non-coding functions of protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are largely ignored. Here, we demonstrate an unexpected non-coding role of FMR1 mRNA in human neurodevelopment. A loss of FMR1 and its protein product, fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) leads to neurodevelopmental disorder fragile X syndrome (FXS). Neurons derived from FXS patients display hyperexcitability and immature morphology, whereas FMRP knockout (FMRP-KO) neurons that retain FMR1 transcript expression do not. Multiomics analyses reveal key metabolic differences between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons. While both FXS and FMRP-KO neurons exhibit reduced mitochondrial respiration, only FXS neurons exhibit elevated glycolysis. We further discover that the FMR1 transcript riboregulates the levels of glycolytic enzyme LDHA by inhibiting binding of LDHA mRNA to insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 2 (IGF2BP2). Finally, FMR1 transcript, independent of FMRP, rescues glycolytic and cellular deficits of FXS neurons. Together, these results suggest that FMR1 is a dual-function RNA in human neurodevelopment.

Graphical Abstract

eTOC blurb Sandoval et al. reported FMR1 is a dual-function RNA with both protein coding and non-coding roles in human neurodevelopment. They showed that FMR1 transcript, independent of FMRP protein, riboregulates glycolysis by inhibiting IGF2BP2 binding to LDHA mRNA.

INTRODUCTION The central dogma of molecular biology places messenger RNAs (mRNAs) as the intermediate step of directional information flow from genes to proteins 1 . The discovery of dual-function RNAs that have both protein coding and non-coding capabilities challenges this doctrine. First discovered in bacteria and plants, then in animals, and recently in human cancer cells, dual-function RNAs have been shown to play important roles in maintaining developmental processes and in regulating biological functions such as RNA splicing, RNA stability, protein synthesis, epigenetic regulation, and gene silencing 2 – 5 . However, most dual-function RNAs discovered to date are non-coding RNAs that produce short peptides with biological functions 2 , 3 . Limited studies have demonstrated non-coding functions of canonical mRNAs during normal cellular processes 6 , 7 or cancer pathogenesis 8 , 9 . Neurons are morphologically and functionally complex and must adapt to external stimuli for the survival of the organism. As such, neurons in the mammalian brain have the highest number and diversity and the most complex regulatory mechanisms of RNAs 10 . Yet few, if any, dual-function mRNAs have been studied in neurons. It has been shown that while Tp53inp2 protein is expressed in skeletal muscle, Tp53inp2 mRNA, without its protein product regulates axonal growth in rat peripheral sympathetic neurons 6 . Therefore, Tp53inp2 is either a protein coding or a non-coding RNA depending on cell types. However, whether mRNA can have both coding and non-coding roles in the same neurons and whether dual-function mRNAs regulate neurodevelopment, especially in humans, remain largely unexplored. Fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common form of inherited intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, affecting about 1 in 4000 males and 1 in 7000 females, is typically caused by full mutational CGG expansion (>200 CGG repeats) in the 5’ untranslated region (UTR) leading to epigenetic silencing of the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 gene ( FMR1 ) and loss of its protein product, fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) 11 – 13 . FXS research has been focusing on FMRP, an RNA binding protein important for neurons through regulation of synaptic protein translation, mRNA stability, RNA transport, and ion channel activities 13 . We have found that FMRP-deficient mouse and human neurons exhibit mitochondrial fragmentation, metabolic deficits, morphological impairment, and altered neuronal activities 14 , 15 . In contrast to FXS, fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) and fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI) are caused by the premutation CGG expansion (55–200 CGG repeats) of the FMR1 gene, leading to increased transcription of CGG-repeat containing FMR1 mRNA 16 . It has been shown that premutation CGG- FMR1 mRNA is able to sequester RNA binding proteins and participate in Repeat Associated Non-AUG (RAN) translation 17 – 20 . Because FXTAS and FXPOI patients retain FMRP protein and do not exhibit intellectual disability, the toxic effects of CGG- FMR1 mRNA has been the focus for pathogenic mechanisms. However, whether FMR1 mRNA, without pathogenic CGG expansion, has regulatory roles in normal cellular functions and neurodevelopment remains unknown. Here, we tested the hypothesis that FMR1 is a dual-function mRNA and FMR1 transcript riboregulates metabolic pathways in human neurodevelopment. We show that FMRP knockout (FMRP-KO) neurons retaining FMR1 mRNA expression do not exhibit the same immature morphology and hyperexcitability deficits found in FXS neurons. Although both FMRP-KO and FXS neurons have reduced mitochondrial function, only FXS neurons have elevated glycolysis. Integrative transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses unveiled significant differences between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons. We discovered that mRNA and protein levels of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA), a key glycolytic enzyme, are upregulated in FXS, but not in FMRP-KO, neurons. The FMR1 transcript binds RNA-binding protein insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA binding protein 2 (IGF2BP2) and inhibits IGF2BP2 binding to LDHA mRNA. The absence of FMR1 transcript in FXS neurons leads to increased binding of LDHA mRNA by IGF2BP2, resulting in elevated LDHA mRNA stability. Finally, exogenous FMR1 transcript alone reduces glycolysis and partially rescues morphological and electrophysiological deficits of FXS neurons. Our data reveals a non-coding function for FMR1 in neurodevelopment through riboregulation of another RNA binding protein and FMR1 transcript alone is sufficient to rescue certain neuronal deficits in FXS. RESULTS FMRP-KO neurons with FMR1 transcript expression exhibit distinct morphological and electrophysiological phenotypes from FXS neurons. We have previously generated three isogenic FMRP-KO (KO) human pluripotent stem cells (hPSC) lines by deleting 7-bases from the exon 3 of the FMR1 gene, yielding hPSC lines expressing mutant FMR1 (Δ FMR1 ) mRNA but not FMRP protein 21 . FXS neurons display impaired morphological development and hyperexcitability 15 , 22 . To investigate potential functions of FMR1 mRNA in the absence of FMRP in human neurodevelopment, we differentiated three FMRP-KO hPSC lines (express FMR1 only, no FMRP), three FXS patient-derived iPSC lines (no FMR1 or FMRP), and five healthy control hPSC lines (express both FMR1 and FMRP) into dorsal forebrain excitatory neurons using our established methods 15 , 22 ( Figure 1A and Table S1 ). At 1-week of differentiation, FXS neurons display decreased dendritic length, small although not significant reduction in number of branches, and no significant change in number processes and total body area, compared to healthy controls (CTRL)( Figures 1A – 1F ), which is consistent with our published observations 22 and literature 23 – 25 . Interestingly, FMRP-KO neurons showed no significant difference in morphology ( Figures 1G – 1K ), when compared to their respective isogenic controls (ISO-CTRL). To assess electrophysiological activity of FMRP-KO and FXS neurons, we performed calcium imaging analyses of neurons transduced with lentivirus expressing a genetic calcium sensor (LV-Syn1-GCaMP7f) ( Figure 1L ). At 3-weeks of differentiation through NGN2 induction, FXS neurons ( Figure 1N ) but not KO ( Figure 1O ) neurons display increased activities (fraction of active frames) compared to controls. In addition, FXS neurons ( Figure 1P ), but not KO neurons ( Figure 1Q ), exhibited decreased Synchronous activity compared to controls. Therefore, the presence of FMR1 transcript alone may have regulatory roles that are important for morphological and electrophysiological development of human neurons. FMRP-KO neurons with FMR1 transcript expression have a different transcriptomic profile from FXS neurons. To investigate the mechanism underlying the non-coding function of FMR1 transcript in human neurons, we performed transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics of CTRL, FXS, and FMRP-KO neurons at 3-weeks of NGN2 induced differentiation ( Figure 2A ). Principal component analysis (PCA) on the differential expressed genes (DEGs) showed a clear separation of the FXS neurons from the CTRL and FMRP-KO neurons, whereas the FMRP-KO neurons clustered with the ISO-CTRL neurons ( Figure 2B ), which is confirmed by hierarchical clustering of the DEGs ( Figure 2C ). Differential expression analysis (EBseq, adj p-value < 0.05, FC > 1.2) revealed major differences between the FXS and KO group (797 DEGs) with a minor change in FMRP-KO neurons compared to their isogenic controls (11 DEGs) ( Figure 2D – 2E and Table S2 ). A comparison with human 15 , 21 , 26 , 27 and mouse 26 , 28 , 29 FMRP target datasets shows that a significant proportion of DEGs are predicted FMRP targets, but with greater overlap with human than mouse FMRP targets ( Figure 2F , Figure S1A , and Table S3 ). Although transcriptomics showed mild reduction of FMR1 transcript levels in KO neurons ( Table S3 ), quantitative single molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) of FMR1 transcript showed significantly reduced FMR1 puncta in FXS, but not in KO, MAP2+ neurons compared to CTRL neurons ( Figure S1B – D ). Gene ontology (GO) analysis of DEGs showed that top biological processes are related to mitochondrial electron transport, energy derivation of organic compounds, and translation in FXS vs KO neurons ( Figure 2G and Table S2 ). We also examined the KEGG and Reactome pathways and noticed overrepresentation of terms related to organelle biogenesis, cell adhesion molecules, and motor proteins ( Figures S1E – 1F ) in FXS vs KO. Additionally, cellular component and molecular function enrichments revealed terms related to cellular respiratory chain complex IV and cytochrome C oxidase activity ( Figure S1G ) in FXS vs KO. On the other hand, the top enriched terms between FXS vs CTRL are DNA replication, chromosome, and transcription ( Figure 2G and Figure S1E – G ). Comparison to published transcriptomic data sets 23 , 26 , 30 showed a greater overlap between our DEGs with those in other FXS iPSC-derived neuron and organoids than those in human fetal tissue ( Figure S1H ). Overall, transcriptomic analyses suggest that the presence of FMR1 transcript alone may attenuate metabolic deficits observed in FXS neurons. FMRP-KO neurons and FXS neurons have distinct proteomic profiles. Since FMRP is known to regulate protein translation, we assessed differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) among CTRL, FXS, and FMRP-KO neurons. In contrast to transcriptomic data ( Figure 2B ), all three groups were well separated ( Figure 3A ), which was also evident in the hierarchical clustering and heatmap visualization ( Figure 3B ). Using t-test on log2 transformed proteomic data (p-value < 0.05, FC > 1.2) we again identified the greatest difference was between the FXS and KO group (787 DEPs) ( Figures 3C – 3D and Table S4 ). Interestingly, the KO vs CTRL group had 97 DEPs that were mainly downregulated in contrast to the 127 DEPs between FXS vs CTRL that were mainly upregulated ( Figures 3C – 3D and Table S4 ). Our DEPs overlapped more extensively with FMRP targets identified in human datasets than with those identified in mouse datasets ( Figure 3E , Figure S2A , and Table S5 ). GO analysis revealed significant overrepresentation of terms related to mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport, aerobic electron transport chain, and cellular respiration in both FXS vs KO and FXS vs CTRL comparisons ( Figure 3F ), suggesting overlapping functions of FMR1 transcript and FMRP protein. However, while top enriched KEGG pathways in FXS vs CTRL are oxidative phosphorylation, reactive oxygen species, the top pathways in FXS vs KO are related to neurodegenerative diseases such as ALS, HTT, prion, and Parkinson’s disease, ( Figure S2B ). Although the Reactome database displays shared terms such as aerobic electron transport chain between FXS vs KO and FXS vs CTRL, complex I biogenesis only in FXS vs KO and collagen degradation only in FXS vs CTRL ( Figure S2C ). Moreover, FXS vs KO comparison has overrepresentation of the terms related to respiratory chain complex I, mitochondrial membrane, ribosomal subunit, and NADH dehydrogenase activity ( Figure S2D ), while most DEPs between KO vs CTRL are related to RNA binding, processing, and protein translations ( Figures S2B – S2D ). Together, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses demonstrate substantial differences in metabolic pathways between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons, supporting FMRP-independent functions of FMR1 transcript. Multiomics integration reveals proteomic changes as the major source of differences between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons. Interestingly, there was a minimal overlap between DEGs and DEPs ( Figures S2E and Table S6 ). Since analysis with or without CTRL2 yielded similar results (5 DEMs including CTRL2 vs 15 DEMs removing CTRL2), we performed downstream analysis without CTRL2. FXS neurons are metabolically different from CTRL and KO neurons, but the KO neurons are more similar to ISO-CTRL neurons. On the other hand, DEMs unique to the FXS vs CTRL comparison were primarily associated with purine metabolism and nucleotide metabolism pathways ( Figure S3E ). title: A cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas reveals intra- and intercellular signaling in Alzheimer's disease
abstract:
Summary Alzheimer’s disease (AD) arises from pathological interactions among diverse brain cell types, but cell-specific proteomic changes remain underexplored. Here, we present deep proteomic profiling of sorted or proximity-labeled brain cells from AD mouse models (5xFAD and App NL-G-F ) at multiple ages, quantifying 13,411 proteins in microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and neurons, with additional spatial information. We identified 3,028 differentially abundant proteins, most of which were absent in bulk proteomic dataset and constructed cell type-specific networks to define functional modules and hub proteins. Comparison with transcriptomic data revealed that ~30% of proteomic changes are RNA-discordant. Further analyses uncovered cross-cell type signaling proteins conserved in human AD brains, such as pleiotrophin (Ptn), which is transcriptionally enriched in astrocytes but accumulates in microglia. Importantly, recombinant PTN activates induced microglia-like (iMG) human cells. Thus, these findings provide a comprehensive cell type-resolved proteomic atlas of AD models, highlighting novel intra- and intercellular signaling events.

eTOC Blurb Using cell type-resolved and spatial proteomics, Zhang et al. map age-dependent protein alterations across Alzheimer’s disease mouse models. Integrative analyses reveal cell-specific networks, plaque-associated responses, and intra- and intercellular signaling, highlighting the contribution of astrocyte-derived pleiotrophin (PTN) to microglial activation.

Introduction Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide 1 , but the molecular mechanisms underlying its cellular heterogeneity are incompletely understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing has substantially advanced AD research by uncovering disease-associated cell subtypes and cellular mechanisms 2 – 6 . RNA-level changes do not capture the full extent of protein-level alterations, particularly in brain tissue composed of postmitotic neurons 7 – 10 . Mass spectrometry (MS) has enabled extensive bulk proteome profiling of AD brain tissue, revealing large-scale protein alterations that appear to be enriched in distinct brain cell types 11 – 13 . However, direct cell type-specific proteomic studies in Alzheimer’s disease remain limited. Proteomic profiling of distinct brain cell types is challenging due to difficulties in isolating specific cell types and limited protein yield from small populations 12 , 14 . To overcome these challenges, several strategies have been developed, including laser capture microdissection (LCM) 15 – 17 , fluorescence- or magnetic-activated cell sorting (FACS or MACS) 18 , translational labeling methods such as BONCAT 19 , and proximity labeling approaches such as TurboID 20 or antibody-mediated biotinylation 21 to capture cell type-specific proteomes. For instance, an early proteomic study employing MACS-MS achieved high proteome coverage of different brain cell types in mouse brain 18 . Compared with MACS, FACS provides higher purity and better resolution, particularly for microglial populations 14 . Alternatively, TurboID-based biotin labeling enabled in vivo neuronal proteome profiling through adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated expression 22 or by Cre-lox transgenic mice 23 , whereas antibody-mediated biotinylation also allowed in situ cell type-specific proteome analysis in mouse brain 24 . The mouse brain is composed of approximately 46% neurons, 20% oligodendrocytes and oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPC), 15% vascular cells, 12% astrocytes, 4% immune cells (mainly microglia), and 3% other cell types 25 . Despite their low abundance, microglia are particularly enriched for the expression of AD risk genes 26 . Distinct microglial subtypes are proposed by markers such as CD63 and CD74, reflecting functional reprogramming relevant to pathogenesis 27 , 28 . But microglial subtype-specific proteomic alterations are largely masked in current bulk tissue analyses. Advancing single-cell-type proteomics is critical for elucidating the molecular pathways that govern cell-specific responses in Alzheimer’s disease. In this study, we generated a cell type-resolved proteomic atlas of two commonly used AD mouse models. Using FACS-sorted microglia (three subtypes), astrocytes, and OPC, along with AAV-based neuronal labeling, we profiled 13,411 proteins at multiple ages in 5xFAD and App NL-G-F mice. We also compared our proteomics data with the results from single cell RNA-sequencing of 5xFAD brain tissue. Hundreds of differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) per cell type were identified, revealing cell type-specific pathways, RNA-protein discordance, and conserved intercellular signaling between mouse and human datasets. Pleiotrophin (Ptn) was identified as a candidate mediator of astrocyte-microglia communication. Finally, the cell type-resolved findings were further supported by LCM-based proteomics and spatial transcriptomic analyses, providing additional spatial context for disease-associated proteomic changes. This atlas highlights AD-related cellular heterogeneity and cell-cell interactions and is available at https://penglab.shinyapps.io/pannda . Results Cell type-resolved proteomics of brain cell types in AD mouse models We developed a cell type-resolved proteomic platform that combined FACS or TurboID-based proximity labeling and 18-plex tandem-mass-tag (TMT) conjugation, extensive two-dimensional liquid chromatography, and tandem mass spectrometry (LC/LC-MS/MS) 29 – 31 ( Figure 1A , Figure S1 ). This strategy enabled systematic profiling of four major brain cell types in two AD mouse models: APP transgenic 5xFAD (FAD) overexpressing human APP and PSEN1 genes with five disease mutations 32 ; and App NL-G-F (NLGF) carrying a humanized App knock-in allele with three pathogenic mutations, resulting in production of humanized Aβ without APP overexpression 33 . The analyzed cell types included three microglial subtypes (MG1-MG3) using Cd11b/Cd63/Cd74 antibody combinations guided by scRNA-seq analysis ( Figure S2 ), as well as astrocytes (AS: ACSA2 + ) and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPC: O4 + ) by FACS ( Figure S3A – D ). Neurons, which could not be efficiently isolated by FACS, were analyzed by AAV-TurboID proximity labeling 22 . It should be mentioned that the O4 antibody recognizes sulfatide expressed in oligodendrocyte lineage cells transitioning from OPC to immature oligodendrocytes 34 ; in this study, we use “OPC” thereafter to refer to this O4 + population. We generally analyzed two mouse models and wild-type (WT) controls at different ages, with approximately six mice per age group, totaling 288 samples. The proteomic analysis was enhanced by a microgram-scale MS workflow 35 and JUMP hybrid database searching method 36 , quantifying 8,220 proteins in MG1, 9,179 in MG2, 9,821 in MG3, 7,947 in AS, 5,520 in OPC, and 10,950 in neurons, totaling 13,411 proteins with 3,028 altered ( Figure 1B and Table S1 , details in the following sections). As expected, Aβ peptides were detected in these cell types from both FAD and NLGF models ( Figure 1C ). Principal component analysis (PCA) further revealed distinct proteomic profiles among cell types, with three microglia subtypes clustering closely ( Figure 1D ). To further verify the analyzed cell type-resolved proteomes, the results were compared to cell-type specific transcriptomes 37 used to define marker genes ( Figure 1E ). Examination of protein levels for the top 30 markers showed clear and consistent cell type enrichment ( Figure 1F and Table S1 ). For example, the microglial marker Itgax (Cd11c) was detected in three MG subtypes relative to other major cell types; the astrocytic phagocytic receptor Megf10 38 was enriched in AS; the oligodendrocyte lineage transcription factor Olig2 39 in OPC; and the postsynaptic scaffold protein Shank2 40 in neurons ( Figure 1G ). Together, these results demonstrate that this cell type-resolved proteomic platform enabled deep profiling of major brain cell populations in AD mouse models. Proteomic alterations in three microglial subtypes We profiled three MG subtypes at 4, 8, and 16 months of age in the WT, FAD and NLGF mice ( Table S2 ). In FACS, the combination of antibody selections against Cd11b (an integrin subunit encoded by Itgam, a microglial marker) 27 , 28 , Cd63 (a tetraspanin associated with endosomal/lysosomal activity) 27 , 28 , and Cd74 (an MHC class II subunit indicative of immune activation) 5 enabled the separation of three microglial populations: MG1: Cd11b + /Cd63 − /Cd74 − ; MG2: Cd11b + /Cd63 − /Cd74 + ; MG3: Cd11b + /Cd63 + ( Figure 2A ). Moreover, comparative proteomic analyses identified a subset of proteins uniquely enriched within each subtype, with the top 15 proteins shown in MG1 (such as Cyba and Cx3cr1), MG2 (Ap1b1 and Plcb2), and MG3 (Gpnmb and Tbxas1) that exhibited strong correlations with the markers Cd11b, Cd74, and Cd63, respectively ( Figure 2B – E and Table S2 ). Based on these subtype markers, MG1 appears to maintain a homeostatic phenotype, while MG2 and MG3 may display responsive and activated states. Consistent with microglia activation in AD, FACS analysis revealed age- and genotype-dependent increases in MG populations in the AD models compared with the controls ( Figure S3E and Figure S4A ). To examine relationships among the three MG subtypes, we performed Pearson correlation analyses using the proteome datasets across ages and genotypes. The MG2-MG3 comparison showed the highest correlation, followed by MG2-MG1 and MG3-MG1, implicating MG3 as the most activated state, MG1 as homeostatic, and MG2 as intermediate ( Figure S4B ). In addition, correlations of the same subtypes between AD model mice (e.g., MG3 in FAD versus MG3 in NLGF) increased with age, reflecting age-dependent microglial activation ( Figure S4C ). To evaluate proteomic alterations within each MG subtype, we performed differentially abundant protein analysis using stringent cutoffs (FAD or NLGF versus WT; false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05, |log 2 FC-z| > 2; Figure 2F and Table S2 ) and focused on consistent DAP changes observed in both AD models ( Figure 2G , Figure S4D , E ). We identified 456, 540 and 696 consistent DAPs in MG1, MG2, and MG3, respectively ( Figure 2H ). MG3 was the most responsive subtype, with 405 unique DAPs, followed by MG2 (285 DAPs) and MG1 (197 DAPs), while 77 DAPs were shared across all subtypes ( Figure 2I ). The genotype-shared DAPs within each microglial subtype were further analyzed for enriched pathways ( Figure 2J and Table S2 ). We next performed Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) 41 on DAPs to delineate their temporal trajectories during disease progression at 4, 8, and 16 months. Four clusters (C1-C4) were identified within each MG subtype ( Figure 2K and Figure S4F ). Functional enrichment revealed distinct protein-protein interaction (PPI) modules in each cluster ( Figure 2L and Figure S4G ). In the case of MG3, C1 (282 proteins) exhibited an early and sustained increase, including proteins such as Gpnmb, Cd68, and Mif; C2 (99 proteins) showed a late increase, featuring inflammatory response proteins such as Ptn, Trem2, and Cd14; C3 (235 proteins) displayed an early decrease, including cell adhesion proteins such as Itga1, Lama1, and Nid1; and C4 (78 proteins) showed a late decrease, encompassing proteins such as Aqp1, Lgals3, and Prdm1. Thus, these results indicate that amyloidosis does not induce a uniform microglial response but instead engages distinct microglial populations with specialized patterns. In addition, we mapped transcriptional regulators and AD risk genes within the MG proteomes and DAPs. A total of 553 transcriptional regulators were detected from the curated database 42 , 31 of which showed consistent changes in both AD mouse models, including Spi1, Ikzf3, and Pparg ( Figure S4H ). Moreover, out of 167 AD risk genes 11 , 89 gene-encoded proteins were identified in MG, 24 of which were consistently altered among microglial subtypes in both mouse models, including Tmem106b, Clu, Trem2, and Apoe ( Figure S4I ). We then mapped our microglial subtype proteomic data to a published bulk RNA-seq dataset stratified by TREM2 expression level 43 ( Figure S4J ). TREM2-associated upregulated transcriptional programs were preferentially represented in MG3, whereas TREM2-associated downregulated programs were preferentially represented in MG1 ( Figure S4K , L ), consistent with the increase in TREM2 protein levels from MG1 to MG3 subtypes. After profiling the FACS-isolated MG subtypes, we used LCM-MS to examine their spatial relationships with amyloid plaques in FAD mice ( Figure S5A ). Plaque-proximal and plaque-distal microglia (MG P and MG D , respectively) were isolated from FAD mice ( Figure S5B ), together with microglia from WT mice (MG WT ). MS analysis identified a total of 6,099 proteins in these samples ( Table S2 ). As expected, Aβ levels were significantly higher in MG P than in MG D ( Figure S5C ). PCA further revealed distinct proteomic profiles among MG WT , MG P and MG D ( Figure S5D ). The specificity of the LCM-isolated MG proteomes was further supported by the enrichment of canonical microglial markers relative to whole-brain lysate ( Figure S5E ). Differential abundance analysis comparing MG P and MG D identified plaque-associated proteomic changes ( Figure S5F ), including 105 proteins showing concordant genotype- and plaque-associated enrichment ( Figure S5G ). Mapping these plaque-associated proteins back to the FACS-defined MG subtypes revealed significantly greater enrichment in MG2 and MG3 than in MG1, with the strongest enrichment observed in MG3 ( Figure S5H , I ). Together, these analyses define three proteome-based MG subtypes that exhibit age- and disease-dependent activation, subtype-specific molecular signatures, spatial relationships to amyloid pathology, and distinct regulatory profiles underlying their diverse responses to amyloid pathology. Proteomic remodeling of brain cells beyond microglia In astrocytes, we applied a similar proteomic workflow to identify astrocyte-specific marker proteins, as well as DAPs in the FAD and NLGF models ( Figure 3A , B and Table S3 ). Some proteins, including Gja1, Mlc1 and Agt, were robustly correlated with the ACSA2 sorting marker encoded by the Atp1b2 gene 44 ( Figure 3B ).
