title: Motor system inefficiency as an activity-dependent amplifier of fatigue in multiple sclerosis
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) fatigue is clinically obvious but mechanistically elusive. It can dominate daily life despite modest disability, stable structural MRI findings, or preserved strength on examination. This Update reviews evidence that an important component of MS fatigue may arise from increased motor-control cost and incomplete recovery after activity. Voluntary muscle activation studies show that some people with MS have incomplete central access to available force, particularly after exertion. Functional imaging studies indicate that apparently preserved movement often depends on expanded recruitment of premotor, cerebellar, striatal, prefrontal, and cingulo-insular systems involved in motor compensation, effort allocation, and body-state monitoring. Metabolic and pathological studies further indicate energetic vulnerability in demyelinated and chronically injured networks, providing biological plausibility for impaired restoration after repeated signalling demands. These findings support a systems framework in which expanded motor-control recruitment may be compensatory when it preserves performance and remains flexible and recoverable, but may amplify MS fatigue when ordinary activity begins from incompletely restored physiological reserve. We outline testable predictions for identifying a motor-cost fatigue phenotype and for designing repeated-measures studies of activity-related fatigue in MS.

title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism)
authors: Van De Water AL et al.
abstract: The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants (48 ASD [13 female], 90 NT [25 female]) viewed six videos (5-20 minutes). Brain activity was measured using functional magnetic resonance imaging. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogenous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.

title: Neotenic expansion of adult-born dentate granule cells reconfigures GABAergic inhibition to enhance social memory consolidation
abstract: Immature adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) show heightened synaptic and structural plasticity and preferentially contribute to hippocampal-dependent memory. Protracted maturation (neoteny) of abDGCs in higher mammals is posited to offset the decline in adult hippocampal neurogenesis by supporting increased plasticity. Here we found that selective, synchronous expansion of 4-week-old immature, but not 8-week-old mature, mouse abDGCs promotes recruitment of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons (INs) in hippocampal CA3 and CA2, increases feed-forward inhibition, decreases social memory interference and enhances social memory consolidation. In vivo local field potential recordings in dorsal CA1 and CA2 revealed increased baseline power, amplitude and duration of sharp-wave ripples, as well as enhanced rate modulation by social experience. Inhibitory neuron-targeted chemogenetic manipulations implicate dorsal CA3 and CA2 INs, including parvalbumin-expressing INs, as necessary and sufficient for social memory consolidation following and sans neotenic expansion of abDGCs, respectively. Our findings suggest that neoteny of abDGCs supports cognition by increasing feed-forward inhibition in DG-CA3 and DG-CA2 and promoting network oscillations that underlie memory consolidation.

title: The neural mechanisms of fast versus slow decision-making
abstract: One hallmark of intelligent behavior is the ability to optimize how much time is devoted to decisions. Yet the principles governing decision timing remain unclear. Here, we developed a novel paradigm for directly comparing decision-making between mice and humans. This approach allowed us to combine widefield and 2-photon imaging in the mouse frontal cortex with optogenetic inhibition to examine the underlying mechanisms. We found that history-dependent refinement of sequences in the medial frontal cortex (MFC), versus a thresholding mechanism in the lateral frontal cortex (LFC), provides a unified logic for decision strategy on a trial-by-trial basis. Notably, behavioral performance and strategy were profoundly disrupted by optogenetic inhibition of the MFC compared with that of the LFC, revealing a dominant cognitive role for MFC in decision selection and timing. These dynamics reflect reinforcement-learning updates that explain timing variability better than sensory evidence. Our findings provide a computational framework that unifies voluntary decision-making across species.

title: Cortical and meningeal neuroimmune interactions contribute to the generation of migraine headaches
abstract: Migraine is a prevalent disorder that ranks as the second leading cause of disability among all diseases. Recent advancements have significantly enhanced our comprehension of its underlying pathophysiology. Growing evidence highlights complex neuroimmune signaling networks-particularly interactions between meningeal nociceptors and resident immune cells-as key contributors to headache generation. The clinical success of anti-calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antibodies underscores the importance of intercellular communication between the dural nociceptive nerves and adjacent resident immune cells such as macrophages in migraine headache. Notably, the intercellular inflammatory interplay is not confined to the meninges. Disturbances within the brain parenchyma potentially act as initiating triggers, as suggested by the presence of aura and premonitory symptoms preceding the headache. Recent experimental discoveries indicate that neuronal stress triggers an inflammatory signaling cascade that, through interactions with astrocytes and microglia, propagates to the meninges, ultimately inducing meningeal neurogenic inflammation and headache. This model is supported by converging experimental evidence and human imaging studies employing PET and quantitative MRI, which document the presence of changes compatible with inflammatory activity within the brain parenchyma and overlying meninges of patients with migraine with aura. Genetic studies identifying several inflammation-related genes and pathways as risk factors for migraine further corroborate this concept. Furthermore, cell-specific transcriptomic analyses of mouse brains have revealed astrocyte-selective activation of nuclear factor kappa B -regulated inflammatory transcriptional pathways after cortical spreading depolarization, the neurophysiological correlate of migraine aura. Owing to their extensive interface with the cerebrospinal fluid, astrocytes are uniquely positioned to release inflammatory mediators to activate meningeal nociceptors and immune cells. Insights from pain research suggest that neuroimmune interactions may be responsible for the widespread parenchymal increases in 18 kDa translocator protein (TSPO) PET signals observed in migraine with aura patients. This discovery also identifies TSPO as a potential player in migraine pathophysiology and novel drug target. In this review, by integrating cellular and molecular findings from peripheral pain and inflammation research, we examine the dynamic interactions between neurons and glia, as well as between meningeal nociceptors and immune cells in the context of migraine headache. This perspective provides a conceptual framework for understanding how nociceptors and glial cells coordinate to signal non-homeostatic brain states-initiating protective, tightly regulated responses without progressing to overt neuroinflammatory disease and provides novel insight into the findings of PET studies involving TSPO.

title: Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds
abstract: Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons. Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons. Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH 4 Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it. Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons. Significance Statement  Foods typically present a complex mixture of tastes. However, understanding how the nervous system processes gustatory signals has traditionally relied on investigations that analyze responses to individual tastes. Our study investigates how mixtures of naturally occurring food tastes activate sensory neurons and how emergent signals arise when combinations of gustatory stimuli excite taste buds. Using in vivo imaging of primary gustatory neurons in mice, we show that sour stimuli suppress neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty tastes. The findings reveal an early, peripheral stage of neural computation that helps explain how complex flavors are encoded.

title: Distinct prelimbic microcircuits control sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain
abstract: The microcircuit mechanisms underlying deactivation and altered output of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a common feature of several chronic pain conditions, are poorly understood. Here, using unbiased in vivo longitudinal multiphoton imaging in the mouse prelimbic cortex (PrL), we show that nerve injury induces sensitization of all classes of GABAergic interneurons and a phenotypic switch from unimodal to polymodal responses. Through circuit interrogation, we identified functions for caudal geminal eminence-derived Prox1 +  interneurons and revealed that distinct classes of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in the PrL have different functions in promoting neuropathic pain. In addition, we show that the sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain engaged two distinct microcircuits, PV + -Rbp4 +  neurons and Prox1 + -Cux2 + /Ntsr1 +  neurons, respectively, to control distinct projection outputs. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for how mPFC guides actions to avoid or overcome pain and how prefrontal deactivation exacerbates neuropathic pain.

title: Spectral envelopes of facial movements predict intention, cortical representations, and neural prosthetic control
abstract: Animals use coordinated facial movements to sample the environment, ingest nutrients, and communicate. Rodents produce rhythmic facial movements during spontaneous behavior and cognitive tasks. Measuring these movements precisely and linking them to neural activity remains challenging. We introduce face-rhythm, an unsupervised pipeline that combines markerless point-tracking, spectral analysis, and non-negative tensor decomposition to reduce facial video to a small set of interpretable components. Applied to videos of mice performing Pavlovian conditioning, a brain-machine interface task, and free behavior, face-rhythm recovers whisking, sniffing, licking, and subtler motifs. The resulting components are consistent across animals, decode task variables and internal states, and explain cortical activity with a low-rank representation. Facial motor cortex neurons are predicted well by a phase-invariant spectral transformation of movements above roughly 0.5 Hz, whereas slower movements retain a phase-variant representation. Face-rhythm compares favorably with deep-learning tracking and embedding methods while yielding an interpretable description of facial behavior.

title: D4Z4 methylation and genetic modifiers influence severity in a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy kindred
abstract: One of the earliest systematic descriptions of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) involved a six-generation kindred tracing back to a single ancestor born in 1775 in Lancashire, England, who later emigrated to Utah in the 1850s. First published in 1950, members of this kindred (K1462) have been followed clinically for decades, with DNA samples archived since the 1980s. Despite sharing the same 5-repeat unit (5RU) D4Z4 contraction on a permissive 4qA haplotype, affected individuals show marked variability in age at onset, clinical severity and disease progression, including within sibships. With long-term follow-up and a shared founder mutation, K1462 is a unique resource for identifying modifiers of disease expression in FSHD. We reintroduce K1462, with enrolment extending into the ninth generation, and perform genomic analysis using modern approaches. Inheritance of the 5RU founder allele was confirmed in 139 individuals, and nanopore Cas9-targeted sequencing determined CpG methylation across the contracted D4Z4 array at base-pair resolution. The 5RU allele showed complete penetrance; however, clinical severity and progression varied widely among affected individuals. Longitudinal analysis of blood-derived genomic DNA demonstrated high stability of D4Z4 CpG methylation within individuals, including samples collected up to 38 years apart, indicating long-term maintenance of the epigenetic state. In contrast, D4Z4 methylation levels differed substantially between individuals and showed a strong inverse correlation with clinical severity. Differences in D4Z4 methylation were observed both within and between families, with a modest but consistent parent-of-origin effect. Whole-genome sequencing analysis found no evidence that rare variants in known FSHD2 genes explained this variability. To assess the contribution of common genetic variation, we performed a pedigree-based genome-wide association analysis of D4Z4 methylation levels, identifying a single genome-wide significant locus on chromosome 15. Variants spanning the promoter and 5' region of HDGFL3, which encodes a PWWP domain chromatin-interacting protein, were associated with increased D4Z4 methylation after accounting for parental transmission, supporting a role for common-variant modulation of methylation in FSHD. These results support a model in which D4Z4 methylation is established through transmission-associated epigenetic resetting, stably maintained within individuals, and quantitatively modified by inherited genetic variation. Together, these findings demonstrate that D4Z4 methylation is a stable, individual-level epigenetic feature that varies across a multigenerational pedigree in a manner that correlates with clinical severity, confirming D4Z4 methylation as a quantitative biomarker and genetically modifiable contributor to disease severity in FSHD.

title: Chronic and subacute phenylalanine effects on brain metabolism in adults with phenylketonuria
abstract: Phenylketonuria (PKU) leads to chronic cerebral exposure to elevated phenylalanine (Phe) despite lifelong dietary treatment, yet the neurometabolic consequences in adulthood remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent alterations in brain metabolism and whether these metabolites respond dynamically to subacute Phe fluctuations. Adults with early-treated PKU (n=30) and healthy controls (n=59) underwent proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS), structural and functional brain MRI to evaluate white matter lesion load (T2-weighted images) and cerebral blood flow (arterial spin labeling), as well as cognitive assessments. Patients additionally participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover intervention with four weeks of oral Phe loading to evaluate subacute metabolic responsiveness. Absolute metabolite concentrations were quantified in predominantly white matter tissue, and associations between blood and brain Phe, white matter lesion load, cerebral blood flow, and cognitive performance were examined. At baseline, patients exhibited higher brain Phe and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) levels, alongside reduced myo-inositol, N-acetylaspartylglutamate (NAAG), and total creatine/phosphocreatine compared with controls. Patients with white matter lesions did not differ in blood and brain metabolites from those without. Four weeks of oral Phe loading increased brain Phe and produced a reversible decrease in myo-inositol, whereas NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds remained unchanged. Blood and brain Phe concentrations were strongly correlated (r=0.83, p<0.001), and their ratio was subject-dependent. No significant associations were observed between metabolite concentrations and regional cerebral blood flow or cognitive performance after correction for multiple comparisons. Adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent neurometabolic alterations involving neuronal-glial metabolism, energy buffering, and astrocytic osmolyte regulation. The findings support a trait-state framework, with stable alterations in NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds reflecting long-standing metabolic changes, superimposed on a dynamically Phe-sensitive astrocytic response indexed by myo-inositol. The absence of strong associations with cerebral perfusion or cognition suggests that these alterations represent upstream biological processes not captured by macroscopic imaging or behavioral measures.

title: Selective and spatially biased activity remodeling following adult-onset sensory loss
abstract: Cross-modal brain plasticity after sensory loss allows an organism to utilize the remaining senses to guide behavior. Two distinct mechanisms support such adaptation: cross-modal recruitment and compensatory plasticity. Cross-modal recruitment refers to the deprived sensory areas gaining responsiveness to the spared senses, while compensatory plasticity indicates enhanced functionality of the spared sensory areas. Widespread synaptic and circuit-level plasticity has been reported to support such cross-modal plasticity. Here we combined whole-brain clearing, light-sheet imaging, and activity labeling using a cFosTRAP2 mouse line to examine the spatial distribution of highly active cells across brain areas following acute sensory manipulations in adult mice of both sexes. Adult-onset vision loss led to an initial decrease in the density of activity-labeled cells in visual areas, including the primary visual cortex (V1), and a parallel increase in the spared primary auditory (A1) and somatosensory barrel (S1BF) cortices. V1 and some higher-order visual areas (HVAs), but not the visual thalamus, exhibited a partial rebound in activity after a week of vision loss. The activity rebound in visual cortices and the enhanced activity observed in A1 were spatially biased. Passively exposing adult-onset blind mice to sound did not further alter activity levels, except for a decrease in the claustrum. Conversely, adult-onset deafening significantly reduced the activity-labeled cell density in auditory and auditory-related areas without clear signs of compensatory plasticity in the spared areas. Our results indicate that adult cross-modal plasticity is largely observed in sensory cortices with rather specific within-area spatial bias, suggesting selective functional adaptations. Significance Statement  This study examined the spatial profile of how the adult brain adapts when one sense is lost. In mice, vision loss caused brain activity to drop in visual areas followed by partial recovery over time, suggesting gradual recruitment of these areas by non-visual information. In parallel, the brain areas for hearing and touch became more active, a sign of compensation. Activity changes were not widespread but limited mainly to sensory areas with some local spatial bias. In contrast, the same duration of hearing loss produced much less evidence of compensation in the spared sensory areas. These findings suggest that the adult brain can reorganize after sensory loss, but this adaptation is selective and region-specific, implying targeted functional compensation.

title: Concomitant Psychotropic Medication Is Associated with Reduced Outcomes of Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Psychotropic medications are frequently prescribed alongside trauma-focused psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet their impact on treatment response remains uncertain. This study emulated target trials to examine the association between psychotropic co-medication at treatment onset and psychotherapy outcomes in a real-world PTSD cohort.

METHODS: A prospective cohort of 6,125 adults with chronic or delayed-onset PTSD received a standardized 2-8 day trauma-focused psychotherapy program, including daily prolonged exposure and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy, at a Dutch psychotrauma center (2021-2024). Target trial emulation with double machine learning with inverse probability of treatment weighting estimated the effects of specific psychotropic co-medications versus non-use on changes in Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) scores (range, 0-80) from pre-to post-treatment.

RESULTS: Mean CAPS-5 scores improved by 25.7 points (Cohen's d = -2.30). Psychotropic co-medication (n = 1,382) was associated with reduced symptom improvement compared with non-use (model-estimated difference = -2.52 points; relative reduction = -9.4%, 95% CI = -10.0 to -8.9; d = -1.11, E = 10.0). This effect persisted at 6-month follow-up (d = -0.42). Antidepressants overall (d = -0.28; follow-up d = -0.56), amitriptyline (d = -0.51), and mirtazapine (d = -0.29) were consistently associated with poorer outcomes across sensitivity analyses. Similar patterns were observed for anticonvulsants, mood-stabilizing anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, fluoxetine, zolpidem, and zopiclone. Sensitivity analyses and E-values indicated robustness to unmeasured confounding.

CONCLUSION: Several psychotropic co-medications were associated with reduced outcomes of evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD. By identifying this as a potentially modifiable factor, psychotherapy outcomes may be optimized. Trials are warranted to evaluate whether tapering or substituting these agents improves outcomes.

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is often treated with trauma-focused psychotherapy, which includes structured methods such as prolonged exposure and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy. These treatments are highly effective for many people. However, many patients also take psychotropic medications, such as antidepressants or sleeping pills, at the time of therapy. It has been unclear whether these medications change how well psychotherapy works. In this study, we followed more than 6,000 adults with PTSD who all received the same intensive psychotherapy program at a specialized treatment center. We compared the treatment results of patients who were using different medications with those who were not using them. To ensure fair comparisons, we applied advanced statistical methods that take into account many individual differences, such as severity of symptoms, past treatment history, and other health problems. Overall, patients showed large improvements after therapy. However, patients who used certain psychotropic medications (such as some antidepressants, antipsychotics, anti-epileptics, and sleeping medications) experienced less symptom improvement compared to those who did not use these drugs. This difference remained visible even 6 months after treatment ended. These findings suggest that certain medications may reduce the benefits of psychotherapy. More research is needed to understand why this happens, and whether temporarily adjusting medication use before therapy could improve results. Such decisions should always be carefully weighed against the possible risks of medication withdrawal or symptom return.

title: Placebo Effect of Verbal Instructions Coupled with Pharmacological Treatment: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Migraine Patients
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Verbal instructions modulate the expectation concerning a given drug. Knowing that the prescribing clinician is positive and enthusiastic toward the prescribed treatment may lead to positive expectations. We tested whether administering strongly positive verbal instructions together with a pharmacological prescription might trigger a placebo effect in migraine patients.

METHODS: Outpatients (n = 102) were randomly assigned to: (a) an experimental condition: the pharmacological prescription was coupled to strongly positive verbal instructions; (b) a control condition: the prescription was coupled to positive verbal instructions. Subjects were assessed before the prescription (T0), 7 days (T1), 15 days (T2), 1 month (T3), 2 months (T4), and 3 months after it (T5). At each assessment point, Headache Impact Test (HIT-6) and two Numeric Rating Scales (NRSs) were proposed. Kellner's scale of change was administered at T1-T5.

RESULTS: Patients who received strongly positive instructions had no HIT decrease (p = 0.177; η2 = 0.034). Patients who received positive instructions had HIT decrease (p = 0.006; η2 = 0.770). No difference was found between the groups. No significant across timepoints change of expectations was observed in the group who received strongly positive instructions (p = 0.433; η2 = 0.021) or in the group who received positive instructions (p = 0.151; η2 = 0.037). Since the first group had a decrease across timepoints of the score while the second group had a peak at T2, difference between them was statistically significant (p = 0.029; η2 = 0.049).

CONCLUSION: Strongly positive verbal instructions did not produce placebo effect.

Verbal instructions can induce positive expectations and, if coupled to a medication prescription, can positively influence the response to it. We tested whether administering strongly positive instructions together with an antimigraine prescription may influence the response to the medication (the so-called placebo effect) in migraine patients. To test such hypothesis, 102 outpatients were assigned to: (a) an experimental condition in which the antimigraine prescription was coupled to strongly positive verbal instructions; (b) a control condition in which the antimigraine prescription was coupled to positive verbal instructions. Subjects were assessed before the prescription, 7 days, 15 days, 1 month, 2 months, and 3 months after the prescription using specific tools which measure migraine severity and expectations related to the medication prescribed. The results showed that patients who received strongly positive instructions had less expectations than those who received positive instructions. In brief, strongly positive instructions did not produce placebo effect and, consequently, did not produce benefit if told to migraine patients.

title: Can we leverage scalable barrier free single session interventions developed for adolescents (13-18 years) for use in young adults? A mixed methods single arm pilot study in the UK
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Many young adults (YA) experience depression symptoms, yet few access appropriate support. Single session interventions (SSIs) offer brief, evidence-based support and can be delivered online, potentially increasing accessibility. SSIs appear acceptable, useful, and efficacious for adolescents which may extend to YA. However, this has not yet been established. This study aimed to explore whether an SSI developed for adolescents would be acceptable and useful to YA, and to identify opportunities for further adaptation.

METHODS: We used a single-arm pre-post intervention within subjects' design. YA in the UK (age 19-25) completed demographics, outcome measures, a behaviour activation-based SSI and gave feedback about the intervention. Demographics and recruitment source were described, and qualitative feedback was analysed using conventional content analysis. Pre-post changes were analysed using linear mixed effects models.

RESULTS: Two-hundred and thirty-two eligible participants consented, 161 started the SSI, and 73 (45.3%) completed it. Most were recruited through a third-party mental health organisation. Participants were predominately White British, assigned female at birth, and heterosexual. Post-intervention programme feedback scale scores indicated that most YA found the SSI acceptable. Participants highlighted both positive and negative aspects in relation to usability, and value. Analyses indicated significant pre-post changes in hope, hopelessness, and perceived control.

CONCLUSIONS: SSIs developed for adolescents appear acceptable and useful, and may produce short term changes in hope, hopelessness and perceived control. Further adaptations could improve age-appropriateness and suitability for YA. Future research could include intervention codesign with YA, and examine whether SSIs influence short- and longer-term clinical outcomes including depression symptoms.

title: Non-pharmacological augmentation of trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Trauma-focused psychotherapies (TFPs) effectively treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet patients show variable response or discontinue treatment. Numerous augmentation strategies have been developed to address these barriers, but the field lacks a framework that extends beyond mechanistic categories as well as a meta-analytic synthesis of their effects.

OBJECTIVE: To develop a classification framework for non-pharmacological augmentation strategies of first-line TFP for PTSD and to meta-analytically evaluate whether these strategies improve treatment outcomes.

METHOD: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing TFP augmented with a non-pharmacological intervention versus TFP alone or an active control (i.e. sham intervention or dose increase). Eight databases were searched to July 2026. Augmentation strategies were qualitatively categorised. Primary outcomes were PTSD symptom severity and response rate; dropout was a secondary outcome.

RESULTS: Fifty RCTs met inclusion criteria. Their augmentations were categorised within a three-level framework comprising targets, mechanisms, and implementation forms. Of these, 39 trials (40 comparisons;  N  = 2,853) were meta-analysed and showed no significant overall effects (symptom severity:  g  = -0.10,  p  = .062; response:  RR  = 1.04,  p  = .111; dropout:  RR  = 0.94,  p  = .489). One subgroup targeting sleep disturbance showed an add-on effect.

CONCLUSIONS: The present findings suggest that augmenting TFP with non-pharmacological interventions does not necessarily lead to incremental efficacy at the overall level, even though small benefits were observed for sleep-focused strategies. Our three-level framework provides a structured approach for conceptualising this heterogeneous field. The absence of a robust overall effect should not be mistaken for evidence that augmentation cannot be effective.

We meta-analysed 39 RCTs ( N  = 2,853) evaluating augmentation of trauma-focused therapy for PTSD and developed a framework classifying add-ons by target, mechanism, and implementationAugmentation showed no overall benefit for PTSD symptoms, response, or dropout.Sleep-focused add-ons were the exception, suggesting that augmentation may be most effective when matched to a specific treatment barrier rather than applied universally.

title: Recruiting a geographically, ethnically and socioeconomically diverse population of postpartum women into a behavioural weight management intervention trial: an evaluation of strategies used in the Supporting MumS (SMS) randomised controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Engaging women in behavioural weight management interventions in the postpartum period has proved challenging. Previous trials of such interventions have frequently experienced issues with participant recruitment and retention and recruited samples have been skewed towards inclusion of women from white ethnicities and more affluent backgrounds. In this paper, we evaluate strategies used to recruit a geographically, ethnically and socioeconomically diverse sample of postpartum women to the Supporting MumS randomised controlled trial (RCT).

METHODS: Two-arm, parallel group, multi-centre RCT. Recruitment took place in five sites across the United Kingdom (UK), selected with consideration of geographic, ethnic and socioeconomic population diversity. Participants were women (including those who gave birth but who do not identify as women), within 6 weeks to 2 years postpartum, with a Body Mass Index of ≥ 25 kg/m 2 . The range of recruitment strategies employed spanned healthcare settings, community settings and social media. Strategies used to recruit over a 12-month period were recorded, and outcomes including numbers expressing interest, screened and randomised, were assessed by site, ethnicity and Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) data.

RESULTS: Over 12 months, 2457 women expressed an interest, 1227 (49.9%) were screened for eligibility and 892 (36.3%) were randomised. The sample included 33.6% of women from minoritised ethnic groups and 53.5% of women who lived in the two most deprived IMD quintiles. Most participants learnt about the study through social media (45.5%), followed by community groups and settings aimed at parents (26.0%), the Born in Bradford's Better Start (BiBBS) cohort (12.5%), friends/family (7.2%), general community settings (5.3%) and healthcare professionals (5.4%). Success of recruitment strategies varied across sites and participant characteristics.

CONCLUSIONS: An ethnically and socioeconomically diverse sample of postpartum women across the four UK countries was recruited within the planned 12-month timeframe. This was achieved by selection of recruitment sites (considering geographical spread and population characteristics), using a range of strategies and tailoring these to local populations, and iteratively adapting strategies employed based on success.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN16299220 ( https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN16299220 ). Prospectively registered on February 10, 2022.

title: Sustainability of Treatment Success 5 Years after Exposure-Based Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Anxiety Disorders
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Achieving sustainable success in the treatment of anxiety disorders remains a central objective in mental health care. Although research has demonstrated the short-term efficacy of psychotherapy, evidence regarding long-term sustainability is limited. This study examined treatment outcomes 5 years after prediction-error-based exposure therapy.

METHODS: For 355 patients (616 eligible; 58% follow-up rate), newly collected follow-up data on anxiety symptoms and psychosocial functioning were compared to pretreatment, posttreatment, and 6-month follow-up data from a multicenter clinical trial characterized by high treatment fidelity.

RESULTS: Improvements in anxiety symptoms and psychosocial functioning that were evident at posttreatment and 6-month follow-up were largely preserved after 5 years. No significant differences emerged between randomized groups of temporally intensified and non-intensified exposure. From 6 months to 5 years, overall remission rates remained stable, with the majority of patients exhibiting no reliable change in symptom severity. Reliable relapse occurred in 4.9% and reliable new remission in 6.5%. Most patients (63.4%) did not seek additional treatment. Among those who did, depression (64.2%) and anxiety (60.5%) were the most frequently cited reasons, although only a minority (6.0%) sought further treatment exclusively for anxiety. Additional treatment during the follow-up period was associated with higher symptom severity throughout assessments.

CONCLUSION: These findings highlight the sustainability and long-term public health benefits of exposure-based CBT for anxiety disorders. Most patients do not need additional treatments for mental disorders even 5 years after treatment. Nevertheless, further efforts are needed to optimize interventions for those patients who do not achieve remission or experience relapse.

title: From evidence to systems: A roadmap for scaling evidence-based psychological interventions via task-sharing across global contexts
abstract: The care gap for psychological interventions for common mental health conditions remains a global challenge. The scaling up of psychological interventions, often through "task-sharing" (training non-mental health specialist providers in community or routine care settings), has emerged as a promising strategy to expand access globally. Yet few interventions have been scaled sustainably in real-world settings. Using the RE-AIM and WHO Health Systems frameworks, we conducted a multiple-case narrative review inclusive of five case studies to illustrate how evidence-based psychological interventions for common mental health problems have been scaled in diverse contexts (United Kingdom, Europe, South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa) and then, applying a political economy perspective, we synthesized the political, economic, and health system factors that shaped their trajectories. We found that scale is most successful when interventions: (1) leverage trusted workforces with political and institutional support for expanded roles; (2) reduce burdens on patients and providers through simplified and accessible service-delivery models; (3) align with high-priority and politically salient policy agendas; (4) are supported by robust monitoring and information systems that enable accountability and legitimacy; (5) are implemented through partnerships between government, technical, or funding actors; (6) remain adaptive to shifts in political will and contextual conditions; (7) are catalyzed by digital technologies that strengthen training, supervision, quality assurance, and routine outcome monitoring; and (8) are supported by sustained advocacy efforts. These lessons highlight that successfully scaling psychological interventions requires a systems and political framework in research design, implementation and dissemination. We conclude by outlining implications for policy and practice to embed interventions within existing service platforms and governance structures to support equitable, sustainable scale-up; and for implementation science, emphasizing the need for future evaluations to measure reach, adoption, and fidelity-to-function.

title: Time in psychoanalysis
abstract: By recognizing the existence of conservative infantile amnesia, psychoanalysis introduced a new category of temporality: timelessness. The contents thus subjected to amnesia escape the influence of time. This unconscious psychic reality is established to counteract the regressive force emanating from the id, in order to fulfil a function: that of thwarting the tendencies to revert to a prior state, even to the inorganic, which are inherent in every drive, and to prevent the disappearance of libidinal cathexes into a 'traumatic timelessness'. Through the regression of sleep, dream work can use this tendency towards extinction to create new psychic content and regenerate narcissistic and object-related cathexis. The dream is the time machine, the fountain of youth available to human beings. The oscillation between experiences of disappearance and those of regeneration, between an endo-perception of discontinuity characterized by experiences of disappearance and eternity, lies at the origin of the notion of temporality, as well as of many devices designed to create the illusion of continuity. Extinction cannot be represented; it is perceived through the traumatic emotions of terror and anxiety. This is why time can only be embodied by the devices that measure it - that is to say, by a method consisting of retaining that which tends to disappear.

title: Transformations in play. Dyadic work inspired by psychoanalytic infant observation
abstract: The article explores the psychoanalytic foundations of Watch Me Play! (WMP), an applied approach first developed to promote understanding of the needs of babies and young children in care, now more widely used to support parent-child relationships and child development. Watch Me Play! is derived from psychoanalytic infant observation and underpinned by key concepts in child development research such as mind-mindedness, joint attention and contingent responsiveness. The relevance of the central psychoanalytic concepts of attention and time in the thinking of Freud, Bion and Birksted-Breen is illustrated in clinical examples from work with the group for whom the approach was first developed: infants and young children who have experienced abuse, neglect and disrupted attachments, together with their foster carers or adoptive parents.

title: Effects of cognitive behavioral therapy on psychological and physical outcomes in adults with rheumatoid arthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
Background Pain and functional limitations associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can substantially impair patients’ psychological and physical well-being. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may alleviate psychological and physical symptoms in patients with RA by modifying maladaptive cognitions and behaviors and promoting adaptive coping with the disease. However, the effect of CBT in RA patients has not been systematically established. Methods PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Embase, and Web of Science were systematically searched from database inception to July 9, 2026, for relevant studies. Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were independently performed by two reviewers. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or adjudicated by a third reviewer. Meta-analyses were primarily implemented through random-effects models. Effect estimates were presented as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Twelve RCTs involving 1,538 participants with RA were incorporated. CBT was associated with lower levels of depression (SMD = −0.35, 95% CI: −0.55 to −0.14, low-certainty evidence), anxiety (SMD = −0.20, 95% CI: −0.32 to −0.08, moderate-certainty evidence), and fatigue (SMD = −0.44, 95% CI: −0.66 to −0.22, low-certainty evidence). At the 6-month follow-up, the pooled SMDs were −0.42 (95% CI, −0.63 to −0.20) for depression and −0.22 (95% CI, −0.43 to −0.01) for anxiety, based on six RCTs with available follow-up data. For sleep, the pooled estimate favored CBT, although this finding was based on only two studies and was supported by very-low-certainty evidence. No statistically significant between-group differences were noted for pain, physical function, or quality-of-life (QoL). Substantial heterogeneity was observed for depression and fatigue, and the 95% prediction intervals crossed the line of no effect for both outcomes. Exploratory subgroup analyses by CBT delivery format revealed no significant differences between subgroups. Conclusion The pooled estimates suggested that CBT may be associated with lower levels of fatigue, anxiety, and depression in patients with RA. However, substantial heterogeneity, prediction intervals crossing the line of no effect, and low certainty of evidence limit the reliability of these outcomes. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261470674 , CRD420261470674.

1 Introduction Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder marked by synovial inflammation that can result in joint pain, structural damage, and functional limitations. The Global Burden of Disease study indicates that RA is still an important public health concern, with its prevalence projected to continue increasing ( 1 ). Persistent joint pain, functional limitations, and joint deformities can substantially impair the psychological and physical well-being of RA patients, further contributing to the overall burden of the disease. Depression and anxiety are among the most prevalent psychological comorbidities in RA patients. Evidence suggests that approximately 16.8% of patients with RA have major depressive disorder, and their risk of developing new-onset depression is about 47% higher than that of individuals without RA ( 2 , 3 ). Anxiety is also common and is linked to pain, impaired physical function, greater disease activity, and poorer quality-of-life (QoL) ( 4 ). Fatigue is another common and burdensome symptom in patients with RA. Recent evidence indicates that substantial fatigue may persist despite treatment with biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic therapies and is closely related to pain, impaired physical function, and psychological factors ( 5 ). The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recognizes fatigue as a common and particularly challenging symptom of inflammatory rheumatic diseases and recommends its routine assessment and management in clinical practice ( 6 ). Sleep disturbances are also common in patients with RA and are associated with poorer physical and psychological QoL, further contributing to the overall disease burden ( 7 ). The combined burden of psychological and physical symptoms can substantially impair health-related QoL, with greater disease activity generally associated with poorer QoL ( 8 ). These challenges highlight the need for feasible and efficient complementary interventions to overcome the multidimensional burden of RA. CBT is a structured psychological intervention that incorporates cognitive restructuring, behavioral strategies, and problem-solving techniques to help patients with chronic conditions cope with symptoms and stress and improve psychological well-being, daily functioning, and adjustment to illness ( 9–11 ). Previous evidence has shown that CBT can attenuate symptoms of depression and anxiety ( 12 ) and is a safe and effective treatment for insomnia ( 13 , 14 ). Few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have examined CBT in RA patients. However, differences in intervention format, duration, and outcome assessment have led to inconsistent findings across studies. Prothero et al. conducted a systematic review of reviews on psychological interventions for RA and reported small to moderate improvements across several biopsychosocial outcomes ( 15 ). However, considerable heterogeneity existed among the included interventions, and the potential influence of group versus individual delivery was not examined. In 2020, Shen et al. performed a meta-analysis focusing specifically on CBT for RA and found significant improvements in anxiety, depression, and fatigue ( 16 ). However, the analysis included only six RCTs, searched the literature up to December 2018, and did not perform subgroup analyses. Since then, five additional RCTs included in the present review have been published. These studies have expanded the evidence base in terms of sample size, CBT delivery formats, and outcome measures. They also provide an opportunity not only to update the overall evidence on CBT effectiveness but also to examine whether treatment effects differ across clinically relevant delivery formats, such as individual versus group CBT and online versus offline CBT. Therefore, an updated meta-analysis was needed. This meta-analysis aimed to examine the effects of CBT on psychological and physical health outcomes in RA patients, provide more comprehensive and robust quantitative evidence, and assess the potential clinical value of CBT as part of comprehensive RA management. 2 Materials and methods This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261470674). The review process and reporting followed the PRISMA and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions statement ( 17 ). Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were independently carried out by 2 reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus, with a third reviewer consulted for unresolved disagreements. 2.1 Search strategy and study selection We searched Cochrane Library, PubMed, Web of Science and Embase for RCTs involving CBT interventions in RA patients from database inception to July 9, 2026, using MeSH and free-text terms combined with Boolean operators. No restrictions on article type were applied. Supplementary Table S1 provides the full search terms and procedures. All retrieved records were saved in EndNote and duplicates were eliminated using the software’s built-in function. The remaining records were then manually checked. Titles and abstracts were first screened and potentially eligible studies were then assessed in full text to determine eligibility. 2.2 Eligibility criteria The PICOS framework was used to establish the eligibility criteria. Population (P): Adults with RA diagnosed according to established diagnostic or classification criteria, or with a diagnosis confirmed by a rheumatologist. Intervention (I): CBT in addition to usual RA treatment or usual care. CBT was defined as a structured psychological intervention incorporating cognitive and behavioral components. Comparison (C): Usual RA treatment, wait-list control, usual care, or usual care supplemented with educational or informational materials. Outcomes (O): Primary outcomes were anxiety, depression, fatigue, pain, and physical function; QoL and sleep were secondary outcomes. Study design (S): RCTs. Studies were excluded if they met one or more of the following criteria: (1) non-RCTs; (2) unavailable full text, including conference abstracts and study protocols; (3) interventions that did not meet the predefined eligibility criteria; (4) no relevant outcome measures; (5) insufficient data for extraction after contacting the corresponding authors; or (6) publications in languages other than English. 2.3 Data extraction Data such as the author, publication year, country, sample size, intervention and control conditions, intervention duration, participant features (sex and age), outcome measures and assessment methods, and assessment time points, were extracted. For multi-arm trials, only the intervention and control groups that met the predefined PICO criteria were included; unrelated study arms were excluded. Details of multi-arm trial handling are provided in Supplementary Table S2 . For essential data not reported in the published articles, the corresponding authors were contacted to request the missing information. 2.4 Risk-of-bias and certainty-of-evidence assessment Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool because the evidence base consisted exclusively of randomized controlled trials. The assessment comprised five domains covering the randomization process, departures from the assigned interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting of results. Domain-level judgments were generated according to the RoB 2 signaling questions and algorithm and were categorized as low risk, some concerns, or high risk. An overall risk-of-bias judgment was then determined for each trial. For the principal outcomes, certainty of evidence (CoE) was evaluated according to the GRADE methodology across five domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. One level was deducted for serious concerns and two levels for very serious concerns, yielding an overall certainty rating of high, moderate, low, or very low. 2.5 Statistical analysis All seven outcomes incorporated in this meta-analysis were continuous outcomes. The mean, standard deviation, and sample size at baseline and post-intervention for the intervention and control groups were extracted. We used the change scores from baseline to post-intervention as the main criteria for the meta-analysis. If data were presented as median and interquartile range, the corresponding mean and standard deviation were computed as described previously ( 18 ). When the standard deviation of the change score was unavailable, it was estimated from the baseline and post-intervention standard deviations according to the method recommended by Follmann et al., with the correlation coefficient assumed to be r = 0.5 ( 19 ). All meta-analyses were conducted in R v4.6.0 using the meta (v8.5–0) and metafor (v5.0–1) packages. As all outcomes were continuous and measured using different scales across RCTs, pooled effects were presented as SMDs with 95% CIs. Outcome directions were harmonized before pooling so that negative SMDs consistently favored CBT. Scales with the opposite direction were reversed. Hedges’ g was used to correct for small-sample bias. Given the potential clinical and methodological heterogeneity in participant features, CBT intervention formats, intervention duration, follow-up periods, and outcome measurement instruments, the primary analyses were implemented through random-effects models. The DerSimonian-Laird method was applied to estimate between-study variance (τ 2 ), with 95% CIs calculated. Fixed-effect estimates were also presented in the forest plots to examine the consistency of effect estimates under different model assumptions. The findings were interpreted primarily based on random-effects models. Cochran’s Q test was employed to test for between-study heterogeneity, and its magnitude was quantified using I 2 . Values of p < 0.10 for Cochran’s Q test or I 2 > 50% were considered indicative of substantial heterogeneity, whereas p < 0.05 denoted statistical significance. To further account for uncertainty due to between-study heterogeneity, 95% prediction intervals were computed for the pooled outcomes. The prediction intervals were derived from the random-effects models using the DerSimonian–Laird estimate of between-study variance, as follows: 95 % PI = μ ˆ RE ± t 0.975 , k − 1 S E 2 ( μ ˆ RE ) + τ ˆ 2 . where μ ˆ RE represents the pooled effect estimate from the random-effects model, S E 2 ( μ ˆ RE ) is the squared standard error of the pooled effect estimate, τ ˆ 2 is the estimated between-study variance, k is the number of studies included in the meta-analysis, and t 0.975 , k − 1 denotes the 97.5th percentile of the Student’s t-distribution with k − 1 degrees of freedom. Exploratory subgroup analyses were conducted for depression, anxiety, and fatigue according to CBT delivery format, comparing individual versus group CBT and online versus offline CBT. For statistically significant primary outcomes, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were implemented. Model sensitivity analyses were also conducted using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation, with and without the Hartung Knapp adjustment, to assess the robustness of the primary findings. Additional study-exclusion sensitivity analyses were performed by excluding studies judged to be at high overall risk of bias and studies using wait-list controls, respectively. Egger’s test was additionally implemented for outcomes with at least 10 included RCTs. As an additional analysis, 6-month follow-up data for depression and anxiety were pooled using change scores from baseline and the same effect-size calculation and random-effects model as in the primary analyses. 3 Results 3.1 Study selection and characteristics of eligible RCTs The database search was performed on 1,006 records, including PubMed, ( n = 159), Embase ( n = 436), Cochrane ( n = 219), and Web of Science ( n = 192). Figure 1 shows the selection process of RCTs. We report on the 12 randomized controlled trials that included 1,538 patients with RA in 7 countries in Table 1 . Three RCTs were carried out in the Netherlands ( 20–22 ), three in the United Kingdom ( 23–25 ), two in Australia ( 26 , 27 ), and one each in the United States ( 28 ), Denmark ( 29 ), Iran ( 30 ), and Germany ( 31 ). CBT interventions were classified by delivery format as group versus individual CBT and online versus face-to-face CBT. 3.2 Risk of bias RoB 2 was employed to evaluate the 12 RCTs included. title: Mindfulness and psychological well-being in older adults: the effect of reminiscence therapy
abstract:
Background This study aimed to examine the effects of reminiscence therapy on psychological well-being and mindfulness among community-dwelling older adults. Methods This pre-test–post-test randomized controlled trial was conducted at XX Community Health Center between May and June 2025. The study was completed with 90 community-dwelling older adults who were randomly assigned to an experimental group ( n = 45) or a control group ( n = 45). Data were collected using the Descriptive Characteristics Form, the Psychological Well-Being Scale, and the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale. Participants in the experimental group received a structured 10-session reminiscence therapy program, whereas the control group received no intervention during the study period. Outcomes were assessed before and immediately after the intervention. A two-way mixed analysis of variance was used to examine the effects of group, time, and the group × time interaction. Results A significant group × time interaction was found for mindful awareness, indicating that changes in Mindful Attention Awareness Scale scores differed significantly between the experimental and control groups, F (1, 88) = 31.415, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.263. Mindful awareness scores increased in the experimental group from 56.71 ± 16.70 at pre-test to 64.27 ± 16.57 at post-test, whereas scores decreased in the control group from 58.00 ± 18.85 to 54.64 ± 17.87. A significant group × time interaction was also observed for psychological well-being, F (1, 88) = 15.196, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.147. Psychological well-being scores increased in the experimental group from 37.00 ± 9.35 to 40.80 ± 10.34, whereas they decreased in the control group from 40.53 ± 14.74 to 36.53 ± 10.91. Conclusions Reminiscence therapy was associated with significantly more favorable changes in mindful awareness and psychological well-being compared with the control condition. These findings suggest that reminiscence therapy may be a useful psychosocial intervention for supporting positive psychological functioning and mindful awareness among community-dwelling older adults. Further studies with larger and more diverse samples, active control conditions, and long-term follow-up assessments are needed to confirm the sustainability and generalizability of these findings. Clinical trial number ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06964399 .

Introduction Improved healthcare services and advances associated with socioeconomic development have contributed to increased life expectancy, resulting in a rapid increase in the proportion of older adults worldwide [ 1 ]. As the older population grows, greater attention is required to the physical, psychological, and social changes associated with aging and their potential effects on health and well-being [ 2 ]. In this context, non-pharmacological interventions have gained importance as approaches that can support healthy aging and address the psychological and social needs of older adults [ 3 , 4 ]. One such intervention is reminiscence therapy, which involves helping individuals recall, reflect on, and share past life events and meaningful experiences, either verbally or silently, often with the support of concrete cues [ 5 ]. The therapeutic purpose of reminiscence, however, may differ according to the characteristics and needs of the target population. While reminiscence-based interventions have also been used in individuals with dementia or cognitive impairment, the present study focuses on community-dwelling older adults without severe dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, related neurological disorders, or major psychiatric disorders. In this population, reminiscence is considered primarily as a psychosocial intervention that may support psychological well-being, life satisfaction, personal identity, self-esteem, autobiographical integration, and emotional adjustment. Consistent with this perspective, reminiscence may help older adults feel stronger, more valued, and more confident and may contribute to the development, maintenance, or reconstruction of personal identity [ 2 , 4 ]. Importantly, evidence obtained directly from healthy older adults supports this psychosocial perspective. Viguer et al. (2017) found that a 10-session reminiscence intervention in 160 healthy older adults reduced depressed mood and improved life satisfaction and psychological well-being; improvements in life satisfaction and some dimensions of psychological well-being were maintained at the three-month follow-up. These findings are particularly relevant to the present study because both the target population and the psychosocial outcomes closely correspond to those examined here [ 6 ]. Mindfulness refers to the capacity to attend to present-moment experiences with awareness and a non-judgmental, accepting attitude toward thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations. In the present study, mindfulness is not conceptualized as the direct product of a formal mindfulness-based intervention. Rather, it is considered a potentially relevant psychological outcome of the reflective processes involved in reminiscence therapy. Reminiscence requires older adults to deliberately evoke, attend to, elaborate, and reinterpret autobiographical experiences. Through this process, individuals may become more aware of their emotional responses and personal meanings associated with past experiences, observe these experiences from a reflective perspective, and integrate them into their current understanding of the self. Such reflective engagement may be associated with greater awareness of emotional responses and personal meanings and may encourage individuals to adopt a more reflective and accepting orientation toward their experiences. Accordingly, although reminiscence therapy differs conceptually from mindfulness-based interventions, its emphasis on attentive reflection, emotional awareness, acceptance, and reinterpretation of autobiographical experiences provides a theoretical rationale for examining mindfulness as an outcome. Mindfulness was therefore included not because reminiscence therapy explicitly teaches mindfulness practices, but because changes in awareness and the way individuals relate to their internal experiences may accompany the reminiscence process [ 7 ]. Accordingly, mindfulness was examined as a theoretically relevant psychological outcome rather than as a direct or expected consequence of formal mindfulness training. In the present study, psychological well-being is conceptualized in accordance with the framework underlying the Psychological Well-Being Scale developed by Diener et al. (2010), rather than as a general construct encompassing all dimensions of subjective or psychological well-being [ 8 ]. Within this framework, psychological well-being refers to flourishing or positive psychological functioning, reflected in perceived purpose and meaning in life, supportive and rewarding relationships, engagement in daily activities, feelings of competence and self-respect, optimism, and the perception that one is functioning well [ 9 ]. This conceptualization is particularly relevant to healthy aging, as maintaining positive psychological functioning becomes increasingly important in the context of the physical, psychological, and social changes associated with later life [ 10 ]. Reminiscence therapy may support these aspects of psychological functioning by enabling older adults to recall, share, and reinterpret meaningful autobiographical experiences, thereby facilitating meaning-making, self-evaluation, emotional balance, and a sense of continuity in life. Accordingly, psychological well-being was selected as a primary outcome of the present study because changes resulting from the reminiscence process may be reflected in older adults’ perceived meaning, competence, positive relationships, and overall optimal psychological functioning. Consistent with this perspective, Ooi et al. (2021) identified psychological well-being as an important component of healthy living among older adults [ 11 ]. In a meta-analysis conducted by Pinquart and colleagues on the effects of reminiscence interventions on psychosocial outcomes, it was found that these interventions had a wide range of therapeutic and preventive effects [ 12 ]. Evidence from clinical populations has also suggested potential psychological benefits of reminiscence therapy. For example, recent studies involving older adults with gastrointestinal or cervical cancer have reported improvements in psychological burden, anxiety or depressive symptoms, and quality of life following reminiscence-based interventions [ 13 , 14 ]. However, these findings were obtained from specific clinical populations and should not be directly generalized to community-dwelling older adults without major medical or psychiatric conditions [ 13 , 15 ]. A systematic review focusing specifically on community-dwelling older adults also reported that reminiscence therapy may contribute to improvements in quality of life and life satisfaction, supporting its potential as a psychosocial intervention for older adults living in the community [ 14 ]. From a nursing perspective, reminiscence therapy has practical relevance as a structured psychosocial intervention that can be integrated into the care of older adults. Nurses, particularly psychiatric nurses, are well positioned to implement reminiscence-based approaches due to their roles in assessing psychological needs, facilitating therapeutic communication, supporting emotional expression, and promoting psychosocial well-being. Through structured reminiscence sessions, nurses can provide opportunities for older adults to express their emotions, reflect on meaningful life experiences, strengthen their sense of identity, and enhance social interaction. Such interventions may also help nurses gain a more individualized and holistic understanding of older adults by providing insight into their personal histories, values, coping experiences, and sources of meaning in life. Therefore, integrating reminiscence-based approaches into nursing and psychiatric nursing practice may contribute to the development of person-centered, non-pharmacological care aimed at supporting psychological well-being and mindfulness in later life [ 16 ]. Recent bibliometric evidence indicates growing scholarly interest in reminiscence therapy and its potential applications in psychological health. However, increased research activity does not itself establish intervention effectiveness, highlighting the need for methodologically rigorous studies examining specific psychological outcomes [ 1 , 17 ]. This highlights the importance of studies on the effects of reminiscence therapy on psychological parameters. Despite the growing body of research on reminiscence therapy, evidence regarding its effects on specific positive psychological outcomes among community-dwelling older adults without significant cognitive impairment remains limited. Previous studies have suggested that reminiscence-based interventions may improve psychosocial outcomes such as life satisfaction, emotional adjustment, and psychological well-being; however, fewer studies have examined psychological well-being in terms of flourishing and positive psychological functioning. Evidence regarding the potential effect of reminiscence therapy on mindfulness is even more limited. Given that the reminiscence process involves deliberate attention to autobiographical experiences, reflection on emotional responses and personal meanings, and the reinterpretation and integration of life experiences, examining mindfulness as a potential psychological outcome may contribute to a better understanding of the broader effects of reminiscence therapy. Therefore, using a randomized controlled design and validated measurement instruments, the present study aimed to examine the effects of reminiscence therapy on psychological well-being and mindfulness among community-dwelling older adults without significant cognitive impairment. Research hypotheses H1: The change in psychological well-being scores over time will differ significantly between the experimental and control groups. H2: The change in mindfulness scores over time will differ significantly between the experimental and control groups. Methods Study design The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT06964399 ). The research was designed as a randomized controlled trial using a pre-test–post-test methodology. This study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines. This trial was retrospectively registered with ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT06964399 ), as recruitment activities (beginning April 10, 2025) had already commenced prior to trial registration (April 24, 2025). Study participants The target population consisted of community-dwelling older adults aged 65 years and over who attended the XX Community Health Center. Participant selection and therapy administration were conducted at the XX Community Health Center in X province. The study preparation began in April 2025, including preparation of the intervention setting and participant recruitment activities. The intervention and data collection were conducted between May and June 2025. The study specifically targeted older adults without severe cognitive impairment, major psychiatric disorders, or neurological conditions that could interfere with participation in group-based reminiscence therapy. The study was not designed to evaluate the effects of reminiscence therapy in individuals with diagnosed dementia or other clinical cognitive disorders; rather, it aimed to examine its effects on psychological well-being and mindfulness among community-dwelling older adults who were able to communicate, participate actively in group sessions, and recall and discuss personal experiences. The required sample size was estimated a priori using G*Power 3.1.9.7 for an F test (ANOVA: repeated measures, within-between interaction). Assuming a medium effect size (Cohen’s f = 0.25), an alpha level of 0.05, statistical power of 0.80, two study groups, and two repeated measurements, with a correlation of 0.50 between repeated measures and a nonsphericity correction of 1.00, the required total sample size was 32 participants. The final sample included 90 participants (45 per group) [ 18 ]. The G*Power calculation did not incorporate an adjustment for clustering by therapy group. Study preparation began in April 2025, including preparation of the intervention setting and participant recruitment activities. The intervention and data collection were conducted from May to June 2025. Data analysis and manuscript preparation were completed in July 2025. Eligibility criteria were assessed through a combination of medical and health-center record review, participant self-report, and researcher assessment during the recruitment interview.
