title: The Session-specific Risk Index (SRI) in psychotherapy: Developing longitudinal session-by-session machine learning algorithms to predict the likelihood of non-response to treatment
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This study aimed to develop and introduce an implementation-oriented, session-specific metric called the Session-specific Risk Index (SRI), which defines the likelihood of treatment non-response in psychotherapy. The SRI integrates baseline information with real-time clinical data from each session, providing a continuously updated probability of non-response to treatment.

METHODS: We used observational data from an outpatient clinic, including 1,010 psychotherapy patients. We compared the performance of elastic net regressions and gradient boosting machines for the prediction of non-response by session 20 using patients' initial sociodemographic, diagnostic and clinical information, combined with data from their symptoms' clinical evolution. Finally, we used the best performing algorithms to define the SRIs.

RESULTS: Elastic net regressions without interaction effects performed the best across the first ten sessions (accuracy = .65-.70; area-under-the-curve = .70 [.70, .71] -.77 [.76, .78]). The use of maximum Youden indices provided optimal SRI thresholds, balancing sensitivity and specificity, to identify patients at high-risk of non-response. Midpoints of SRI groups strongly correlated with proportion of patients not responding to treatment within those groups (weighted correlation= .85, 95%CI [.83-.86]).

CONCLUSION: These findings positioned the SRI as an implementation-oriented, timely-sensitive index to determine the risk of non-response to therapy session-by-session. If implemented in clinical practice, SRIs might enhance precision in mental health care going beyond baseline models of treatment personalization.

title: Long-term acquisition and maintenance of cognitive behavioral therapy skills through a smartphone-based intervention: A secondary analysis of the RESiLIENT trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is assumed to confer longer-term benefit partly through the acquisition and maintenance of therapeutic skills, but evidence on these processes after smartphone-based CBT remains limited in subthreshold depression. This exploratory secondary analysis of the RESiLIENT randomized controlled trial examined 50-week changes in five CBT skill domains: behavioral activation (BA), cognitive restructuring (CR), problem solving (PS), assertion training (AT), and behavioral therapy for insomnia (BI).

METHODS: The reported comparisons involved 3280 participants with baseline PHQ-9 scores of 5 or higher assigned to nine CBT intervention arms or the weekly self-check control arm. Self-reported skill enactment was assessed at baseline and weeks 6, 26, and 50. Standardized mean differences versus self-check were reported for 135 CBT contrasts. P-values and confidence intervals used a Dunnett approximation within each domain and visit.

RESULTS: Estimated changes in CR skill scores favored several intervention arms over self-check, whereas changes in BA skill scores favored the intervention in some comparisons. Estimated between-group differences in PS, AT, and BI skill scores were generally small. At week 50, standardized mean differences for BA + CR versus self-check were 0.26 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.46) for BA and 0.27 (0.07 to 0.47) for CR. The corresponding CR estimate in the CR arm was 0.21 (0.01 to 0.41). These estimates illustrate exploratory patterns and do not establish superiority of one intervention or skill domain.

CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory study describes varying patterns of change across self-reported CBT skill domains over 50 weeks following a brief smartphone-based intervention. These findings may inform future research on the persistence of CBT skill use and its relationship with longer-term clinical outcomes.

title: Perspectives on temporality in psychoanalysis
abstract: The text presents three complementary approaches to temporality in psychoanalysis-pedagogical, metapsychological, and clinical-all conceiving psychic time as multiple, non-linear, and structured through Nachträglichkeit oraprès-coup. Wang Chenyang examines Lacanian temporality through logical time, anticipation, the signifier and scansion. The past gains meaning retrospectively, while transference allows the subject's relation to time and desire to unfold and change. Bernard Chervet traces psychic time to discontinuity, loss, and drive extinction, distinguishing the repressed's preservative timelessness from traumatic atemporality. Because time has no direct representation, it is figured through rhythms, movement, and measuring devices. Temporalisation uses unconscious preservation to create continuity, work through loss and open future possibilities. Rosine Perelberg explores how coexisting temporalities are transformed in clinical practice, integrating Freudian, British, and French perspectives. She emphasises Green's heterochrony, Birksted-Breen's reverberation time and the organising role of après-coup. Analysis can represent and reorganise experiences frozen by trauma. Together, the papers unite conceptual rigour and clinical sensitivity, framing psychic change as a transformation in the experience of time.

title: Unseen mothers: a psychoanalytic community responds to perinatal mood distress
abstract: Perinatal mood disturbances are prevalent yet often not seen. Internal psychic pressures contribute to women downplaying such disturbances. Additionally, stressed maternal health providers frequently fail to provide these women with support in getting to the mental health care they need. These distressed mothers can fall through the cracks of the maternal health care system. This paper details the successful development of a psychoanalytic society's community outreach program that offers affordable and accessible therapy for pregnant women and new mothers. The SPRING Project has become a valued resource in the community and significantly altered the sponsoring psychoanalytic society's relationship to the external world. The Project has been life changing for many in the community and, in turn, has established a portal for psychoanalysts to become community psychoanalysts. With case examples, the author highlights the receptivity of pregnant women and new mothers to psychoanalytic treatment at this transformative time of life. It is posited that unconscious social defenses in medical practices may contribute to overcompartmentalization and obstacles to promoting access to necessary mental health care and unwittingly intertwine with a new mother's wish for self-sufficiency.

title: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface training for upper-limb rehabilitation after subacute stroke: A randomized sham-controlled trial
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether motor imagery (MI) based brain-computer interface (BCI) training improves upper-limb motor function in patients with subacute stroke compared with a high-fidelity sham-BCI control, and to explore accompanying structural and resting-state functional MRI changes.

METHOD: In this participant-blinded randomized controlled trial, 32 patients with subacute stroke were randomized to a MI-based BCI group or a high-fidelity BCI sham-control group (n = 16 each). Both groups received dose-matched training (30 min/session, 5 sessions/week for 4 weeks) in addition to standard rehabilitation. Upper-limb motor outcomes were assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE; primary outcome), Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), Motor Assessment Scale (MAS), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI). Structural MRI and resting-state functional MRI were acquired at baseline and post-intervention to assess gray matter volume (GMV) and functional connectivity (FC).

RESULTS: Both groups showed significant improvement after the intervention. Compared with the sham-control group, the MI-based BCI group demonstrated greater gains in FMA-UE and secondary motor outcomes (WMFT and MAS), whereas the difference in MBI was not statistically significant. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a within-group increase in GMV in the contralesional supplementary motor area (SMA) in the MI-based BCI group; however, no significant between-group GMV difference was observed. The MI-based BCI group also exhibited increased resting-state FC between the SMA and the ipsilesional cerebellar lobule IX and fusiform gyrus. Changes in FC were associated with improvements in FMA-UE, WMFT, and MBI, but not MAS.

CONCLUSION: Compared with a high-fidelity sham-control group, MI-based BCI group training was associated with greater upper-limb motor recovery in patients with subacute stroke, accompanied by changes in structural and functional neuroimaging measures involving motor-related regions and connections. Larger randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are required to confirm durability and clinical relevance.

title: Surprise Resets the Mind: An Adaptive Online Reset in Working Memory Selection
abstract: Human cognition rapidly adapts to unexpected events in dynamic environments, but it remains unclear whether expectation violations rapidly influence the selection of attended information into working memory. Using the attribute-amnesia paradigm, we introduced expectation violations during the surprise trial to test whether unexpected changes improve reporting of a target feature that had been attended and used but was normally not reported. Across six experiments (total  N  = 250 college students, aged 17-27 years; 149 females), expectation violations reliably improved surprise-trial report of this feature, indicating greater availability in working memory. This effect occurred not only when the violation concerned the target, but also when it involved broader contextual or auditory changes, suggesting that the effect cannot be characterized simply as enhanced visual attention to the target. These findings suggest that expectation violations trigger a rapid, flexible adjustment of working-memory selection, highlighting its role in dynamically managing information under uncertainty.

title: Uncovering internal sensory evidence reveals the nature of confidence computation in multi-alternative perceptual decision making
abstract:
A central goal of perceptual decision making is to determine the computations underlying choice and confidence in complex, multi-alternative tasks. However, revealing these computations requires knowledge of the internal sensory evidence upon which the computations operate. Unfortunately, unlike for 2-choice tasks, there is no established method in multi-alternative tasks to determine how stimuli are transformed into internal sensory evidence. Here we address this critical gap by developing a novel modeling paradigm that reveals how the brain transforms external stimuli into internal sensory evidence during multi-alternative decision making in the context of numerosity tasks. Across three experiments that feature 2-, 3-, and 5-choice conditions, we show that the internal sensory evidence in our numerosity task can be described with a simple, 2-parameter equation that fits data for up to 12 conditions. Critically, the ability to model the internal sensory evidence allowed us to test six theories of confidence computation. Our results support a model where confidence reflects the raw evidence difference between the top two alternatives. These results establish a new numerosity paradigm in which a 2-parameter equation can be used to determine the internal sensory evidence for a potentially unlimited number of multi-alternative conditions and reveal the confidence computation in multi-alternative tasks.

Introduction Humans possess the metacognitive ability to assess the accuracy of their own decisions through confidence ratings ( Fleming, 2024 ; Mamassian, 2020 ; Rahnev, 2021 ). Accurate metacognition is important in many domains, such as learning and the ability to engage in sequential decisions ( Aguilar-Lleyda et al., 2020 ; Hainguerlot et al., 2018 ; Schunk & Ertmer, 2000 ). A critical goal in the field is identifying the computational mechanisms behind confidence in complex, multi-alternative tasks ( Rahnev et al., 2022 ). However, revealing these computations requires knowledge of the internal sensory evidence upon which the computations operate. But unlike for 2-choice tasks, there is currently no well-established paradigm that allows modeling how external stimuli are converted into internal sensory evidence for multi-alternative tasks ( Miyoshi et al., 2024 ; Shekhar & Rahnev, 2024a ). Only a few papers have examined the computation underlying confidence in n-choice tasks via cognitive modeling. Li & Ma (2020) designed a cloud task where participants indicated the color of the cloud from which a black dot originated. Comay et al. (2023) used a different task where participants judged which of three shapes has the largest area. The two papers reached different results about the confidence computation, with Li & Ma favoring a model where confidence reflects the difference in probability between the top two options, whereas Comay et al. favored a model where confidence reflects the difference in probability between the top choice and the average of all other choices. More importantly, all models tested by Li & Ma (2020) and Comay et al. (2023) were probability-based models. Such models are known as “explicit-Bayes” models ( Xue & Rahnev, 2026 ): they necessitate a complex computation that considers the likelihood of all possible stimulus states given a certain percept and applies Bayes’ theorem to convert these likelihood functions into probabilities ( Locke et al., 2022 ). This contrasts fundamentally with evidence-based models, which give confidence based directly on the raw internal sensory evidence without requiring complex inference to derive probabilities ( Locke et al., 2022 ; Xue et al., 2024 ). More recently, Miyoshi & Sakamoto (2025) used an evidence accumulation framework and compared a model where confidence is based on a combination of early and late evidence with a model where confidence is based on the Softmax computation. Overall, no prior work has used cognitive modeling to compare the full range of viable confidence models, including probability- and evidence-based models, in the context of multi-alternative tasks. Some prior work has compared probability- and evidence-based models in the context of 2-choice tasks ( Adler & Ma, 2018 ; Aitchison et al., 2015 ; Locke et al., 2022 ; Xue et al., 2024 ). Aitchison et al. (2015) used a two-interval forced-choice contrast discrimination task and found that confidence appeared Bayesian (probability-based) when subjects reported their decision and confidence sequentially, but results were mixed in a simultaneous response design. Adler & Ma (2018) used two orientation categorization tasks that varied sensory reliability and found evidence against a fully Bayesian, probability-based account of confidence, but their preferred heuristic models do not fit neatly into a simple probability- versus evidence-based categorization. Locke et al. (2022) used a two-interval spatial discrimination task and found that most observers were better described by evidence-based models than by probability-based models, although individual differences existed. Xue et al. (2024) used an orientation discrimination task and informed participants about the difficulty level of each trial, finding that evidence-based models better fit the data than probability-based ones. Thus, the literature on 2-choice tasks tends to favor evidence-based models, but not only is this problem still open for 2-choice tasks, it is unclear how the 2-choice results would generalize to multi-alternative tasks. A recent paper used artificial neural networks to compare probability- and evidence-based models in multi-alternative tasks ( Shekhar et al., 2025 ). Participants completed an 8-choice handwritten digit discrimination task and their performance was compared to that of RTNet, a neural network model of human perceptual decisions ( Rafiei et al., 2024 ). Shekhar et al. then generated confidence ratings produced by RTNet using both probability- and evidence-based computations and compared these ratings to the ones obtained from the human participants. Shekhar et al. found that the best match was provided by a model where confidence reflects the difference in evidence for the top two choices. However, the use of artificial neural networks instead of cognitive modeling has several limitations. First, unlike cognitive models that can be tuned to human behavior, RTNet provides only an imperfect model of human internal activations ( Rafiei et al., 2024 ). Second, the approach involved no formal model fitting, as that is computationally difficult for neural networks, and instead simply equated RTNet’s accuracy to the average human accuracy. Finally, the qualitative signatures examined, including effects of task difficulty, speed-accuracy trade-off, and the folded-X pattern, are well-established behavioral benchmarks for confidence models in general but do not specifically probe the computational challenges unique to multi-alternative tasks, such as how additional weak options or changes in the number of choices affect confidence. Thus, while artificial neural networks allow modeling of very complex tasks (e.g., handwritten digit discrimination), they cannot yet replace cognitive modeling, which allows close fitting of individual participants and the use of tasks that probe more detailed behavioral signatures. Our study directly addresses these critical gaps by building a novel modeling paradigm that successfully establishes the transformation of stimuli into internal sensory evidence for multi-alternative numerosity tasks. This advancement enables the mapping of a potentially unlimited number of conditions in multi-alternative numerosity tasks using as few as two free parameters, while providing a broader template for analogous mappings in other perceptual domains. Critically, our approach enables a comprehensive test of evidence- and probability-based confidence models in multi-alternative tasks. We also identify three behavioral signatures specific to multi-alternative confidence that provide strong qualitative constraints on confidence models and go beyond the general benchmarks examined in previous work. Our results provide strong evidence that a particular evidence-based model – according to which confidence reflects the difference in raw evidence between the highest and second-highest sensory evidence – best explains confidence in multi-alternative tasks. Methods Participants Experiment 1 featured 15 participants (8 female; mean age = 19.3 years) who completed 1,440 trials each over two sessions. Experiment 2 featured 25 participants (12 female; mean age = 20.0 years) each completing a total of 576 trials in a single session. Experiment 3 featured 28 participants (12 female; mean age = 19.8) each completing 960 trials in a single session. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and signed informed consent. Experimental procedures were approved by the Georgia Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board. Experimental design Each trial in all three experiments began with a fixation point at the center of the screen for a duration of 500 ms, followed by the presentation of the stimulus for 500 ms in Experiments 1 and 2 , or 600 ms in Experiment 3 ( Figure 1A ). A one-second inter-trial interval was provided between trials, with 15-second breaks between blocks. Trials from different conditions were randomized and intermixed throughout the whole experiment. Between runs, participants could take breaks of unlimited duration and continue the experiment by pressing any key when ready. The stimulus was a cloud of dots with a radius of 8 degrees of visual angle (231 pixels) consisting of either three different colors in Experiment 1 , two or three colors in Experiment 2 , and three or five colors in Experiment 3 . Dots of different colors were randomly positioned throughout the display area, with no clustering based on color or numerical dominance. In Experiments 1 and 2 , the colors were red (RGB: 255, 32, 32), green (RGB: 0, 180, 0), and blue (RGB: 15, 15, 255). In Experiment 3 , five colors were used: purple, yellow, green, red, and blue, with the exact RGB values being adjusted for each individual separately (see below). Individual dots had a diameter of 5 pixels in all experiments. In Experiment 3 , before the presentation of the stimulus, we presented a condition cue (500 ms) that indicated the number of dots for each choice option. Specifically, the cue displayed the condition number along with the exact dot counts listed in descending order from the most to the least dominant color (e.g., ‘Condition 1: [100, 80, 60]’). Participants also learned the mapping between condition numbers and dot distributions during the training phase prior to the main experiment. For all experiments, after the presentation of the stimulus, a response screen was presented until the participants provided a decision. The participants’ task was to indicate which was the dominant color (i.e., the color with the most dots) in the cloud of dots. We ensured that each color appeared equally often in each position from the dominant to the one with fewest dots. In Experiments 1 and 2 , participants used keyboard buttons ‘Z’, ‘X’, and ‘C’ for red, green, and blue respectively. In Experiment 3 , participants used the mouse to click on a box with the name of the correct color. After the participants gave their response, a confidence screen appeared and was presented until the participants made a confidence response on a 4-point scale. In all experiments, participants indicated their confidence level using the keyboard. We note that we refer to our task as a “numerosity task” because this is how we described it to our participants. Because dots were uniform in size and randomly distributed throughout the display area, other variables such as color density are perfectly correlated with numerosity. Participants could in principle rely on other variables to perform the task, but that would not affect either our modeling approach or conclusions. Experiment 1 Experiment 1 was completed over two sessions. Each session consisted of 3 runs with 5 blocks per run, and each block contained 48 trials. In total, participants completed 1,440 trials across the two sessions. The experiment included 12 conditions with varying dot number distributions ( Table ). Conditions 1–6 and 7–12 were designed to maintain similar evidence ratios while using different absolute numbers (conditions 7–12 used approximately 85.7% of the dot numbers in conditions 1–6). However, due to the constraint that dot numbers must be whole integers, small deviations in ratios were unavoidable. Experiment 2 Participants in Experiment 2 completed the experiment in a single session consisting of 3 runs with 4 blocks per run, with each block containing 48 trials, totaling 576 trials per subject. The experiment included 6 conditions, where Conditions 1–3 and 4–6 were perfectly matched in their ratios, with Conditions 4–6 using exactly 80% of the dot numbers in Conditions 1–3 ( Table 1 ). For instance, in Conditions 1 vs. 4, the ratios are identical: 100:75:75 vs. 80:60:60, both yielding .75 for the ratio between second highest and highest dots. Experiment 3 Experiment 3 consisted of 6 runs, with each run containing 4 blocks, and each block containing 40 trials (total of 960 trials per participant). The study included two main manipulations: the number of colors presented (either 3 or 5 colors) and eight different dot number distributions ( Table 1 ). Before beginning the main experiment, participants in Experiment 3 completed a color calibration phase. During calibration, participants were presented with displays containing dots of the five different colors and were instructed to adjust the colors until all of them were equally noticeable to them. After each selection, that color’s intensity was either increased or reduced by multiplying its RGB values by a factor of .92 or 1/.92 (~1.087), while maintaining the original RGB ratios. Each color could be reduced by no more than 80% of its original intensity. This process continued until participants had made at least five adjustments and indicated that all colors appeared equally noticeable by selecting an “Equal” option that became available after the minimum adjustments. Across all three experiments, we tested a substantially broader range of conditions than previous multi-alternative confidence studies. Experiment 1 included 12 conditions, Experiment 2 included six conditions, and Experiment 3 included eight conditions with both 3-choice and 5-choice tasks. title: Event-general concepts guide semantic generalizations during verb learning cross-linguistically
abstract: Languages vary in how they map the conceptual components of events onto verbs. For example, some languages, such as English, often encode the manner of spontaneous motion in verbs (e.g., run), while others, such as Spanish, make greater use of verbs that encode the path of motion (e.g., enter). Such verb lexicalization biases are known to be malleable for spontaneous-motion verbs in English. In the present study, we probed the scope and malleability of such biases cross-linguistically. We found that both English-speaking and Spanish-speaking learners can learn new verb lexicalization biases from a few exposures and extend them to novel verb meanings within the same semantic class - in both previously documented and new domains (spontaneous motion - Experiment 1; caused motion - Experiment 2). Furthermore, speakers of both languages could extend verb biases across semantic classes (from spontaneous motion to caused motion - Experiment 1; and from caused motion to spontaneous motion - Experiment 2). These findings indicate that verb lexicalization biases are flexible higher-order semantic generalizations that draw from conceptual dimensions that cross-cut specific event types and support verb learning across languages.

title: Exploring cognitive and emotional predictors of adaptive information search
abstract: Adaptive information search often requires balancing competing cognitive goals. In selecting an information search strategy, individuals may face a trade-off between the speed and efficiency of information acquisition. Evidence suggests that individual differences explain variability in how people trade-off deliberation time and accuracy when making decisions. However, less is known about how individuals might differ in how they balance search speed and efficiency in information-rich environments that require sequential information sampling and flexible goal coordination. In our exploratory study, N = 127 participants played a novel variant of the code-breaking game Mastermind in three conditions: in the speed condition, participants were incentivized for rapid game completion; in the efficiency condition for using few queries; and in the mixed condition for both. We assessed individual differences in numeracy, working memory, state and trait emotion, personality and thinking styles in a pretest. Our results suggest that both numeracy and working memory predict information search behaviour across these conditions. Higher numeracy and working memory scores were associated with improved performance and more effective information search strategies across conditions, particularly under time pressure. Emotional predictors showed smaller and condition-dependent effects. State emotional dominance was negatively associated with performance in the mixed condition, suggesting a modulating role of emotional dominance in the coordination of competing demands. State emotional valence was negatively associated with performance under the speed incentive, potentially reflecting a relationship between emotional valence and time-sensitive goal-directed behaviour. Our exploratory findings stress the relevance of considering individual differences in research on adaptive information search.

title: Mind the cueing design: Order effects mask benefits of congruency pre-cues
abstract: Evidence that individuals proactively adjust cognitive control in response to pre-cues signaling upcoming distraction has been surprisingly sparse, raising questions about the limits of volitional control. The present study tested whether this pattern reflects genuine constraints in proactive control engagement or methodological limitations of standard pre-cueing designs. Across two pre-registered experiments, we examined the role of cueing order (i.e., whether participants started with informative or uninformative pre-cue blocks) in the commonly used between-block design and evaluated an alternative within-block design in which informative and uninformative pre-cues were randomly intermixed. In Experiment 1, the standard approach of collapsing cueing order conditions yielded null pre-cue benefits for the between-block comparison, mirroring what is often observed in the literature. However, when considering cueing order, benefits emerged when informative cues were encountered first (cued-first group) but not when they appeared second (uncued-first group). In contrast, the within-block comparison produced reliable pre-cue benefits regardless of cueing order. Experiment 2 replicated the within-block pre-cue benefit using a fully intermixed design without the cueing order manipulation. Together, these findings indicate that sparse evidence for pre-cue benefits may partly reflect design-related constraints rather than limits in proactive control. Why pre-cue benefits depend on cueing order remains an open question, but the present findings reveal that the intermixed cueing design offers a more sensitive and reliable method for detecting cue-based control adjustments-with important implications for prominent theories of cognitive control.

title: Assessing advanced theory of mind in middle childhood: psychometric evaluation and responsiveness to training of a comprehensive AToM battery
abstract: This study examined the psychometric properties and responsiveness to training of a comprehensive Advanced Theory of Mind (AToM) Battery in middle childhood. In Study 1, 168 eight- to nine-year-old children participated (M age  = 8.61 years, SD = 0.64; 88 girls, 79 boys, one preferred not to say). Children completed the AToM Battery, the Strange Stories task, and measures of language, inhibition, working memory, and nonverbal intelligence. Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) largely supported the proposed three-factor structure. At the same time, the CFA indicated that several items, particularly within the Social Reasoning component, showed comparatively weak loadings. The AToM Battery showed moderate convergent validity with the Strange Stories task, r = .37, p < .001. Language ability significantly predicted overall AToM performance, R 2  = .16, with effects primarily driven by the Social Reasoning component, R 2  = .15. In Study 2, 126 children completed the battery at pretest, posttest, and follow-up after participating in either a conversation-based training or a control training. Linear mixed-effects models indicated general improvements over time across groups. Training-specific gains emerged most consistently for Recognition of Transgressions of Social Norms at posttest [t(247.20) = 3.45, p < .001] and follow-up [t(247.20) = 3.23, p = .001]. Stability correlations in the control group indicated moderate temporal stability over a three-month interval, r = .55, p < .001. Overall, the findings support the AToM Battery as a multidimensional and psychometrically useful measure of advanced social-cognitive reasoning, while highlighting the importance of considering language demands and subscale-specific responsiveness.

title: Distinct Amygdala-Frontopolar and Amygdala-Medial Temporal Pathways Support Temporal Memory for Emotional Events
abstract: Growing evidence suggests that emotion shapes temporal aspects of memory-such as remembering when an event occurred-yet the neural bases of these effects remain unclear. Prior work indicates that temporal context representations in memory are supported by the functions of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and prefrontal regions, including hippocampus, perirhinal cortex, and lateral frontopolar cortex (FPl). These regions have privileged access to amygdala-originated affective signals that may mediate emotional influences on temporal memory. To test whether these candidate pathways shape temporal memory for emotional events, participants encoded trial-unique negative and positive images in the scanner, followed by a surprise temporal memory task. We found that more negative stimuli were associated with greater amygdala activation and lower temporal memory error for when emotional images occurred. Replicating and extending prior work, higher stimulus-evoked multivoxel pattern similarity in the hippocampus and FPl was associated with higher temporal memory error. Notably, greater amygdala responding to emotional images predicted higher between-trial pattern similarity in the hippocampus but lower within- and between-trial similarity in FPl. Amygdala engagement was also correlated with greater perirhinal activation, which in turn predicted stronger item memory and a recency bias in temporal memory estimates. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct-and opposing-modulatory effects of amygdala-FPl and amygdala-MTL pathways on temporal memory, with the potential to sharpen and blur memory for when emotional events occurred.

title: You process it, yet miss the change: a magic-based demonstration of a novel form of change blindness
abstract: Previous research on change blindness has demonstrated that perceptual changes can sometimes go undetected despite preserved access to pre-change information. In the present study, we investigated whether change blindness can occur even when pre-change information is consciously and actively processed. Participants (N = 40) observed opaque cups filled with water (pre-change information) while mentally manipulating the liquid as part of an insight problem-solving task. After a memory digit-span task, the cups were turned upside down without any liquid spilling (post-change information). This magic trick relied on superabsorbent powder secretly placed in the cups beforehand. Strikingly, most participants did not spontaneously report surprise, and subsequent reports (e.g., explicitly acknowledging that they had failed to notice the water's disappearance) provided more direct evidence of change blindness for a substantial subset. This occurred despite participants having actively processed the initial state of the cups and encoded both the pre- and post-change information. These findings highlight fundamental limits in adults' ability to monitor the coherence of their environment. We discuss the mechanisms underlying this novel form of change blindness, notably in relation to the phenomenon of event boundaries.

title: Development of the mental timeline and mental number line in preschool children
abstract: Humans routinely use space to represent abstract concepts such as time and number, yet little is known about whether these spatial representations emerge through shared or independent developmental processes. The present study investigated the development of the mental timeline and mental number line in English-speaking preschoolers (N = 71; M age  = 4.37, 38 female). Children completed two card arrangement tasks in which they spatially organized sequences of temporal events and numerical magnitudes, along with an assessment of early literacy skills. Across both domains, children predominantly created linear spatial arrangements, demonstrating an emerging tendency to organize abstract concepts sequentially in space. Children produced left-to-right arrangements more frequently for temporal sequences than for numerical magnitudes, suggesting that the mental timeline may become systematically organized earlier than the mental number line. However, individual differences in directional preferences were related across domains: children who more consistently represented temporal order from left to right were also more likely to represent numerical magnitudes from left to right. In addition, older children showed a greater tendency to produce left-to-right arrangements, and though early literacy scores also predicted this tendency, the relation was no longer significant after accounting for age. These findings suggest that the mental timeline and mental number line become increasingly aligned with culturally dominant spatial conventions during the preschool years. Our results support the view that experience with culturally determined directional information contributes to the development of spatial representations of abstract concepts.

title: Does the mirror have magic? The moderating role of self-awareness intensity on sharing behavior in 3- to 6-year-old children
abstract: This study examined whether theintensityof self-awareness induction moderates sharing behavior in 3- to 6-year-old children. Two experiments employed distinct sharing paradigms. Experiment 1 used a dictator-game sticker-sharing task. Experiment 2 used a balloon-sharing task. Both adopted a between-subjects design that crossed three self-awareness conditions with two age groups. The three conditions were: anenhanced mirror-selfcondition (mirror plus self-relevant cues), amirror-selfcondition (mirror only), and a control condition (no mirror). The two age groups were 3-4 years and 5-6 years. The results showed that, in both tasks, children in theenhanced mirror-selfcondition shared significantly more than those in the control condition. In the balloon task, they also shared significantly more than those in themirror-selfcondition, whereas themirror-selfand control conditions did not differ. Meanwhile, children aged 5-6 years shared significantly more than those aged 3-4 years across both tasks. Among the 3- to 6-year-old preschoolers studied here, these findings indicate that the reliability of the mirror-self effect may depend on thestrengthof self-awareness induction. Higher-intensity self-awareness induction appears to more reliably promote prosocial behavior in preschoolers. The results support the continuity hypothesis of objective self-awareness theory, help resolve prior inconsistencies regarding the stability of mirror effects, and offer empirically grounded implications for fostering prosocial development.

title: Inferring basic and complex emotions across the lifespan: The influence of face masks and autistic traits
abstract: Since Covid-19, wearing face masks has been more commonplace. Mixed findings exist regarding the impact of face masks on emotion recognition. This study investigated the recognition of basic and complex emotions from dynamic facial expressions portrayed with and without a face mask across the life-span whilst also examining the influence of autistic traits. 376 participants (112 children, aged 6-11, 74 males, 38 females; 101 adolescents, aged 12-15, 62 males, 34 females; 163 adults, aged 16-87, 44 males, 119 females) completed an online facial expression recognition task with newly created and validated stimuli of five basic and five complex emotions. Findings revealed that participants had lower recognition accuracy for masked compared to unmasked faces overall, [Formula: see text]  = .18. Children and adolescents with a higher number of autistic traits were generally less accurate in both conditions, r = -.22 and -.30 respectively. Moreover, higher levels of autistic traits were linked to lower accuracy for masked faces in children, [Formula: see text]  = .07, but not in adolescents, [Formula: see text]  = .02, or adults, [Formula: see text]  < .001. These findings highlight the challenges face masks pose to emotion recognition, particularly for children with higher levels of autistic traits.

title: [Suicide crises in adolescents]
abstract: Suicide and suicide attempts amongst young people are a major public health issue. The Covid crisis has starkly highlighted the rise in self-harm as a means of emotional regulation and the inadequacy of resources in child and adolescent psychiatry. Care must include an assessment and management of both the individual and the adolescent's environment.

title: Clinico-demographic Profile and Associated Factors of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autism Spectrum Disorder is a neurodevelopmental disorder with symptoms manifesting in early childhood.

OBJECTIVE: To determine the clinical and sociodemographic profile of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and identify associated factors.

METHOD: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among children diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Children were recruited consecutively at the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Unit, Kanti Children's Hospital, Nepal. The study duration was from 1st August 2023 to 31st January 2024. The study was approved by Institutional Review Board of Kanti Children's Hospital. A semi-structured proforma and Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition were used to assess the children. Data were entered and analysed using IBM SPSS version 16.0.

RESULT: The sample included 145 children. Mean age of diagnosis was 44.1 months (SD ± 18.7). Majority of them were 119 (82.1%) male, 85 (58.6%) belonged to nuclear family, and 69 (47.5%) were single child. Male to female ratio was 4.5:1. The mean paternal and maternal ages at the time of conception were 32.1 years (SD ± 6.5) and 27.7 years (SD ± 5.2), respectively. Most common source of referral was doctors/ health workers 66 (45.5%), parents themselves 45 (31%) and relatives 15 (10.3%). The main reason for visit was speech delay 135 (93.1%) and poor socio emotional reciprocity 76 (52.4%). Mean childhood autism rating score was 34.9 (SD ± 4.3), with 108 (74.4%) having mild-to-moderate autism severity. Sibling status was significantly associated with autism severity (p= 0.042) as children without siblings were more likely to exhibit mild to moderate symptoms compared to those with one or more siblings.

CONCLUSION: The study shows higher rate of Autism Spectrum Disorder among males and diagnosis at an early age. Presence of a sibling may affect autism severity.

title: Cross-sectional analysis of the association between exclusive breastfeeding duration and Autism Spectrum Disorder odds in U.S. preschool children: a nationally representative study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The association between breastfeeding and Autism Spectrum Disorder remains unclear, with existing evidence showing inconsistency. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between breastfeeding patterns and ASD in a national sample of preschool children.

METHODS: Data from the 2018-2023 National Survey of Children's Health (N = 48,158) were analyzed. Breastfeeding was categorized into four mutually exclusive groups based on official NSCH methodology: never breastfed, breastfed < 6 months, breastfed ≥ 6 months non-exclusively, and exclusively breastfed for 6 months. Multivariable weighted logistic regression models examined the association between breastfeeding patterns and ASD, adjusting for confounders. Dose-response was evaluated by modeling breastfeeding category as an ordinal variable (0-3) in fully adjusted models, with polynomial contrasts assessing linearity of trends. Subgroup analyses stratified by age, sex, race/ethnicity, parental education, household size, poverty level, low birth weight, and preterm status tested effect heterogeneity via likelihood ratio tests. Robustness to unmeasured confounding was quantified using E-values for the primary exposure-outcome association.

RESULTS: The weighted prevalence of ASD was 3.0%. Compared to never breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months was associated with significantly lower ASD odds in fully adjusted models (OR = 0.61, 95% CI:0.44-0.86). A significant linear trend was observed, with ASD odds decreasing by 16% for each increase in breastfeeding category (OR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.76-0.93). Polynomial contrasts further indicated the steepest reduction in odds occurred at the transition to exclusive breastfeeding. Subgroup analyses revealed significant effect modification (P for interaction < 0.05) and stronger inverse associations with lower ASD odds among 3-year-olds, non-Hispanic White children, children of college-educated parents, and those from single-child households.

CONCLUSION: Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months was associated with lower odds of ASD in U.S. preschool children, with a graded inverse association across increasing breastfeeding exposure categories. This association was modified by sociodemographic and biological factors, underscoring the importance of contextualizing feeding practices within broader family and social environments in neurodevelopmental research.

CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: [Native language rejection and foreign language dominance in autism: empirical evidence and clinical and educational policy recommendations]
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may be associated with a wide range of atypical language patterns. Over the past two decades, an increasing number of scientific publications have documented a phenomenon in which autistic children acquire a foreign language - most commonly English - instead of their native language as their primary means of communication, often exclusively through exposure to media content (YouTube videos, cartoons, computer games). The literature refers to this phenomenon as "unexpected bilingualism", "paradoxical language dominance", or "non-interactive language acquisition". The present review article summarizes the available empirical and case-based evidence, analyzes possible explanations for the phenomenon, and discusses its clinical and educational implications. We argue that autistic children's preference for a foreign language is not an independent pathological symptom, but rather a possible consequence of the cognitive and autonomic nervous system profile characteristic of autism; a phenomenon that educational systems should recognize and actively support rather than attempt to suppress. Keywords: autism; autism spectrum disorder; non-interactive language acquisition; unexpected bilingualism; paradoxical language dominance; native language rejection; interpersonal distance; homeschooling; online education; educational policy.

title: ["Stagnation-dryness" theory and syndrome differentiation-based treatment of tic disorder comorbid with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children]
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder(ADHD) is one of the most common comorbidities of tic disorder(TD) in children. Clinically, children with TD often present with inattention, hyperactivity, and emotional irritability. TCM has unique advantages in treating the co-occurrence of these two conditions. This article provides an in-depth theoretical and clinical exploration of the challenging issue of TD comorbid with ADHD in children and innovatively proposes "stagnation-dryness engendering wind, and dysfunction of the pivotal mechanism" as the core pathogenesis, systematically constructing an explanatory framework that integrates TCM theory with modern scientific mechanisms. According to this framework, factors such as emotional disruption and external pathogens first lead to Qi stagnation. This "stagnation" corresponds to abnormalities in neural circuit regulation in modern neuroscience. Qi stagnation then disrupts fluid distribution, generating internal dryness. Prolonged stagnation transforming into fire further scorches fluids into dryness. This "dryness" corresponds to immune-metabolic abnormalities in modern medicine. Ultimately, extreme dryness generates internal wind, which disturbs the clear orifices above and traverses the meridians and collaterals. This "wind" corresponds to neuroelectrophysiological abnormalities. The primary disease location involves the liver and gallbladder, often triggered by the Taiyang and Taiyin systems, and chronic progression may extend to the heart and kidney in the Shaoyin system. Targeting this pathogenesis, the fundamental treatment principle is "dispersing stagnation, promoting fluid movement, regulating the pivotal mechanism, and extinguishing wind". Clinically, formulations containing Bupleuri Radix, such as Xiaochaihu Decoction, Sini Powder, Dachaihu Decoction, and Chaihu Jia Longgu Muli Decoction, are recommended for staged pivotal regulation treatment. Detailed differentiation and modification strategies are provided for five major syndrome patterns, i.e., externally-contracted wind pathogen, liver hyperactivity with wind stirring, phlegm-heat stirring wind, spleen deficiency with liver hyperactivity, and upper heat with lower cold, offering a comprehensive and precise pattern-based treatment plan. By deeply integrating the "stagnation-dryness(fire)-wind" pathogenesis chain with modern multi-omics evidence, this study provides a solid theoretical foundation and an effective clinical pathway for the TCM diagnosis and treatment of TD comorbid with ADHD in children.

title: Antipsychotic Use in Children and Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder
journal: Child Adolesc Psychiatr Clin N Am
abstract: Antipsychotic medications may be effective for the management of irritability, aggression, and other mental health disorders in youth with autism spectrum disorder and other neurodevelopmental disorders including intellectual disability. While these medications may significantly improve safety outcomes and quality of life, autistic youth may be at greater risk of overprescribing, side effects, and insufficient monitoring. Best practice includes clarifying target symptoms/behaviors, using lowest effective doses, ensuring first-line behavioral and environmental interventions, collaboratively working with parents/guardians and other care team members, utilizing creative strategies to follow gold-standard monitoring guidelines, and deprescribing when able.

title: Clozapine in Children and Adolescents: Indications, Efficacy, and Safety
journal: Child Adolesc Psychiatr Clin N Am
abstract: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic but it remains underutilized. This review synthesizes evidence for clozapine use in children and adolescents, including additional indications such as suicidality, aggression, autism, and catatonia. Children have differences in pharmacokinetics, dosing, and side effect profiles. Although side effects can include agranulocytosis, myocarditis, and metabolic effects, regular laboratory and vital sign monitoring and adjunctive treatments can mitigate these risks. Persistent barriers often delay initiation, but increased education and systems-level changes can reduce barriers to clozapine use. Recent regulatory changes and emerging evidence support earlier and more widespread use of clozapine in appropriately selected pediatric populations.

title: Examining the Effectiveness of a Dual Executive Function Training Package: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Abstract Background Executive function (EF) refers to the cognitive processes that enable goal-directed regulation of thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Two interrelated domains are commonly distinguished: “cool” EF, which involves abstract cognitive processes, and “hot” EF, which involves regulation in emotionally or motivationally charged contexts. Children with special educational needs (SEN) frequently show difficulties across both domains, yet most interventions target one in isolation. Objective The present study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a dual EF training package for 3 of the most prevalent SEN groups: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), specific learning difficulties (SpLD), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Methods A total of 288 primary school students aged 6 to 12 years with a diagnosis of ADHD, ASD, or SpLD will be recruited. Participants will be randomly assigned to either an intervention or a waitlist control group, stratified by diagnosis. Each intervention group (n=48) will receive the dual EF training program. Participants in the waitlist control group will continue to receive usual educational and clinical support (standard care) during the study period and will be offered the dual EF program upon completion of the study. Preintervention and postintervention assessments will include neuropsychological tests of EF, teacher- and parent-reported behavioral ratings, and measures of disability impact, school satisfaction, and social participation. Changes in outcome measures will be examined using a mixed-design analysis, with diagnosis (ADHD, ASD, and SpLD) and group (experimental vs waitlist control) as between-participant factors and time (pretest vs posttest) as the within-participant factor. Baseline scores will be included as covariates where appropriate. The analysis will assess overall intervention effects and whether changes over time differ by intervention condition and diagnosis, with significant interactions followed by appropriate post hoc comparisons. Results The study was funded by Advance Children Medical and Education Foundation Limited from September 2025 to December 2026 and received ethical approval. Recruitment commenced in early 2026, and 30 participants with ADHD, 30 with ASD, and 45 with SpLD had been enrolled by June 2026. Baseline assessments were completed for all participants. Further data collection and data analysis are scheduled for completion by early 2027, with the results to be submitted for publication thereafter. Conclusions This study will evaluate the effectiveness of a theme-based dual EF program that integrates hot and cool EF within a structured curriculum. Findings will provide evidence of the potential of this approach to support EF and related outcomes in children with SEN and may inform future research and inclusive educational practices.

Introduction Executive functions (EFs) are a set of higher-order cognitive processes that enable children to regulate their thoughts, emotions, and behaviors in pursuit of goals. Core domains include working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility, often referred to as cool EFs because they are typically measured in abstract, decontextualized contexts [ 1 ]. Cool EFs are top-down cognitive processes that are logically based or mechanistic [ 2 ] and operate in affectively neutral contexts [ 3 ]. In contrast, hot EF refers to regulation in affectively or motivationally charged situations, encompassing delay discounting, affective/risky decision-making, and interpersonal and social behavior [ 3 ]. Both domains are crucial for children’s learning, adaptation, and participation, but they rely on partially distinct neural systems and show different developmental trajectories [ 4 ]. Importantly, recent models emphasize that hot and cool EF should not be viewed as isolated constructs but rather as interconnected components along a continuum [ 3 , 5 ]. In real-world learning and social contexts, cognitive and affective demands are often intertwined. For example, sustaining working memory while managing frustration or planning actions while negotiating peer dynamics highlights the need for interventions that address both hot and cool domains simultaneously. EF difficulties are particularly salient in the context of special educational needs (SEN). Children with SEN are disproportionately likely to present with impairments in both hot and cool EF, which underpin many of the learning and behavioral challenges they face in schools [ 6 ]. Among these, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and specific learning difficulties (SpLD) are the 3 most prevalent conditions worldwide, and they are consistently associated with executive dysfunction [ 7 , 8 ]. ADHD, ASD, and SpLD are all characterized by combined hot and cool EF deficits. In ADHD, cool EF weaknesses in working memory, inhibition, and sustained attention [ 6 , 9 ] are compounded by hot EF problems such as poor delay of gratification, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation [ 10 ]. ASD presents with cool EF impairments in flexibility, planning, and working memory [ 11 , 12 ]. It also shows hot EF deficits in emotion regulation, reward processing, and theory of mind [ 13 , 14 ]. SpLD is often framed as academic skill deficits. However, it also involves cool EF challenges in working memory, processing speed, and attention [ 15 ], as well as hot EF challenges related to frustration tolerance and motivation [ 8 ]. Despite this dual profile, many existing interventions have focused disproportionately on one side of the EF spectrum, typically emphasizing cool EF while neglecting hot EF. To provide meaningful support for children with SEN, a more comprehensive approach is needed, one that systematically integrates both domains. Existing EF interventions provide partial solutions but leave important gaps. Cognitive training studies, such as Re et al [ 16 ], have demonstrated that children with ADHD symptoms can improve in attention, inhibition, and working memory following structured training. These domains reflect cool EF, and while the program successfully enhanced cognitive performance, the gains were largely confined to laboratory tasks, with modest evidence of generalization to socioemotional or classroom functioning. Hot EF, such as emotional regulation or social reasoning, was not directly addressed. A more ecological approach is seen in the cognitive-functional (Cog-Fun) intervention for ADHD [ 17 ]. Cog-Fun is an occupational therapy program that emphasizes metacognitive strategy use, planning, organization, and self-monitoring in daily life. Parents are also coached to support the application of strategies at home. While Cog-Fun is effective in improving organization, homework performance, and children’s self-directed behavior, its focus remains on cool EF, with only indirect influence on hot EF domains such as emotional regulation and motivation through parent involvement. More recent work has explicitly attempted to integrate hot EF. Shuai et al [ 18 ] developed an EF training package for children with ADHD that included not only core cool EF skills (working memory, inhibition, planning, flexibility, and verbal fluency) but also hot EF components such as emotional regulation. Their results showed improvements in both cognitive control and social understanding, underscoring the value of a dual-domain approach. However, the scope of hot EF was narrow, confined to theory of mind tasks and behavioral ratings of emotional control, and the program was delivered in a clinic-based format, limiting scalability and ecological validity in school contexts. Similarly, Jasni et al [ 19 ] implemented a psychosocial group intervention combining cognitive skills training with social skills and emotional regulation exercises. Although not framed explicitly in hot-cool EF terms, the program recognized the importance of targeting both domains. Children showed improvements in EF performance and social behavior. Yet the hot EF elements were integrated only loosely with cognitive training, and the lack of a systematic framework to connect the 2 domains limited the intervention’s conceptual clarity and generalizability. Research on EF interventions in ASD and SpLD reveals similar limitations. For ASD, interventions often focus on improving planning, flexibility, and organization through structured tasks or cognitive-behavioral strategies, targeting cool EF deficits [ 20 ]. Some studies incorporate social skills training, which overlaps with hot EF, but these are typically run as separate programs [ 21 , 22 ] rather than integrated EF training. This fragmented approach fails to address the interdependence of cognitive and socioemotional regulation, both of which are impaired in ASD [ 13 ]. In SpLD, interventions predominantly target working memory, inhibition, or attention to support reading or mathematics performance. These cool EF-focused programs have demonstrated efficacy in improving task-related outcomes [ 23 ], but they neglect hot EF processes such as self-regulation, frustration tolerance, and motivational control, which are equally important for sustaining learning in students with SpLD [ 8 ]. The absence of a hot EF component leaves a gap in addressing the broader challenges faced by students with SpLD in daily classroom participation [ 24 ]. Together, these findings demonstrate that while ADHD, ASD, and SpLD are all characterized by combined deficits in hot and cool EF, most existing interventions are narrow in scope, either focusing almost exclusively on cool EF or including only partial and unsystematic coverage of hot EF. Furthermore, interventions are often delivered in clinical rather than classroom contexts, which constrains ecological validity and limits opportunities for students to practice EF in authentic academic and social environments. These limitations highlight the need for a comprehensive, classroom-based intervention that systematically integrates both hot and cool EF domains, such as the dual EF training package described in the present study. Existing EF interventions have tended to adopt a fragmented architecture, with cool and hot EF components treated as separate strands rather than as interdependent processes. Cognitive training programs often prioritize laboratory-based tasks of working memory, inhibition, or flexibility, while socioemotional curricula focus on behavioral regulation or social skills, but the 2 are rarely integrated within a coherent structure. This separation is at odds with contemporary models conceptualizing EF as a continuum, in which cognitive and affective regulation are dynamically interlinked [ 3 , 5 ]. In everyday contexts, children must simultaneously hold information in mind, resist distraction, and adapt flexibly while also regulating frustration, negotiating peer relationships, and maintaining motivation. An intervention that addresses only one side of this continuum risks producing narrow, domain-bound effects with limited generalization. Theoretical and empirical precedents suggest that integration is both necessary and feasible. Frameworks such as the expected value of control model [ 25 ] highlight how motivational and affective signals shape the allocation of cognitive control, underscoring the need to cotrain these systems within a unified framework. Similarly, approaches to self-regulated learning [ 26 ] and early childhood curricula such as Tools of the Mind [ 27 , 28 ] demonstrate the benefits of coupling cognitive strategies with emotion regulation and motivational scaffolding within the same area of focus. Yet, most existing efforts remain partial, addressing affect only indirectly or situating cognitive and affective training in parallel modules rather than within a unified sequence. Taken together, prior studies demonstrate that EF is malleable and that both cognitive and socioemotional interventions can yield measurable benefits. However, they also reveal persistent limitations: most interventions either focus narrowly on cool EF or address hot EF only incidentally, and few are implemented in ecologically valid, classroom-based contexts. The current study seeks to evaluate the effectiveness of a dual EF training package designed to address these gaps by explicitly integrating cool and hot EF within a coherent, school-based curriculum. The program adopts a theme-based, paired structure in which each cool EF skill is systematically linked to its hot EF counterpart within the same chapter. To our knowledge, it represents the first intervention to use a systematically matched hot-cool EF design across an entire curriculum. This theoretically grounded and ecologically valid model is expected to yield improvements not only in core EF performance but also in broader functional outcomes most relevant to children with SEN. Methods Participants A priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7; Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf) to determine the required sample size for the planned analysis of the primary outcomes (ie, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and inhibition). The study will use a 2 × 3 × 2 factorial repeated-measures ANOVA, with intervention condition (experimental vs waitlist control) and diagnostic group (ADHD, ASD, and SpLD) as between-participant factors and time (pretest vs posttest) as the within-participant factor. The power analysis was therefore based on the planned factorial repeated-measures analysis rather than on a simple 2-group comparison.
