title: Metaphorical perceptions of caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder regarding the caregiving process
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the metaphorical perceptions of caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) regarding the caregiving process. The study was conducted with 46 participants responsible for the care of children with ASD. Data were collected between March and April 2026 using a metaphor form. The first part of the form included questions regarding sociodemographic characteristics, while the second part included the statement, "Caring for a child with autism spectrum disorder is like … because …" to identify participants' metaphorical perceptions of the caregiving process. Participants produced 46 metaphors, which were analyzed using content analysis and grouped into five themes: love, belonging, and hope; struggle and resilience; patience, acceptance, and adaptation; uncertainty, learning, and discovery; and intensive care and dependency. Regarding emotional valence, 28.3% of the metaphorical expressions were classified as positive, 37.0% as negative, and 34.7% as mixed. The theme of love, belonging, and hope had the highest frequency (28.3%). Descriptive cross-tabulations were also used to present the distribution of metaphor themes according to caregiving support, psychological support, and education about ASD. As no inferential statistical tests were performed, these distributions were interpreted descriptively and were not considered evidence of statistically significant differences, associations, or causal effects. Overall, the findings demonstrate that caregivers' metaphorical perceptions of caring for a child with ASD reflect a multidimensional experience encompassing emotional attachment and hope as well as struggle, adaptation, uncertainty, and dependency.

title: Goal Management Training for Adolescents with ADHD: A Multi-Center Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial
abstract:
Non-pharmacological interventions targeting executive functions (EF), such as Goal Management Training (GMT), may augment treatment as usual (TAU) for adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). We examined whether GMT plus TAU improves EF, ADHD symptoms, and functional impairment more than TAU only. In this preregistered multi-center randomized controlled trial, 116 participants (M age = 14.69 years; 66% female) were randomized to GMT plus TAU or TAU only. GMT comprised seven weekly 2-hour group sessions, supplemented by parent and teacher sessions. TAU was standard outpatient mental health services. Outcomes were assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks. The primary outcome was the parent-reported Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF-2), Global Executive Composite (GEC). Secondary outcomes were teacher-, self-, and parent-reported BRIEF-2 subdomains; parent- and teacher-reported ADHD Rating Scale-IV scores; and parent-reported functional impairment measured with the Weiss Functional Impairment Rating Scale–Parent Report (WFIRS-P). GMT plus TAU showed no additional benefit over TAU only. Intention-to-treat analyses showed no significant between-group difference in GEC (adjusted b = − 2.12, 95% CI [− 7.64, 3.41], p = .449, d = − 0.14), parent-reported ADHD symptoms ( d = − 0.27, p = .323) or other secondary outcomes (all p > .10). Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05874791 ; registered April 14, 2023).

Introduction Clinical guidelines recommend a multimodal approach to the management of adolescent attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), typically combining psychoeducation, pharmacological treatment, and psychosocial interventions (Coghill et al., 2023 ; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE], 2018 ; Wolraich et al., 2019 ). Although pharmacological treatments demonstrate robust effects on core ADHD symptoms, the evidence for corresponding improvements in everyday functioning is less consistent (Cortese et al., 2018 ; Sibley et al., 2025 ). Reliance on medication as a standalone treatment may therefore restrict response domains, as pharmacotherapy alone often fails to yield improvements in executive function (EF) and real-world functioning domains more reliably addressed through non-pharmacological interventions (Sibley et al., 2025 ). Non-pharmacological and pharmacological interventions may thus be considered complementary as medication reduces core symptom burden, particularly in the short term, whereas psychosocial and training-based interventions target the EF difficulties essential to long-term everyday functioning (Sibley et al., 2025 ; Wolraich et al., 2019 ). EF refers to a set of top-down cognitive control processes, including working memory, planning, and self-regulation, that are orchestrated largely by the prefrontal cortex to enable goal-directed behavior (Diamond, 2013 ). EF difficulties are common among youth with ADHD and are associated with poorer academic performance (Dvorsky & Langberg, 2014 ), reduced quality of life (Barkley & Fischer, 2019 ), and elevated rates of comorbid psychopathology (Orm et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2022 ). Adolescence may represent a particularly opportune period for EF-focused interventions, as executive abilities continue to mature while academic, social, and organizational demands intensify (Ekman et al., 2022 ; Selemon, 2013 ). Several evidence-based psychosocial interventions for adolescents with ADHD target EF difficulties by combining direct skill-building with behavioral support (Rios-Davis et al., 2023 ; Sibley et al., 2023 ). This is particularly evident in programs addressing organization, time management, and planning (OTMP), which employ multi-component delivery to target the behavioral manifestations of EF difficulties (Rios-Davis et al., 2023 ; Sibley et al., 2016 ). Organizational Skills Training (OST), for instance, integrates skills sessions for youth with parent and teacher consultations to promote everyday use of these strategies (Bikic et al., 2017 ; Nissley-Tsiopinis et al., 2024 ). Such EF-focused programs yield moderate-to-large gains in organizational behaviors, whereas effects on core inattention and academic achievement are generally modest (Bikic et al., 2017 ; Nissley-Tsiopinis et al., 2024 ). Specialized CBT for adolescents that integrates metacognitive, emotion-regulation, and planning strategies also shows promise for EF-related outcomes in meta-analyses; yet individual trial results remain inconsistent, particularly for core ADHD symptoms (Haugan et al., 2022 ; Qiu et al., 2023 ). Similarly, computerized cognitive training targeting domain-specific difficulties (e.g., working memory) often produces robust near-transfer to trained tasks but limited far-transfer to everyday functioning, academic outcomes, or core ADHD symptoms, particularly in masked evaluations (Veloso et al., 2020 ; Westwood et al., 2023 ). These findings motivate interest in metacognitive approaches such as Goal Management Training (GMT), which includes strategies for monitoring and sustaining goal-directed behavior in real-world contexts (Lenartowicz et al., 2024 ; Stamenova & Levine, 2019 ). GMT, a group-based, manualized intervention grounded in models of goal neglect and supervisory attentional control, is primarily a cognitive rehabilitation intervention using metacognitive strategy training to address executive difficulties through goal management, attentional control, and self-monitoring (Duncan et al., 1996 ; Norman & Shallice, 1986 ; Robertson & Levine, 2013 ). The hypothesized GMT change mechanism is improved metacognitive control of goal-directed behavior by training participants to interrupt automatic responding, reactivate task goals, and monitor ongoing behavior against those goals (Robertson & Levine, 2013 ). The intervention uses the core “stop-and-think” strategy and mindfulness-based attention regulation to support these processes (Kabat-Zinn, 2005 ; Levine & Stamenova, 2018 ). Originally developed to target EF difficulties following acquired brain injury (Robertson, 1996 ), GMT has since been adapted for a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions (Haugen et al., 2021 ; In de Braek et al., 2017 ; Jensen et al., 2021 ; Stubberud et al., 2013 ). GMT has shown promise for improving everyday EF and emotional outcomes in adults with ADHD. One study reported that GMT added to psychoeducation and counseling significantly improved clinician-rated cognitive functioning (In de Braek et al., 2017 ). An exploratory study found enhancements in performance-based inhibitory control, with gains maintained at six-month follow-up, alongside self-reported improvements in productivity and ADHD symptoms (Jensen et al., 2021 ). In a randomized controlled trial (RCT), GMT did not yield additional gains in perceived EF relative to routine care but was associated with a greater reduction in anxiety symptoms (Hanssen et al., 2023 ). Despite these encouraging findings in adult populations, GMT for adolescents remains largely unexplored. A small pilot study ( n = 6) demonstrated good adherence, reductions in functional difficulties, and preliminary improvements in everyday EF (Sadeghi et al., 2024 ), underscoring the need for larger controlled studies in this age group. Current Study Evidence-based psychosocial interventions for adolescents with ADHD often comprise multiple components and can be effective, but their complexity may increase implementation burden in routine clinical settings (Rios-Davis et al., 2023 ; Sibley et al., 2023 ). This raises the question of whether a more focused metacognitive strategy-training approach such as GMT can provide additional functional benefits when added to routine care. The present study evaluates a developmentally adapted, group-based version of GMT as a standardized, EF-focused adjunct to TAU. This model, adapted from the pediatric version of GMT (Brandt et al., 2021 ), employs a youth group format to leverage therapeutic advantages of peer-based intervention for adolescents, including normalization and shared peer learning (Haugan et al., 2022 ). To engage systemic support and facilitate the transfer of learned metacognitive strategies to everyday life, GMT is supplemented by structured, separate guidance sessions for parents and teachers (Haugan et al., 2022 ; Nissley-Tsiopinis et al., 2024 ). This context-sensitive approach, teaching and supporting EF skills within everyday activities and in close collaboration with key adults, is consistent with principles from pediatric neurorehabilitation (Ylvisaker et al., 2005 ). At the same time, the present model retains a focused, standardized EF-oriented format. The objective of this RCT was to evaluate the efficacy of group-based GMT combined with treatment as usual (TAU), compared with TAU only, in improving everyday EF, ADHD-related symptoms and functional impairment in adolescents with ADHD at 12 weeks post-intervention. Everyday EF in ADHD is commonly assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function, Second Edition (BRIEF-2; Gioia et al., 2015 ), a multi-informant rating scale of EF in everyday contexts. The BRIEF-2 Global Executive Composite (GEC) captures overall EF difficulties across key domains, including working memory, planning, and self-monitoring, and is intended to reflect real-world functioning. In the present trial, the primary outcome was parent-reported BRIEF-2 GEC. Secondary outcomes were BRIEF-2 subdomains rated by parents, teachers, and adolescents, as well as parent- and teacher-reported ADHD Rating Scale-IV (ADHD-RS-IV; DuPaul et al., 1998 ) total scores and subscales. Functional impairment in everyday life was assessed as an additional secondary outcome with the Weiss Functional Impairment Rating Scale–Parent Report (WFIRS-P; Weiss et al., 2005 ), which captures impairment across six life domains and complements the symptom-focused BRIEF-2 and ADHD-RS-IV. We hypothesized that both groups would demonstrate improvements from baseline to post-intervention, but that adolescents receiving GMT plus TAU would show significantly greater improvements in parent-rated everyday EF (the primary outcome) than those receiving TAU only. We further expected that GMT plus TAU would lead to greater reductions in ADHD symptoms, as well as improvements across additional informants (self and teacher) and on secondary BRIEF-2 indices and ADHD-RS-IV subscales, and more pronounced improvements in functional impairment as measured by the WFIRS‑P at the 12‑week follow‑up. Methods Study Design and Procedure This preregistered multi-center RCT was conducted across three child and adolescent mental health outpatient clinics in South-Eastern Norway. Recruitment and intervention took place between fall 2023 and summer 2025. A total of 116 adolescents were included and distributed across sites ( n = 43, 39, and 34). The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05874791 ). All three clinics belong to the same public specialist mental health care system in Norway. The trial included one site located in an urban hospital setting and two sites located in small-town/rural hospital settings, reflecting typical outpatient ADHD services within the region. Randomization was stratified by site to guard against potential systematic differences between clinics, patient populations, and clinicians. In all primary analyses, site was included as a categorical covariate. All participants continued to receive TAU in Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services throughout the trial, in line with national and international guidelines for ADHD care (Norwegian Directorate of Health, 2016 ; Wolraich et al., 2019 ). Following baseline assessment (T1), participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either GMT plus TAU or TAU only. Randomization was implemented by an individual independent of the study, using a computerized parallel-group allocation system with block randomization (fixed block size of four) stratified by recruitment site to ensure balanced group assignment. A priori power calculations were conducted based on a two-group longitudinal design, following previous work in pediatric EF interventions (Kurowski et al., 2014 ). These analyses indicated that 60 participants per randomization arm (total N = 120) were required to detect a small-to-moderate standardized effect on the primary outcome ( f = 0.30) with 84% power at a two-sided significance level of α = 0.05. The final sample was N = 116. The study complied with the ethical guidelines for research involving children and the CONSORT 2010 guidelines for reporting randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010 ). The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics (REK), South-Eastern Norway (identifier: 420217). Eligible participants were first approached by their clinician. For adolescents younger than 16 years, clinicians requested permission to contact parents; adolescents aged 16 years or older were contacted directly. Adolescents and parents received verbal and written information about the study. Before baseline assessment, written informed consent was obtained electronically using BankID (a Norwegian national digital identification system) from adolescents aged 16 years or older and from the parents or legal guardians of adolescents younger than 16 years. Adolescents younger than 16 years also provided assent. Participant data are stored securely using the University of Oslo’s Services for Sensitive Data (TSD). All participants received a 30 USD gift card for completing post-measures. Baseline (T1) assessments included self-, parent-, and teacher-reported BRIEF-2 measures (Gioia et al., 2015 ) and parent- and teacher-reported ADHD symptoms using the ADHD Rating Scale–IV (DuPaul et al., 1998 ), as well as parent-reported functional impairment using the WFIRS-P (Weiss et al., 2005 ). Post-intervention (T2) assessments were conducted 12 weeks after the start of the intervention by trained research assistants who were masked to treatment allocation and not involved in delivering the intervention. For the per-protocol sensitivity analysis, major protocol deviations were predefined in the Statistical Analysis Plan (S​AP; Dyresen, 2023 ​).​ ​These included (a) attendance at fewer than five GMT sessions, (b) initiation or discontinuation of ADHD medication during the intervention period, and (c) T2 assessments conducted outside the predefined 3-month assessment window. Adverse events were monitored throughout the trial; none were reported in either group.
